Concept = an idea to understand. Hardware / Chip / Firmware = physical security components and the low-level code inside them. Standard / Specification / RFC / Protocol / Algorithm / Format / Extension = official rules, message exchanges, maths and data layouts. Key / Certificate = specific cryptographic keys and certificates. Product / Service / Software / Tool / Command / Library = things you buy, run or program with. Attack / Incident = known weaknesses and real-world failures. Role / Organisation / Regulation / Certification / Career / Resource = people, bodies, laws, credentials and learning material.

docs.title: Status labels
docs.text:
Current, Legacy, Deprecated, Emerging

Current = widely used and recommended today. Legacy = still found and worth knowing, but being replaced. Deprecated = being removed or no longer trusted; plan to migrate away. Emerging = new, announced or just being adopted.

docs.title: Domain labels
docs.text:
Silicon, Firmware & Boot, Platform & OS, Trusted Execution, Cloud, Web PKI, Private PKI, Devices & IoT, Mobile, General

Where the entry mainly lives: inside the chip (Silicon), in the boot chain (Firmware & boot), the operating system (Platform & OS), protected enclaves and confidential VMs (Trusted execution), cloud services, the public certificate system used by browsers (Web PKI), organisations' own certificate authorities (Private PKI), connected devices, phones, or across all of them (General).

docs.title: About this guide
docs.text: This guide is for students and self-learners. Specification versions, product names, CA/Browser Forum rules, root-program policies and dates were checked for accuracy as of late 2026, but this field changes quickly — certificate lifetimes are shrinking on a published schedule, root certificates expire and get distrusted, and post-quantum standards are still rolling out. Always confirm details with the Trusted Computing Group, NIST, the IETF, the CA/Browser Forum and the browser root programs. Product names and trademarks belong to their owners. Everything here is described for defensive use: protecting, verifying and recovering your own systems.

docs.title: Chapter 6: PKI & X.509 Certificates, In Depth
docs.text: This chapter opens up the certificate itself and the machinery around it: who issues and checks certificates, every X.509 field and extension, file formats, signature algorithms including post-quantum ML-DSA, how clients build and validate chains, revocation, Certificate Transparency, TLS, trust stores and the tools professionals use daily. Root CAs and their governance come next in Chapter 60, and running your own CA in Chapter 70.

docs.title: 6.1 What PKI Is: Binding Names to Keys
docs.text:
Public key infrastructure (PKI) is the whole system — people, rules, software and hardware — that lets strangers trust that a public key really belongs to a named website, person or device. A certificate authority (CA) checks who you are, then signs a small digital document called a certificate that links your name to your public key. Anyone who trusts that CA can check its signature and so trust the link.

The certificate lifecycle in seven steps. Most real-world failures happen in the last box: missed renewals and slow revocation.

Think of it like…

PKI works like passports: a government checks your identity once and issues a hard-to-forge document, and border officers around the world accept it because they trust the issuing government's stamp — not because they know you personally.

Real-world example

Lumen Bikes launches shop.lumenbikes.example. Its web server generates a key pair and sends the public key to a CA in a signing request. The CA confirms Lumen controls the domain and signs a certificate saying 'this key belongs to shop.lumenbikes.example for the next 200 days'. When Ada opens the shop, her browser checks that signature chain back to a root in its trust store and only then shows the page without a warning.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The subscriber generates a key pair and keeps the private key secret (ideally in an HSM, TPM or locked-down file).
  2. It sends a certificate signing request (CSR) containing the public key and the names it wants certified.
  3. The CA, or its registration authority, validates domain control or identity according to its published policy.
  4. The CA signs the certificate; for public TLS it is also logged in Certificate Transparency logs.
  5. Relying parties validate the chain to a trust anchor and check dates, names, permitted uses and revocation.
  6. Before expiry the certificate is renewed (ideally automatically); if the key is compromised it is revoked.

Who uses it

Web developers, system administrators, security engineers, PKI engineers, identity and IoT teams — anyone who deploys HTTPS, VPNs, Wi-Fi 802.1X, signed email, signed software or device identity.

Key takeaway

Memorise the definition: a certificate is a CA-signed binding of a public key to an identity, valid for a stated period and for stated purposes — every other PKI concept refines one part of that sentence.

Going deeper

  • The public 'Web PKI' is governed by browser and OS root programs plus the CA/Browser Forum Baseline Requirements; a private PKI follows only its owner's rules. The cryptography is identical — what differs is who decides which roots are trusted.
  • PKI gives authentication and integrity through signatures. In TLS 1.3 the certificate key only signs the handshake; the session keys come from ephemeral (EC)DHE or hybrid ML-KEM key exchange, so the certificate is not what encrypts traffic.
  • Core standards: ITU-T X.509 defines the certificate, IETF RFC 5280 profiles it for the internet, RFC 6960 defines OCSP, RFC 6962 Certificate Transparency, RFC 8555 ACME and RFC 3647 the CP/CPS framework.
  • Public TLS lifetimes are shrinking under CA/B Forum ballot SC-081: a 200-day maximum from 15 March 2026, 100 days from March 2027 and 47 days from March 2029 — Chapter 60 covers the ballot, Chapter 70 the automation it forces.
  • Alternatives to hierarchical PKI each trade convenience for accountability: OpenPGP's web of trust, SSH trust-on-first-use, DNSSEC-based DANE and TLS raw public keys (RFC 7250).
  • Non-repudiation is partly legal: a signature only proves much if the key was well protected, policies were followed and audit evidence exists — which is why qualified signatures require certified signing devices.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Believing the certificate encrypts your traffic — it authenticates the server; TLS negotiates separate session keys.
  • Reading the padlock as 'this site is honest' — a DV certificate proves only domain control, and phishing sites get them too.
  • Thinking a certificate contains the private key — it holds only the public key; the private key stays with the subscriber (a .p12 bundle is a different thing).

docs.title: Try it: See the identity, issuer and validity a real website presents
docs.text:
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -dates -ext subjectAltName

docs.text: Name What it does Example PKIX and LAMPS working groupsIETF · Organisation · General IETF PKIX (closed 2013) wrote the internet X.509 profile; its successor LAMPS maintains PKIX and S/MIME, including the post-quantum certificate RFCs. RFC 5280 came from PKIX, while RFC 9881 for ML-DSA certificates and the composite-signature drafts came from LAMPS. Public-key certificateITU-T X.509 / RFC 5280 · Certificate · General A CA-signed data structure binding a public key to a subject name for a validity period and a set of permitted uses. The certificate for shop.lumenbikes.example says this ECDSA P-256 key belongs to that hostname from 1 April to 18 October 2026, for server authentication only. Proof of possessionRFC 2986 / RFC 4211 · Concept · General Evidence that a requester actually holds the private key for the public key being certified, usually by signing the CSR with it. The CA checks the CSR's self-signature before issuing, so nobody can get a certificate for Ravi's public key without his private key. Certificate profileCA CP/CPS; CA/B Forum BRs §7 · Concept · General A template fixing which fields, extensions, key types and lifetimes a class of certificates must have; CAs publish profiles in their CPS. Northwind's TLS profile fixes ECDSA P-256 keys, the serverAuth EKU, the DV policy OID and a 199-day maximum, and a linter checks each certificate. Level of assuranceCA/B validation types; eIDAS low/substantial/high · Concept · General How much confidence a certificate's identity checks provide, such as DV versus OV versus EV, or eIDAS levels low, substantial and high. Harbourview accepts DV certificates for marketing sites but requires OV for customer portals and qualified certificates for signing contracts. ITU-T X.509ITU-T (also ISO/IEC 9594-8) · Standard · Current · General The international standard defining certificate and CRL formats; first published in 1988, with the extensible version 3 format arriving in the 1990s. When a textbook says 'X.509 certificate' it means this structure, whether it secures HTTPS, smart cards, VPNs or electric-car chargers. RFC 5280IETF PKIX working group (2008) · RFC · Current · General The IETF profile of X.509 for the internet: which fields and extensions to use, how to encode them, and the path validation algorithm. Developers writing certificate parsers in Go, Rust or Java follow RFC 5280 section 4 for fields and section 6 for chain validation. Certificate lifecyclePKI operations practice · Concept · General The stages every certificate passes through: key generation, request, validation, issuance, logging, deployment, monitoring, renewal, and revocation or expiry. Priya's team tracks 1,200 certificates; most outages happen at renewal, so they automate it with ACME and alert 30 days before expiry. Web of trust (OpenPGP)OpenPGP community (RFC 9580) · Concept · Legacy · General A decentralised model where users sign each other's keys and decide personally whom to trust, instead of relying on central CAs. Open-source developers have long held key-signing parties at conferences to cross-sign OpenPGP keys before trusting each other's signed releases. Trust on first use (TOFU)SSH and similar protocols · Concept · General Accepting a key the first time you see it and warning if it later changes; simple, but blind to an attack on that first connection. SSH saves a server's host key in known_hosts at first login and shows a loud warning if the key is different next time. Raw public keys (RFC 7250)IETF TLS working group (2014) · RFC · Current · Devices & IoT A TLS option to authenticate with a bare public key instead of a certificate, for closed systems that distribute keys some other way. A small IoT gateway pre-loaded with its sensors' public keys uses RFC 7250 to skip certificate parsing on constrained devices.

docs.title: 6.2 The Cast: CA, RA, VA, Subscriber, Relying Party and Trust Anchor
docs.text:
A PKI has a small cast of roles with precise names. The certificate authority (CA) signs certificates; the registration authority (RA) checks who is asking; the validation authority (VA) tells others whether a certificate is still good; the subscriber owns the certificate; the relying party is whoever checks it; and the trust anchor is the key everyone has agreed to trust at the top.

Who talks to whom in a PKI. The relying party never contacts the RA; it trusts the CA's signature and checks status with the VA.

Think of it like…

Think of a driving licence: the licensing office's front desk checks your documents (RA), the back office prints and signs the licence (CA), you carry it (subscriber), a police officer checks it (relying party), the officer's radio check for suspensions is the VA, and the officer's trust in the national licensing agency is the trust anchor.

Real-world example

Greenleaf University's help desk acts as the RA: staff show an ID card before an S/MIME certificate is approved. The university's issuing CA, whose key sits in an HSM, signs the certificate. Professor Okafor is the subscriber and agrees to protect her key. When a student's mail client opens her signed email, it is the relying party: it builds a chain to the university root it has been told to trust and asks the VA's OCSP service whether the certificate is revoked.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. An applicant (person or organisation) requests a certificate and supplies evidence.
  2. The RA function verifies identity or control; a public CA must perform domain validation itself.
  3. The CA signs the certificate and publishes its policies, CA certificates and revocation data in a repository.
  4. Once issued, the applicant becomes the subscriber, bound by the CA's subscriber agreement.
  5. A relying party validates the chain up to a trust anchor in its trust store and queries status from the VA (CRL or OCSP).

Who uses it

PKI engineers and architects, CA compliance staff, identity and access management teams, auditors, and developers integrating certificate validation into applications.

Key takeaway

In interviews, separate 'subject' (who the certificate names) from 'subscriber' (who is contractually responsible) — for a server certificate they differ.

Going deeper

  • The CA/Browser Forum Baseline Requirements (section 1.3.2) let a public CA delegate parts of identity validation to a Delegated Third Party, but never domain or IP address validation — the CA's own systems must do that.
  • RFC 5280 calls every non-CA certificate holder an 'end entity'; a CRL issuer may be a separate entity from the CA, signalled through the CRL Distribution Points cRLIssuer field and an indirect CRL.
  • A delegated OCSP responder certificate carries the id-kp-OCSPSigning EKU (1.3.6.1.5.5.7.3.9) and usually the id-pkix-ocsp-nocheck extension, so clients do not try to check the responder's own revocation status.
  • RFC 5914 defines a TrustAnchorInfo format (public key, name, optional constraints), showing that a trust anchor is fundamentally a key, not necessarily a self-signed certificate — though most stores hold self-signed roots.
  • In CA/B Forum vocabulary, browser and OS vendors are 'Certificate Consumers' and CAs are 'Certificate Issuers'; both vote on ballots, and root programs turn the results into enforceable policy (Chapter 60).
  • Separation of duties matters: in well-run CAs, the people who approve requests (RA officers) cannot also operate the CA signing system, and every action is logged for the annual audit.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Calling the browser 'the CA' — the browser is the relying party; it only decides which CAs to trust.
  • Assuming the RA signs anything — the RA approves; only the CA's private key signs certificates and CRLs.
  • Treating 'trust anchor' and 'root CA' as identical in every system — some products can anchor trust at an intermediate or a bare public key.

docs.title: Try it: Find the CA and validation-authority endpoints named inside a certificate
docs.text:
openssl x509 -in cert.pem -noout -issuer -subject \
  -ext authorityInfoAccess,crlDistributionPoints,certificatePolicies

docs.title: Key chips, standards, protocols, products & terms
docs.text: Name What it does Example Issuing CARFC 5280 / CA hierarchy practice · Role · General The CA whose key actually signs end-entity certificates; usually an online intermediate in an HSM, while the root stays offline (Chapter 60). Northwind's issuing CA receives Lumen Bikes' CSR, confirms the validation evidence and signs the certificate with its HSM-held key. Registration Authority (RA)RFC 5280 / RFC 3647 · Role · General The function that verifies applicants' identity or control before the CA signs; it may be part of the CA or a separate trusted party. A university's IT help desk acts as RA, checking staff ID cards before approving S/MIME certificate requests that the CA then signs. Delegated Third PartyCA/B Forum Baseline Requirements §1.3.2 · Role · Web PKI An outside party a public CA uses for some validation tasks; the BRs forbid delegating domain and IP address validation itself. A CA uses a local partner to verify company registration documents for OV certificates, but its own systems perform the DNS challenge. Validation Authority (VA)PKI architecture term · Role · General A service that answers 'is this certificate still valid?', usually by publishing CRLs or running an OCSP responder for one or more CAs. A government PKI runs a central VA so ministries' applications query one OCSP service instead of each issuing CA separately. Delegated OCSP responderRFC 6960 · Role · General A responder holding its own CA-issued certificate with the id-kp-OCSPSigning EKU, allowed to sign status answers on the CA's behalf. Northwind's issuing CA signs a short-lived responder certificate so its busy OCSP servers never need access to the CA key itself. SubscriberCA/B Forum BRs definitions · Role · General The person or organisation to whom a certificate is issued and who agrees to the CA's terms, including protecting the private key. Lumen Bikes Ltd is the subscriber; if its key leaks, it must ask the CA to revoke the certificate within its agreement's timelines. ApplicantCA/B Forum BRs definitions · Role · Web PKI The person or organisation requesting a certificate; it becomes the subscriber once the certificate is issued. Before validation completes, Lumen Bikes is just an applicant whose ACME account has placed an order. Subject vs subscriberRFC 5280 §4.1.2.6; CA/B Forum BRs · Concept · General The subject is the entity a certificate describes — a hostname, person, device or CA — named in the Subject field and the SAN extension. For a server certificate the subject is shop.lumenbikes.example, while the subscriber is the company that runs it. End entity (leaf)RFC 5280 · Role · General Any certificate holder that is not a CA — servers, users, devices; their certificates are called leaf or end-entity certificates. A smart thermostat's device certificate is an end-entity certificate: Basic Constraints says cA=FALSE, so it can never issue certificates. Relying party agreementCA repository documents; RFC 3647 · Concept · General CA terms for those who rely on its certificates, limiting liability and stating checks they must perform, such as revocation status. Harbourview's lawyers learn a CA's warranty applies only if the bank checked revocation status before relying on a partner's certificate. Trust anchor format (RFC 5914)IETF RFC 5914 / RFC 5937 · Format · Current · General A TrustAnchorInfo structure holding a trusted public key, name and optional constraints, showing an anchor need not be a self-signed certificate. A constrained device stores only its manufacturer's root public key and name as its trust anchor, rather than a whole certificate. Certificate ConsumerCA/Browser Forum bylaws · Role · Web PKI CA/Browser Forum term for software makers that ship trust stores and enforce rules, such as Apple, Google, Microsoft and Mozilla. When Certificate Consumers vote for a ballot such as SC-081, their root programs then require CAs to follow it. RepositoryRFC 3647 / CA/B Forum BRs §2 · Concept · General The public place where a CA publishes its CP/CPS, CA certificates, CRLs and terms, so relying parties can check them. Following a certificate's CRL Distribution Point leads to the CA's repository, which also hosts its latest CPS document.

docs.title: 6.3 X.509 v3 Anatomy, Field by Field
docs.text:
Every X.509 certificate has the same three-part shape: a 'to-be-signed' body full of fields, the name of the signature algorithm, and the CA's signature. The body says which version it is, its serial number, who issued it, when it is valid, who it is for, the public key, and a list of extensions. Learning to read these fields is the most useful single PKI skill.

Inside an X.509 v3 certificate. Everything except the last layer is inside tbsCertificate and covered by the CA's signature.

Think of it like…

A certificate is like a notarised form: the boxes on the form (name, dates, reference number) are the body, and the notary's stamp at the bottom covers every box — change any box and the stamp no longer matches.

Real-world example

Ravi runs openssl x509 -text on his shop's certificate. He sees Version 3, a long random serial number, Issuer 'C=US, O=Northwind Trust, CN=Northwind TLS Issuing CA 1', Not Before and Not After dates 200 days apart, a Subject of CN=shop.lumenbikes.example, an EC P-256 public key, about ten extensions, and finally an ecdsa-with-SHA384 signature from the intermediate's P-384 key. Every field he will ever troubleshoot is on that one screen.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The CA assembles TBSCertificate: version, serialNumber, signature algorithm, issuer, validity, subject, subjectPublicKeyInfo and extensions.
  2. It DER-encodes TBSCertificate, hashes those exact bytes and signs the hash with its private key.
  3. It wraps the result as Certificate ::= SEQUENCE { tbsCertificate, signatureAlgorithm, signatureValue }.
  4. A verifier re-hashes the received TBSCertificate bytes and checks the signature with the issuer's public key.
  5. Only if the signature verifies does the verifier trust any field inside — dates, names, key and extensions.

Who uses it

Anyone troubleshooting TLS, VPN or code-signing errors; PKI engineers designing certificate profiles; developers parsing certificates; security analysts investigating suspicious certificates.

Key takeaway

Remember the order: version, serial, signature, issuer, validity, subject, SPKI, extensions — then signatureAlgorithm and signatureValue outside the signed part.

Going deeper

  • RFC 5280 caps serial numbers at 20 octets and requires them to be positive; the Baseline Requirements demand at least 64 bits of CSPRNG output, defeating chosen-prefix collision attacks like the 2008 MD5 rogue CA.
  • Validity dates use UTCTime (two-digit year) through 2049 and GeneralizedTime from 2050; notAfter 99991231235959Z means 'no well-defined expiry', used for some device certificates.
  • The inner 'signature' field and the outer 'signatureAlgorithm' must be identical; the duplication prevents an attacker swapping the algorithm identifier outside the signed bytes.
  • Distinguished names are sequences of RDNs whose attributes are OIDs: CN 2.5.4.3, O 2.5.4.10, OU 2.5.4.11, C 2.5.4.6. Since September 2022 the Baseline Requirements no longer allow OU in public TLS subscriber certificates (ballot SC47).
  • Hostnames live in the SAN extension; browsers stopped falling back to the Common Name years ago (Chrome 58 in 2017), and RFC 9525 (2023) formally removed CN-ID matching.
  • A typical ECDSA TLS leaf is about 1-1.5 KB in DER; most of that is names, extensions, embedded SCTs and the signature — the 65-byte P-256 public key is a small part.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Looking for the fingerprint inside the certificate — tools compute it as a hash over the whole DER; it is not a field.
  • Assuming 'Version: 3 (0x2)' is a typo — versions count from zero, so v3 is encoded as 2.
  • Matching hostnames against the Subject CN — only SAN entries count for modern clients.

docs.title: Try it: Read every field, then just the serial and fingerprint
docs.text:
openssl x509 -in cert.pem -noout -text
openssl x509 -in cert.pem -noout -serial -fingerprint -sha256
# Windows:
certutil -dump cert.cer

docs.title: Key chips, standards, protocols, products & terms
docs.text: Name What it does Example tbsCertificateRFC 5280 §4.1 · Format · General The 'to-be-signed' body holding every field and extension; the CA signs exactly these DER-encoded bytes. Changing a single byte in tbsCertificate, say the expiry year, makes the CA's signature fail verification instantly. versionRFC 5280 §4.1.2.1 · Format · General Indicates the X.509 version; virtually every certificate is v3, encoded as integer 2 because counting starts at zero. openssl x509 -text prints 'Version: 3 (0x2)' — the hex shows the raw encoded value. serialNumberRFC 5280 §4.1.2.2 / BRs §7.1 · Format · General A positive integer of up to 20 bytes, unique per issuing CA; public TLS CAs must include at least 64 random bits. CRLs and OCSP identify revoked certificates by issuer plus serial, such as 04:a1:9f:...:3c, never by domain name. signature (algorithm identifier)RFC 5280 §4.1.1.2 / §4.1.2.3 · Format · General The algorithm the CA used, such as ecdsa-with-SHA256; repeated outside tbsCertificate as signatureAlgorithm, and both copies must match. A certificate showing sha256WithRSAEncryption (1.2.840.113549.1.1.11) was signed by an RSA CA key over a SHA-256 hash. issuerRFC 5280 §4.1.2.4 · Format · General The distinguished name of the CA that signed this certificate; it must match the subject field of the issuer's own certificate. Issuer 'C=US, O=Let's Encrypt, CN=R11' tells clients to look for a CA certificate with exactly that subject name. validity (notBefore / notAfter)RFC 5280 §4.1.2.5 · Format · General The window in which the certificate may be accepted; UTCTime encoding through 2049, GeneralizedTime from 2050 onward. A public TLS certificate issued in April 2026 may be valid for at most 200 days under the current Baseline Requirements. subjectRFC 5280 §4.1.2.6 · Format · General The distinguished name of the certificate holder; in public TLS it may be nearly empty because the names belong in the SAN. A DV certificate's subject often holds only CN=shop.lumenbikes.example, with no organisation, city or country attributes. subjectPublicKeyInfo (SPKI)RFC 5280 §4.1.2.7 · Format · General The subject's public key plus its algorithm identifier, such as id-ecPublicKey with curve P-256; pins and key identifiers are hashes of it. Two certificates renewed with the same key share an identical SPKI, so an app pinning the SPKI hash survives the renewal. extensionsRFC 5280 §4.1.2.9 / §4.2 · Format · General The v3 list of extra fields, each with an OID, a criticality flag and a DER value; detailed in the next section. A typical leaf has about ten: SAN, Key Usage, EKU, Basic Constraints, AKI, SKI, AIA, CRL DP, Certificate Policies and SCTs. signatureValueRFC 5280 §4.1.1.3 · Format · General The CA's signature over the DER-encoded tbsCertificate, stored as a BIT STRING after the signatureAlgorithm field. For an ECDSA P-256 CA it is about 70-72 bytes; for an ML-DSA-65 CA it would be 3,309 bytes. Distinguished Name (DN)ITU-T X.501 / RFC 5280 · Concept · General An ordered list of attribute-value pairs (RDNs) such as C, O, OU and CN, each identified by an OID, forming a hierarchical name. CN=Aoife Byrne, O=Harbourview Bank, C=IE names a person; CN is OID 2.5.4.3 and O is 2.5.4.10. Common Name (CN)X.520 attribute 2.5.4.3 · Concept · Legacy · General A DN attribute once used for hostnames; browsers now match only SANs, and the BRs require any CN to repeat a SAN value. Chrome 58 (2017) stopped falling back to CN, so internal certificates without a SAN suddenly failed in the browser. Fingerprint (thumbprint)Computed by tools, not stored · Concept · General A hash of the entire DER certificate, computed by software to identify it; the value is not stored inside the certificate. certutil shows a SHA-1 'Cert Hash' and openssl x509 -fingerprint -sha256 gives 32 bytes; both identify a certificate in allow-lists. issuerUniqueID / subjectUniqueIDX.509 v2; RFC 5280 §4.1.2.8 · Format · Deprecated · General Optional v2 fields for handling reused names; RFC 5280 says conforming CAs must not generate them. Linters such as zlint raise an error when a public TLS certificate carries a subjectUniqueID field.

docs.title: 6.4 Certificate Extensions in Depth
docs.text:
Extensions are the labelled add-ons in a version 3 certificate that say what the key may be used for, which names it covers, whether it belongs to a CA, and where to find the issuer and revocation information. Each extension has a unique number (an OID), a value, and a 'critical' flag telling software whether it may ignore the extension if it does not understand it.

Typical extensions: CA certificate vs TLS leaf

Issuing CA certificate TLS server leaf Basic Constraints critical, CA:TRUE, pathlen:0 CA:FALSE Key Usage critical, keyCertSign, cRLSign critical, digitalSignature Extended Key Usage serverAuth (constrains below) serverAuth Subject Alt Name usually absent DNS names / IP addresses Name Constraints optional, permitted subtrees not allowed AKI / SKI AKI = root's SKI; own SKI AKI = CA's SKI AIA / CRL DP root cert URL, root CRL issuer cert URL, CRL shard Certificate Policies CA/B OIDs or anyPolicy e.g. 2.23.140.1.2.1 (DV) SCT list absent 2-3 embedded SCTs

The same extension means different things depending on whether the certificate belongs to a CA.

Think of it like…

If the certificate is an ID card, extensions are the endorsements printed on the back: 'may drive lorries', 'valid in these countries only', 'issued by office no. 12, call this number to check it'.

Real-world example

Lumen Bikes' security engineer compares two certificates. The issuing CA certificate has Basic Constraints CA:TRUE with pathlen:0, Key Usage keyCertSign and cRLSign, and an EKU limited to serverAuth. The shop's leaf has CA:FALSE, Key Usage digitalSignature, EKU serverAuth, three DNS names in the SAN, AKI matching the CA's SKI, an AIA caIssuers URL, a CRL Distribution Point, the DV policy OID and two embedded SCTs. Reading those lines tells her exactly what each certificate may do.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The certificate profile (CA policy or a template) decides which extensions to include, their values and criticality.
  2. The CA encodes each as Extension ::= SEQUENCE { extnID OID, critical BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE, extnValue OCTET STRING }.
  3. During validation, software parses every extension; an unrecognised critical extension makes the certificate invalid.
  4. CA-level extensions (Basic Constraints, Name Constraints, policy constraints) constrain everything issued below.
  5. Leaf-level extensions (SAN, Key Usage, EKU) are matched against how the certificate is actually being used.

Who uses it

PKI architects writing certificate profiles, CA engineers, AD CS template owners, developers debugging 'certificate not valid for this purpose' errors, and auditors checking BR compliance.

Key takeaway

Know the two classic confusions cold: Key Usage (cryptographic operations, like digitalSignature) versus Extended Key Usage (application purposes, like serverAuth), and AKI (issuer's key ID) versus SKI (this certificate's key ID).

Going deeper

  • Key Usage bits: digitalSignature(0), nonRepudiation/contentCommitment(1), keyEncipherment(2), dataEncipherment(3), keyAgreement(4), keyCertSign(5), cRLSign(6), encipherOnly(7), decipherOnly(8). An ECDSA TLS key needs only digitalSignature; keyEncipherment matters only for TLS 1.2 RSA key transport.
  • RFC 5280 requires Basic Constraints to be critical in CA certificates. pathLenConstraint counts the intermediate CA certificates allowed below; pathlen:0 means 'may issue only end-entity certificates'.
  • EKU in a CA certificate effectively constrains everything below it. The Chrome Root Program's June 2026 deadline for dedicated serverAuth hierarchies is why public CAs such as Let's Encrypt dropped clientAuth in 2026.
  • SAN name types include dNSName, iPAddress, rfc822Name (email), uniformResourceIdentifier (e.g. spiffe:// workload IDs) and otherName (e.g. Microsoft UPN 1.3.6.1.4.1.311.20.2.3 for smart-card logon). If the subject DN is empty, the SAN must be marked critical.
  • Name Constraints (permittedSubtrees / excludedSubtrees) make 'technically constrained' sub-CAs possible; enforcement is reliable in modern clients, but a constrained CA should also be limited by EKU.
  • Other extensions worth recognising: Policy Mappings (2.5.29.33), Inhibit anyPolicy (2.5.29.54), Subject Information Access, the CT precertificate poison (1.3.6.1.4.1.11129.2.4.3), TLS Feature/Must-Staple (1.3.6.1.5.5.7.1.24), noRevAvail (RFC 9608) and Microsoft template OIDs such as 1.3.6.1.4.1.311.21.7.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Mixing up Key Usage and EKU — a certificate with keyUsage digitalSignature but no serverAuth EKU still fails as a TLS server certificate in strict clients.
  • Putting hostnames only in the CN — modern clients read only the SAN.
  • Marking a new or private extension critical 'for safety' — every client that does not understand it will reject the certificate.
  • Assuming every certificate has an OCSP URL in AIA — many now have only a CRL Distribution Point, and short-lived ones may have neither.

docs.title: Try it: Print just the extensions that matter, and define them when making a lab certificate
docs.text:
openssl x509 -in leaf.pem -noout -ext \
  basicConstraints,keyUsage,extendedKeyUsage,subjectAltName,authorityKeyIdentifier,authorityInfoAccess,crlDistributionPoints,certificatePolicies

# lab profile snippet (openssl.cnf)
[ v3_leaf ]
basicConstraints = critical, CA:FALSE
keyUsage = critical, digitalSignature
extendedKeyUsage = serverAuth
subjectAltName = DNS:shop.lumenbikes.example, DNS:www.lumenbikes.example

docs.title: Key chips, standards, protocols, products & terms
docs.text: Name What it does Example Basic ConstraintsRFC 5280 §4.2.1.9 (OID 2.5.29.19) · Extension · Current · General States whether the certificate belongs to a CA (cA TRUE/FALSE) and, optionally, pathLenConstraint: how many intermediate CAs may follow below it. An issuing CA with 'CA:TRUE, pathlen:0' can sign leaf certificates but not another sub-CA; every leaf carries CA:FALSE. Key UsageRFC 5280 §4.2.1.3 (OID 2.5.29.15) · Extension · Current · General A bit string of permitted cryptographic operations such as digitalSignature, keyEncipherment, keyAgreement, keyCertSign and cRLSign; usually marked critical. A CA certificate sets keyCertSign and cRLSign; an ECDSA TLS leaf sets only digitalSignature. Extended Key Usage (EKU)RFC 5280 §4.2.1.12 (OID 2.5.29.37) · Extension · Current · General Application purposes as OIDs: serverAuth 1.3.6.1.5.5.7.3.1, clientAuth .3.2, codeSigning .3.3, emailProtection .3.4, timeStamping .3.8. A VPN gateway rejects a user certificate lacking clientAuth even though its signature and dates are fine. Subject Alternative Name (SAN)RFC 5280 §4.2.1.6 (OID 2.5.29.17) · Extension · Current · General The identities the certificate covers: dNSName, iPAddress, rfc822Name email, URI and otherName such as Microsoft UPN. One certificate lists DNS:lumenbikes.example, DNS:www.lumenbikes.example and DNS:*.api.lumenbikes.example. Name ConstraintsRFC 5280 §4.2.1.10 (OID 2.5.29.30) · Extension · Current · Private PKI CA certificates only: permitted and excluded name subtrees that every certificate below must respect, such as only names under harbourview.example. Harbourview's partner gets a sub-CA permitted only for partner.harbourview.example, so even if compromised it cannot issue for other domains. Authority Key Identifier (AKI)RFC 5280 §4.2.1.1 (OID 2.5.29.35) · Extension · Current · General Identifies the issuer's public key, normally by copying the issuer's Subject Key Identifier, helping clients choose the right issuer when names repeat. After a CA rekeys under the same name, AKI tells clients which of two 'Northwind Issuing CA' certificates actually signed. Subject Key Identifier (SKI)RFC 5280 §4.2.1.2 (OID 2.5.29.14); RFC 7093 · Extension · Current · General A short identifier of this certificate's own public key, often a SHA-1 hash of the key bits or a truncated SHA-256 hash. Chain-building code matches the leaf's AKI 3B:9F:... against an intermediate's SKI 3B:9F:... before trying the signature. Authority Information Access (AIA)RFC 5280 §4.2.2.1 (OID 1.3.6.1.5.5.7.1.1) · Extension · Current · General Pointers to issuer resources: caIssuers (URL of the issuing CA certificate) and, optionally, ocsp (URL of the OCSP responder). A Windows client missing the intermediate downloads it from the caIssuers URL, http://crt.northwind-ca.example/issuing.crt, and completes the chain. CRL Distribution Points (CDP)RFC 5280 §4.2.1.13 (OID 2.5.29.31) · Extension · Current · General URLs where the issuer publishes the CRL that would list this certificate if revoked; standard in public TLS certificates now that OCSP is optional. Let's Encrypt began adding CRL URLs to its certificates on 7 May 2025, the same day it removed OCSP URLs. Certificate PoliciesRFC 5280 §4.2.1.4 (OID 2.5.29.32) · Extension · Current · General Policy OIDs naming the rules the certificate was issued under, plus optional CPS URLs; public TLS uses CA/B OIDs like 2.23.140.1.2.1 (DV). An EV certificate carries 2.23.140.1.1, telling relying software the stricter Extended Validation checks were performed. Embedded SCT listRFC 6962 (OID 1.3.6.1.4.1.11129.2.4.2) · Extension · Current · Web PKI Signed Certificate Timestamps proving the precertificate was submitted to Certificate Transparency logs; browsers require them for public TLS. openssl shows 'CT Precertificate SCTs' with entries naming each log ID, timestamp and signature. Critical flagRFC 5280 §4.2 · Concept · General A Boolean on each extension: if critical and the software does not understand it, the certificate must be rejected; non-critical ones may be ignored. Basic Constraints is critical in CA certificates so legacy software that cannot parse it fails safe instead of trusting a leaf as a CA. Policy Constraints and Inhibit anyPolicyRFC 5280 (OIDs 2.5.29.36, 2.5.29.54) · Extension · Current · Private PKI CA-certificate extensions steering policy processing: requireExplicitPolicy, inhibitPolicyMapping and inhibitAnyPolicy. Bridge PKIs such as the US Federal PKI combine these with policy mappings so agencies accept only certificates of equivalent assurance.

docs.title: 6.5 ASN.1, DER, PEM and Certificate File Formats
docs.text:
Certificates are described in a notation called ASN.1 and stored as compact binary bytes using DER. Because binary is awkward to paste into emails or config files, it is often wrapped as PEM: Base64 text between BEGIN and END lines. Around these sit container formats — CSRs for requests, PKCS #7 for chains, PKCS #8 for private keys and PKCS #12 for a password-protected key-plus-certificate bundle.

From abstract syntax to the file on disk. Each layer wraps the one below; signatures are always computed over the DER bytes.

Think of it like…

ASN.1 is the blueprint, DER is the house built exactly to it, PEM is the same house photographed and posted as a printable picture, and PKCS #12 is a locked removal van holding the house keys and the deeds together.

Real-world example

Tomás receives 'server.cer' from a colleague and nginx refuses it. He runs head -1 server.cer and sees binary garbage, so it is DER. openssl x509 -inform DER -in server.cer -out server.pem converts it, and the PEM file now starts with -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----. For the Windows IIS box he then bundles key and chain into a .pfx with openssl pkcs12 -export.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Specifications define structures in ASN.1, e.g. Certificate ::= SEQUENCE { tbsCertificate, signatureAlgorithm, signatureValue }.
  2. DER encodes each value as tag-length-value bytes with exactly one valid encoding, so signatures are reproducible.
  3. PEM Base64-encodes the DER bytes and adds a label line such as CERTIFICATE, PRIVATE KEY or CERTIFICATE REQUEST.
  4. Containers group objects: PKCS #10 for requests, PKCS #7/CMS for chains, PKCS #8 for keys, PKCS #12 for key + chain.
  5. Tools convert between them; the content, not the file extension, determines the format.

Who uses it

System administrators moving certificates between Linux, Windows, Java and appliances; developers using crypto libraries; PKI engineers; anyone who has ever had to 'convert a PFX to PEM'.

Key takeaway

When a file will not load, first identify it: 'BEGIN' text means PEM (read the label); binary starting with 0x30 0x82 is DER; a password prompt usually means PKCS #12 or an encrypted PKCS #8 key.

Going deeper

  • DER is tag-length-value: 0x30 is a SEQUENCE, 0x02 INTEGER, 0x06 OBJECT IDENTIFIER, 0x03 BIT STRING, 0x04 OCTET STRING, 0xA0/0xA3 context-specific tags such as [0] version and [3] extensions; 0x82 means 'length in the next two bytes'.
  • PEM labels come from RFC 7468: CERTIFICATE, CERTIFICATE REQUEST, PRIVATE KEY, ENCRYPTED PRIVATE KEY, PUBLIC KEY, X509 CRL and PKCS7. Legacy labels RSA PRIVATE KEY and EC PRIVATE KEY indicate PKCS #1 and SEC 1 formats.
  • A CSR (PKCS #10, RFC 2986) carries requested extensions in a PKCS #9 extensionRequest attribute (1.2.840.113549.1.9.14) and is signed by the requester's own key as proof of possession; the CA decides what actually goes into the certificate.
  • OpenSSL 3 creates PKCS #12 files with AES-256-CBC, PBKDF2 and an HMAC-SHA256 MAC by default; some older systems and appliances only read RC2/3DES files, which needs the -legacy option.
  • Java's default keystore type has been PKCS #12 since Java 9 (JEP 229); JKS remains readable, and keytool -importkeystore migrates between them.
  • A .p7b 'certs-only' bundle is a degenerate CMS SignedData with no content and no signers — just a bag of certificates (and optionally CRLs).

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Trusting file extensions — .cer and .crt can be either PEM or DER; inspect the content.
  • Sending a .pfx and its password in the same email — share the password through a separate channel.
  • Putting the private key into the 'certificate' field of a server config, or the chain in the wrong order — the leaf must come first, followed by its issuer.

docs.title: Try it: Make a CSR, inspect raw ASN.1 and convert between formats
docs.text:
openssl req -new -newkey ec -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -noenc \
  -keyout lab.key -out lab.csr -subj "/CN=lab.example" -addext "subjectAltName=DNS:lab.example"
openssl req -in lab.csr -noout -text -verify
openssl asn1parse -in cert.pem -i | head -20
openssl x509 -in cert.pem -outform DER -out cert.der
openssl pkcs12 -export -inkey lab.key -in cert.pem -certfile chain.pem -out lab.p12
openssl pkcs12 -in lab.p12 -info -noout

docs.title: Key chips, standards, protocols, products & terms
docs.text: Name What it does Example ASN.1ITU-T X.680 series · Standard · Current · General Abstract Syntax Notation One: a language for describing data structures like Certificate ::= SEQUENCE { ... } independently of how they are encoded. RFC 5280's appendix defines TBSCertificate in ASN.1; code generators in Go, Rust and Java turn it into parsers. DERITU-T X.690 · Format · Current · General Distinguished Encoding Rules: the single canonical binary encoding of ASN.1 used for certificates, so signer and verifier hash identical bytes. A certificate's DER bytes start 30 82 05 1c — a SEQUENCE tag followed by a two-byte length of 1,308 bytes. BERITU-T X.690 · Format · Legacy · General Basic Encoding Rules: DER's flexible parent allowing several encodings of one value; tolerated in some CMS messages but not in certificates. Old PKCS #7 files from some tools use BER indefinite lengths, which strict DER-only parsers refuse. PEMRFC 7468 (textual encodings) · Format · Current · General Base64-encoded DER wrapped in -----BEGIN label----- and -----END label----- lines, so binary objects survive email, configs and copy-paste. nginx's certificate file holds two PEM blocks labelled CERTIFICATE: the leaf first, then the intermediate. Object Identifier (OID)ITU-T X.660 / IANA / national registries · Concept · General A globally unique dotted number naming algorithms, extensions, attributes and policies, such as 2.5.29.17 for Subject Alternative Name. openssl shows an unknown extension 1.3.6.1.4.1.311.21.7; an OID lookup reveals Microsoft's certificate template information. PKCS #10 CSRRFC 2986 · Format · Current · General Certificate Signing Request: subject name, public key and requested extensions, signed with the matching private key as proof of possession. Ravi runs openssl req -new to create shop.csr, pastes it into the CA portal, and keeps shop.key on the server. PKCS #7 / CMSRFC 2315 / RFC 5652 · Format · Current · General Cryptographic Message Syntax: a container for signed or encrypted data; a 'certs-only' .p7b file carries a chain without keys. Windows exports a chain as .p7b; openssl pkcs7 -print_certs -in chain.p7b turns it into PEM for a Linux server. PKCS #12 (.p12 / .pfx)RFC 7292 · Format · Current · General A password-protected bundle of a private key, its certificate and chain; the usual way to move identities between Windows, macOS, Java and browsers. Aoife imports her S/MIME identity into Outlook from aoife.p12, using a password IT sent through a separate channel. PKCS #8RFC 5208 / RFC 5958 · Format · Current · General A generic private-key container for any algorithm, optionally password-encrypted; PEM labels PRIVATE KEY or ENCRYPTED PRIVATE KEY. OpenSSL 3 writes new keys as PKCS #8 by default, so generated files start with -----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----. PKCS #1 and SEC 1 key filesRFC 8017 / RFC 5915 · Format · Legacy · General Older algorithm-specific private-key encodings, labelled RSA PRIVATE KEY (PKCS #1) and EC PRIVATE KEY (SEC 1). A 2014 server key starts 'BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY'; openssl pkey -in old.key -out new.key converts it to PKCS #8. JKS (Java KeyStore)Oracle / OpenJDK · Format · Legacy · General Java's proprietary keystore format; since Java 9 the default keystore type is PKCS #12, and JKS remains for compatibility. Tomás migrates an old Tomcat keystore with keytool -importkeystore -srcstoretype JKS -deststoretype PKCS12. Certificate file extensionsConventions, not standards · Concept · General .pem, .crt, .cer, .der, .key, .csr, .p7b and .p12/.pfx are naming conventions only; the content decides the real format. A '.cer' from one admin is DER while another '.cer' is PEM; head -1 shows a BEGIN line only for PEM. Full-chain bundleServer configuration convention · Format · Current · Web PKI A PEM file concatenating the leaf certificate and then its intermediates, in order, so a server can send the complete chain. certbot writes fullchain.pem and privkey.pem; pointing nginx at cert.pem alone causes missing-intermediate errors. CRL fileRFC 5280 §5 · Format · Current · General A signed CertificateList in DER or PEM (label X509 CRL) listing revoked serial numbers with dates and reasons. openssl crl -inform DER -in ca.crl -noout -text prints thisUpdate, nextUpdate and every revoked serial.

docs.title: 6.6 Certificate Types: TLS, Client, S/MIME, Code, Document, Device and Qualified
docs.text:
All certificates share the X.509 format, but they are issued for different jobs and under different rulebooks. TLS server certificates prove a website's name; client certificates prove a user or device; S/MIME certificates sign and encrypt email; code-signing and document-signing certificates prove who published software or signed a file; and qualified certificates carry special legal weight in the EU. The EKU, the policy OIDs and the level of identity checking tell them apart.

Three public certificate families compared (2026)

TLS server S/MIME Code signing EKU serverAuth (.3.1) emailProtection (.3.4) codeSigning (.3.3) Identity checked Domain; + org for OV/EV Mailbox; + org or person Organisation or individual Rulebook TLS BRs + EV Guidelines S/MIME BRs (since 2023) Code Signing BRs Max lifetime 200 days (from Mar 2026) 825 days (strict/multipurpose) 460 days (from Mar 2026) Key storage rule Subscriber's choice Subscriber's choice Hardware (HSM/token) since 2023

Each family has its own CA/Browser Forum rulebook, EKU and maximum lifetime.

Think of it like…

Like different kinds of official ID — a passport, a work badge, a notary's seal and a professional licence — all are cards with a photo and a stamp, but each is checked differently and accepted for different purposes.

Real-world example

Harbourview Bank holds an OV TLS certificate for its website, a wildcard for *.api.harbourview.example, client certificates on staff laptops for VPN, sponsor-validated S/MIME certificates for email, an EV code-signing certificate for its desktop app, a document-signing certificate for PDF statements, and — for EU open-banking APIs — a QWAC. Each one comes from a different profile with a different EKU and lifetime.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Decide the use: server TLS, client authentication, email, code, documents, device identity or legal signatures.
  2. Pick the validation level the use requires: DV, OV, EV, mailbox/individual validation, or qualified (eIDAS).
  3. The CA issues under the matching rulebook — TLS Baseline Requirements, S/MIME BRs, Code Signing BRs or ETSI/eIDAS.
  4. The certificate carries the matching EKU and policy OIDs, which relying software checks.
  5. Keys are protected as required: hardware is mandatory for public code signing and for qualified signatures.

Who uses it

Web and platform teams buying certificates, software release engineers, email and identity administrators, legal/compliance teams handling e-signatures, and IoT manufacturers.

Key takeaway

Memorise the CA/B policy OIDs: 2.23.140.1.2.1 DV, 2.23.140.1.2.2 OV, 2.23.140.1.2.3 IV, 2.23.140.1.1 EV — they appear on every public TLS certificate.

Going deeper

  • EV company names disappeared from the address bar in Chrome 77 and Firefox 70 (2019); EV still exists but its value is now mainly contractual and for some regulated sectors.
  • Wildcards (RFC 9525 rules) match exactly one label in the leftmost position: *.lumenbikes.example covers shop.lumenbikes.example but not lumenbikes.example or a.b.lumenbikes.example. EV certificates may not contain wildcards.
  • The S/MIME BRs took effect on 1 September 2023 with mailbox-, organisation-, sponsor- and individual-validated types in Legacy, Multipurpose and Strict generations; Legacy issuance ended on 15 July 2025, and ballot SMC013 (2025) allows experimental ML-DSA and ML-KEM certificates.
  • Code Signing BRs have required subscriber keys in hardware (FIPS 140-2 Level 2 or Common Criteria EAL4+ HSMs or tokens) since 1 June 2023.
  • Ballot CSC-31 capped code-signing certificate validity at 460 days for certificates issued from 1 March 2026; RFC 3161 timestamps (Chapter 70) keep signatures verifiable after the certificate expires.
  • Public TLS certificates are leaving client authentication: the Chrome Root Program requires dedicated serverAuth hierarchies by June 2026, so Let's Encrypt stopped issuing clientAuth in 2026 and organisations need private CAs for mTLS.
  • Qualified certificates under eIDAS (Regulation 910/2014, amended by 2024/1183 'eIDAS 2.0') are issued by qualified trust service providers on EU Trusted Lists and marked with QCStatements (RFC 3739, ETSI EN 319 412-5); PSD2 QWACs add the payment provider's authorisation details.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Thinking EV or OV gives stronger encryption — all types use the same algorithms; only the identity checks differ.
  • Expecting *.example.com to cover example.com — add the apex as a separate SAN entry.
  • Using a public TLS certificate as a client certificate for mTLS — clientAuth is being removed from public TLS hierarchies; use a private CA.

docs.title: Try it: Identify a certificate's type from its policy OIDs and EKU
docs.text:
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -ext certificatePolicies,extendedKeyUsage,subjectAltName
# 2.23.140.1.2.1 = DV, .2.2 = OV, 2.23.140.1.1 = EV

docs.title: Key chips, standards, protocols, products & terms
docs.text: Name What it does Example Domain Validated (DV) certificateCA/B Forum TLS BRs; OID 2.23.140.1.2.1 · Certificate · Current · Web PKI Proves only control of the domain names, checked by DNS, HTTP or TLS-ALPN challenges; contains no verified organisation name. Let's Encrypt issues only DV certificates, so a hobby blog and a large bank using it get the same assurance level. Organization Validated (OV) certificateCA/B Forum TLS BRs; OID 2.23.140.1.2.2 · Certificate · Current · Web PKI Adds a vetted organisation name and location to domain validation; the CA checks registration records and the requester's authority. Harbourview Bank's OV certificate shows O=Harbourview Bank plc when users open certificate details, not in the address bar. Extended Validation (EV) certificateCA/B Forum EV Guidelines; OID 2.23.140.1.1 · Certificate · Current · Web PKI The strictest TLS identity vetting, covering legal, physical and operational existence; it no longer gets special address-bar treatment. Chrome 77 and Firefox 70 moved EV company names out of the address bar in 2019 after research showed users ignored them. Wildcard certificateRFC 9525 / CA/B Forum TLS BRs · Certificate · Current · Web PKI A certificate with a name like *.example.com covering any single label in that position, but not the apex or deeper subdomains. *.lumenbikes.example covers shop. and api. but not lumenbikes.example itself or eu.api.lumenbikes.example. Multi-domain (SAN) certificateCA/B Forum TLS BRs · Certificate · Current · Web PKI One certificate listing several distinct names in its SAN, sometimes sold as UCC; every name must be validated separately. A hosting firm puts 40 customer domains in one certificate; when one customer leaves, the whole certificate must be reissued. IP address certificateCA/B Forum TLS BRs; RFC 5280 iPAddress · Certificate · Current · Web PKI A TLS certificate whose SAN contains an iPAddress instead of a DNS name; public CAs must validate control of that address. Since January 2026 Let's Encrypt issues IP address certificates, but only through its six-day short-lived profile. Client authentication certificateEKU clientAuth 1.3.6.1.5.5.7.3.2 · Certificate · Current · Private PKI Identifies a user, device or service to a server in mutual TLS, VPN or 802.1X, using the clientAuth EKU. Bluefin Logistics' warehouse scanners present client certificates from a private CA when joining Wi-Fi with EAP-TLS. S/MIME certificateCA/B Forum S/MIME BRs (effective 1 Sep 2023) · Certificate · Current · Web PKI Signs and encrypts email using the emailProtection EKU; the S/MIME BRs define mailbox-, organisation-, sponsor- and individual-validated types. Aoife's sponsor-validated certificate names her and Harbourview Bank, so recipients' mail clients show a verified signature. Code signing certificateCA/B Forum Code Signing BRs · Certificate · Current · General Signs software with the codeSigning EKU; keys must be in hardware since June 2023 and validity is capped at 460 days since March 2026. Lumen's app team signs installers through a cloud HSM service and timestamps each signature so it stays valid after expiry. Document signing certificateRFC 9336 id-kp-documentSigning; Adobe AATL · Certificate · Current · General Signs PDFs and office documents using the documentSigning EKU (1.3.6.1.5.5.7.3.36) or vendor EKUs, trusted via lists like Adobe's AATL. A council's planning approvals show as validly signed in Acrobat because the issuing CA is on the Adobe Approved Trust List. Device certificateIEEE 802.1AR, vendor PKIs · Certificate · Current · Devices & IoT Identifies hardware rather than a person or domain, often installed at manufacture; IEEE 802.1AR IDevIDs are covered in Chapter 40. Each smart meter leaves the factory with a certificate holding its serial number, letting the utility authenticate it remotely. Qualified certificateeIDAS 910/2014 + 2024/1183; ETSI EN 319 412 · Certificate · Current · General An EU certificate issued by a qualified trust service provider, marked with QCStatements (RFC 3739), for legally recognised signatures and seals. Marta's qualified certificate on her national ID card creates qualified electronic signatures equivalent to handwritten ones across the EU. QWACeIDAS Article 45; ETSI EN 319 411/412 · Certificate · Current · Web PKI Qualified Website Authentication Certificate: an eIDAS certificate binding a website to a verified legal entity; eIDAS 2.0 requires browsers to recognise them. Open-banking APIs under PSD2 use QWACs carrying the payment provider's authorisation number, so banks and fintechs can identify each other.

docs.title: 6.7 Keys and Signature Algorithms in Certificates (Including Post-Quantum)
docs.text:
A certificate holds one public key and is signed by its issuer's key, and each of those uses a named algorithm. Today almost all public certificates use RSA or elliptic-curve ECDSA with SHA-256 or SHA-384. Post-quantum algorithms such as ML-DSA now have official X.509 identifiers, but they are much larger and not yet trusted by browsers for public websites.

Public key + signature size per certificate. Post-quantum signatures are 25-80 times larger than ECDSA, which is why chain size now matters.

Think of it like…

Choosing a signature algorithm is like choosing the kind of lock on a safe: older heavy locks (RSA), compact modern ones (ECDSA, Ed25519), and new quantum-proof locks (ML-DSA) that are very strong but far bulkier to fit.

Real-world example

Northwind's lab issues three test certificates for the same host: ECDSA P-256 (about 1 KB), RSA-2048 (about 1.3 KB) and ML-DSA-65 (about 5.5 KB). A three-certificate ML-DSA chain plus handshake signature adds roughly 15 KB, while the ECDSA chain adds under 3 KB. The team keeps ECDSA for the public site, tests ML-DSA internally with OpenSSL 3.5, and follows the IETF and Chrome plans before committing.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The subscriber picks a key algorithm (RSA, ECDSA curve, EdDSA or ML-DSA) and generates the key pair.
  2. The SPKI records it with an OID, e.g. id-ecPublicKey + prime256v1, or id-ml-dsa-65.
  3. The issuer signs with its own key's algorithm, recorded as signatureAlgorithm, e.g. ecdsa-with-SHA384.
  4. Clients advertise acceptable algorithms (TLS signature_algorithms_cert) and reject certificates they cannot verify.
  5. Policy (BRs, root programs, CNSA 2.0, NIST deprecation dates) decides which algorithms are allowed and for how long.

Who uses it

PKI architects choosing hierarchy algorithms, security engineers planning post-quantum migration, HSM and firmware engineers, and developers whose libraries must parse new OIDs.

Key takeaway

Remember the sizes: P-256 public key 65 bytes and signature about 72; RSA-2048 signature 256 bytes; ML-DSA-65 public key 1,952 bytes and signature 3,309 bytes.

Going deeper

  • The TLS Baseline Requirements allow only RSA (at least 2048-bit, modulus divisible by 8) and ECDSA on P-256, P-384 or P-521; Mozilla narrows ECDSA to P-256 and P-384. Ed25519 is valid X.509 (RFC 8410) but barred from public TLS.
  • RFC 9881 (October 2025) defines ML-DSA-44/65/87 in X.509 with OIDs 2.16.840.1.101.3.4.3.17-19 and allows only 'pure' ML-DSA in certificates; RFC 9909 (December 2025) does the same for SLH-DSA and RFC 9935 (March 2026) for ML-KEM public keys.
  • No browser root program accepts ML-DSA TLS certificates yet. In February 2026 Chrome said it has no immediate plan to add post-quantum X.509 roots and is developing Merkle Tree Certificates in the IETF PLANTS working group instead.
  • Hybrid authentication comes in two styles: composite ML-DSA (one key and signature combining ML-DSA with RSA/ECDSA/EdDSA; draft-ietf-lamps-pq-composite-sigs, approved and in the RFC Editor queue in 2026) and non-composite pairs of certificates linked by RFC 9763.
  • Key exchange moved first: hybrid X25519MLKEM768 is already the default in major browsers and OpenSSL 3.5, stopping 'harvest now, decrypt later'. Signatures must be quantum-safe only before a quantum attacker exists, but long-lived roots need planning now.
  • NIST IR 8547 (initial public draft, November 2024) proposes deprecating 112-bit classical signatures such as RSA-2048 after 2030 and disallowing RSA and ECDSA after 2035; CNSA 2.0 sets earlier dates for US national-security systems (Chapter 70).

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming Ed25519 works for public websites — it is not permitted by the Baseline Requirements, so browsers will not accept it from public CAs.
  • Believing RSA-4096 is 'quantum-safe' — Shor's algorithm breaks RSA of any size; only post-quantum algorithms resist it.
  • Thinking ML-DSA certificates can be deployed on public sites today — they are standardised but not yet trusted by browser root stores.
  • Confusing SHA-1 certificate signatures (banned) with SHA-1 key identifiers in SKI (still fine — not used for security).

docs.title: Try it: Generate classical and post-quantum lab keys (ML-DSA needs OpenSSL 3.5+)
docs.text:
openssl genpkey -algorithm EC -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -out p256.key
openssl genpkey -algorithm ED25519 -out ed25519.key
openssl genpkey -algorithm ML-DSA-65 -out mldsa65.key
openssl req -new -x509 -key mldsa65.key -subj "/CN=pq-lab" -days 30 -out mldsa65.crt
openssl x509 -in mldsa65.crt -noout -text | head -15
wc -c p256.key mldsa65.crt

docs.title: Key chips, standards, protocols, products & terms
docs.text: Name What it does Example RSA in certificates (rsaEncryption)RFC 8017 (PKCS #1); OID 1.2.840.113549.1.1.1 · Algorithm · Current · General The classic public-key algorithm; public TLS requires at least 2048-bit keys, and sha256WithRSAEncryption remains common for CA signatures. Northwind's RSA-4096 root signs RSA-2048 intermediates, producing 512-byte signatures; those intermediates sign leaves with 256-byte signatures. RSA-PSSRFC 8017; OID 1.2.840.113549.1.1.10 · Algorithm · Current · General A provably secure RSA signature padding; mandatory for RSA handshake signatures in TLS 1.3 but rarely used inside certificate signatures. A TLS 1.3 server with an RSA certificate signs CertificateVerify with rsa_pss_rsae_sha256 even though its certificate uses PKCS #1 v1.5. ECDSA P-256FIPS 186-5; curve OID 1.2.840.10045.3.1.7 · Algorithm · Current · General Elliptic-curve signatures on NIST P-256: about 128-bit security, a 65-byte public key and roughly 72-byte signatures; a common default for TLS keys. Ravi chooses P-256 for shop.lumenbikes.example; handshakes are faster and the certificate smaller than with RSA-2048. ECDSA P-384FIPS 186-5; curve OID 1.3.132.0.34 · Algorithm · Current · General ECDSA on the larger P-384 curve with about 192-bit security, popular for root and intermediate CA keys and national-security profiles. ISRG Root X2, Let's Encrypt's ECDSA root, uses a P-384 key and signs with ecdsa-with-SHA384. Ed25519RFC 8032; RFC 8410; OID 1.3.101.112 · Algorithm · Current · Private PKI EdDSA on Curve25519: fast, deterministic, 32-byte keys and 64-byte signatures; valid in X.509 but not permitted for public TLS. An internal mTLS mesh issues Ed25519 workload certificates, while its public website still uses ECDSA for browsers. Ed448RFC 8032; RFC 8410; OID 1.3.101.113 · Algorithm · Current · General EdDSA on Curve448 with about 224-bit security; standardised for certificates but seldom used outside specialised systems. A researcher creates an Ed448 test certificate with openssl genpkey -algorithm ED448 to check a parser's coverage. SHA-2 signature algorithm OIDsNIST FIPS 180-4; RFC 4055 / RFC 5758 · Algorithm · Current · General Hash choices encoded in signature OIDs, e.g. sha256WithRSAEncryption and ecdsa-with-SHA256; SHA-384 usually pairs with P-384 keys. ecdsa-with-SHA384 (1.2.840.10045.4.3.3) on an intermediate means the root hashed it with SHA-384 before signing with P-384. SHA-1 certificate signaturesFIPS 180-4; CA/B Forum BRs · Algorithm · Deprecated · General Signatures using SHA-1, banned for new public TLS certificates from 2016 and rejected by browsers in 2017 after the SHAttered collision. An old intranet appliance still presents a SHA-1-signed certificate; modern browsers refuse it, so the admin must reissue. ML-DSA certificatesNIST FIPS 204; RFC 9881 (Oct 2025) · Algorithm · Emerging · General NIST's lattice-based post-quantum signature; RFC 9881 defines ML-DSA-44, -65 and -87 in X.509 with OIDs 2.16.840.1.101.3.4.3.17-19. Using OpenSSL 3.5, a lab issues an ML-DSA-65 test chain; each certificate is about 5.5 KB versus about 1 KB for ECDSA. SLH-DSA certificatesNIST FIPS 205; RFC 9909 (Dec 2025) · Algorithm · Emerging · General Stateless hash-based post-quantum signatures relying only on hash-function security; tiny keys but signatures from about 7.8 KB to 50 KB. A firmware vendor considers SLH-DSA for a rarely used, long-lived root because its security rests only on hashes. ML-KEM certificateNIST FIPS 203; RFC 9935 (Mar 2026) · Certificate · Emerging · General A certificate carrying an ML-KEM encapsulation key instead of a signing key, for post-quantum key establishment such as encrypted S/MIME. Under S/MIME ballot SMC013, a CA could experimentally issue Aoife an ML-KEM certificate so senders encrypt mail to her quantum-safely. Composite ML-DSAIETF LAMPS draft-ietf-lamps-pq-composite-sigs · Algorithm · Emerging · General One key and signature combining ML-DSA with RSA, ECDSA or EdDSA under a single OID; both must verify. In the RFC Editor queue in 2026. id-MLDSA65-ECDSA-P256-SHA512 (OID 1.3.6.1.5.5.7.6.45) stays secure if either ML-DSA or P-256 is later broken. Related certificates (RFC 9763)IETF LAMPS (June 2025) · RFC · Emerging · General A non-composite hybrid approach: separate traditional and post-quantum certificates for one entity, linked by a RelatedCertificate extension. A defence contractor gives each server an ECDSA and an ML-DSA certificate linked by RFC 9763, so clients can verify either or both.

docs.title: 6.8 Chain Building and Path Validation
docs.text:
A server's certificate is trusted only if software can build a chain from it, through one or more intermediate CA certificates, up to a root it already trusts — and then check every link. Path building finds a possible chain; path validation checks signatures, dates, CA flags, name rules, key usages and revocation along it. Most 'certificate errors' you will ever fix are failures in one of these two steps.

What a client checks before trusting a certificate. Failing any step makes the path invalid; the client may then try another path.

Think of it like…

It is like checking a reference letter: the letter is signed by a manager, whose authority is confirmed by a director, whose identity you already know. If any signature is missing, forged or expired, the whole chain of vouching collapses.

Real-world example

Ravi deploys shop.lumenbikes.example with only cert.pem. Chrome on his laptop shows a padlock because it fetches the missing intermediate using the AIA URL, and Firefox works because it preloads known intermediates. But the company's Python stock-sync job fails with 'unable to get local issuer certificate'. He switches nginx to fullchain.pem, reruns openssl s_client -showcerts, sees two certificates sent, and every client now builds the chain.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Collect candidates: the server-sent chain, local intermediate caches, preloaded intermediates and AIA downloads.
  2. Build a path from leaf to a trust anchor by matching issuer to subject names and AKI to SKI.
  3. For each certificate verify the signature, validity dates and that issuers have Basic Constraints CA:TRUE within pathLen.
  4. Apply name constraints and policy rules, then check Key Usage and EKU for the intended purpose.
  5. Check revocation (CRLite, CRLSets, CRL or OCSP depending on client) and match the hostname to a SAN entry.
  6. If this path fails, try alternative paths (e.g. via a cross-sign) before reporting an error.

Who uses it

Site reliability engineers, DevOps and platform teams, application developers, support engineers, and security testers who must explain why one client trusts a certificate and another does not.

Key takeaway

Servers must send the leaf and all intermediates (never needed: the root). Test with a client that does not fetch missing intermediates, such as openssl s_client or curl, not with a desktop browser.

Going deeper

  • RFC 5280 section 6 defines validation with state variables such as working_public_key, working_issuer_name, max_path_length, permitted/excluded subtrees and valid_policy_tree; RFC 4158 gives guidance on path building, which is a graph search with possibly many valid paths.
  • Different verifiers behave differently: Chrome uses its own verifier with the Chrome Root Store; Firefox uses mozilla::pkix with intermediate preloading; Windows CryptoAPI and Apple platforms fetch missing intermediates via AIA; OpenSSL, Go and Java generally do not.
  • When DST Root CA X3 expired on 30 September 2021, OpenSSL 1.0.2 clients failed despite a valid path to ISRG Root X1, because they did not stop at the first trusted certificate; OpenSSL 1.1.0+ does.
  • Validation time is normally 'now', but code-signing verification can use a trusted RFC 3161 timestamp, so a signature made while the certificate was valid keeps verifying after expiry.
  • In TLS 1.3 the leaf must come first; other certificates may be in any order and clients should tolerate extras, but sending the root wastes bytes and an outdated cross-sign can steer old clients onto expired paths.
  • Browsers' error codes map to steps: NET::ERR_CERT_AUTHORITY_INVALID / SEC_ERROR_UNKNOWN_ISSUER (no path), NET::ERR_CERT_DATE_INVALID (dates), NET::ERR_CERT_COMMON_NAME_INVALID (hostname), NET::ERR_CERT_REVOKED (revocation).

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Testing only in Chrome or Firefox — they hide missing intermediates that break curl, Python, Java and many devices.
  • 'Fixing' errors with curl -k, verify=False or a trust-all TrustManager — this disables authentication entirely and invites man-in-the-middle attacks.
  • Putting the intermediates in the wrong order or using last year's intermediate after the CA changed its issuing hierarchy.

docs.title: Try it: Show the chain a server sends and validate a lab chain yourself
docs.text:
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com -showcerts </dev/null
openssl verify -CAfile root.pem -untrusted intermediate.pem leaf.pem
openssl verify -CAfile root.pem -untrusted intermediate.pem \
  -purpose sslserver -verify_hostname shop.lumenbikes.example leaf.pem

docs.title: Key chips, standards, protocols, products & terms
docs.text: Name What it does Example Certification path (chain)RFC 5280 §6 · Concept · General The ordered chain from leaf to trust anchor where each certificate's issuer matches the next one's subject and its signature verifies. www.greenleaf.example → Let's Encrypt R11 → ISRG Root X1 is a three-certificate path; the root comes from Ada's trust store. Path buildingRFC 4158 (informational) · Concept · General Finding candidate chains from a leaf to any trust anchor using names, AKI/SKI, supplied intermediates, caches and AIA downloads. With a cross-signed intermediate available, Ada's laptop finds two possible paths and prefers the one ending at a root it trusts. RFC 5280 path validation algorithmIETF RFC 5280 §6 · RFC · Current · General The step-by-step checks for each certificate: signature, validity, revocation, name chaining, Basic Constraints, path length, name constraints and policies. Go's crypto/x509, Java's PKIX CertPathValidator and mozilla::pkix all implement this algorithm, with small differences in edge cases. Intermediate certificate in the chainServer configuration practice · Certificate · Web PKI A CA certificate between leaf and root that servers must send in the handshake; clients usually do not store intermediates themselves. After installing only cert.pem, Ravi's site works in Chrome but curl reports 'unable to get local issuer certificate'. AIA chasingRFC 5280 AIA caIssuers · Concept · Web PKI Downloading a missing intermediate from the leaf's AIA caIssuers URL during validation; done by Windows, Apple platforms and Chrome, but not OpenSSL-based tools. A server missing its intermediate looks fine to Chrome users yet breaks the company's Python scripts and curl health checks. Intermediate preloadingMozilla Firefox (CCADB data) · Concept · Web PKI Firefox ships all publicly disclosed intermediate CA certificates from the CCADB, so it can complete chains without AIA fetching. Firefox validates Ravi's incomplete chain because it already knows the CA's intermediate, while his Go-based monitoring tool still fails. Cross-signed certificateCA practice; see Chapter 60 · Certificate · Web PKI A CA certificate for an existing key signed by a different CA, creating alternative paths; Chapter 60 covers root cross-signing strategy. Old Android phones trusted Let's Encrypt through ISRG Root X1 cross-signed by DST Root CA X3 until that cross-sign expired in 2024. Trusted-first path selectionOpenSSL 1.1.0+ default behaviour · Concept · General Stopping chain building at the first locally trusted certificate instead of following the server's longest chain to an expired root. When DST Root CA X3 expired on 30 September 2021, OpenSSL 1.0.2 clients failed while OpenSSL 1.1.x clients found the ISRG Root X1 path. RFC 9525 service identityIETF (2023), obsoletes RFC 6125 · RFC · Current · General Rules for matching a hostname to a certificate: use SAN DNS or IP entries only, wildcards only as the whole leftmost label, no CN fallback. A client for api.lumenbikes.example accepts DNS:*.lumenbikes.example but rejects a certificate whose only match is CN=api.lumenbikes.example. 'unable to get local issuer certificate'OpenSSL verify error 20 · Concept · General The chain cannot reach a trusted root: usually a missing intermediate, or a CA bundle that lacks the (private) root. Fix it by serving fullchain.pem, or for a private CA by adding its root to the client's bundle — never by disabling verification. 'certificate has expired' / 'not yet valid'OpenSSL verify errors 10 and 9 · Concept · General The current time is outside a certificate's validity window, caused by a genuine expiry or by a wrong clock on the client. A field device with a dead clock battery boots believing it is 2000, so every certificate looks 'not yet valid'. Developers at Bluefin see this from pip behind the corporate proxy until IT adds the inspection root to Python's CA bundle.
