Kenji's home-lab dashboard with a self-signed certificate shows this until he installs his lab root in the browser's trust store.

docs.title: 6.9 Revocation: CRLs, OCSP, Stapling, CRLite and Short-Lived Certificates
docs.text:
Revocation is how a CA cancels a certificate before it expires — for example when its private key leaks. The CA publishes signed lists of revoked serial numbers (CRLs) or answers one-at-a-time questions (OCSP). In practice online checking proved slow, unreliable and bad for privacy, so browsers now push revocation data to users, OCSP is being switched off, and certificates are getting so short-lived that revocation matters less.

How revocation evolved. The trend is from online lookups toward pushed lists and certificates too short-lived to need revoking.

Think of it like…

Revocation is like a shop's list of stolen credit cards: the till can download the whole list each morning (CRL), phone the bank for every card (OCSP), or the bank can issue cards that only work for a week so a stolen one soon becomes useless (short-lived certificates).

Real-world example

Ravi accidentally commits shop.key to a public GitHub repository. He revokes the certificate through his ACME client with reason keyCompromise, and the CA adds the serial to its next CRL shard and blocks the key. Within hours, Firefox's CRLite update and the CA's CRL reflect it; Chrome blocks it only if Google adds it to CRLSets. Because the shop had switched to six-day certificates, the exposed certificate would have expired within days anyway.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The subscriber or CA decides to revoke and records a reason code (e.g. keyCompromise, superseded).
  2. The CA adds the serial to its next CRL (or CRL shard) and, if it runs OCSP, starts answering 'revoked'.
  3. Browsers aggregate CA CRLs centrally and push compact updates (Firefox CRLite, Chrome CRLSets).
  4. Other clients download the CRL from the CDP URL, query OCSP, or read a stapled OCSP response in the handshake.
  5. Short-lived certificates sidestep the process: they expire before revocation could reliably propagate.

Who uses it

Incident responders handling key leaks, CA operations staff, browser and OS security teams, enterprise PKI administrators and anyone running VPN, Wi-Fi or smart-card authentication that relies on CRLs.

Key takeaway

Know the 2023-2026 story: CA/B ballot SC-063 made OCSP optional from 15 March 2024, Let's Encrypt removed OCSP URLs on 7 May 2025 and shut its responders on 6 August 2025, and Firefox replaced OCSP with CRLite.

Going deeper

  • Baseline Requirements timelines: revoke within 24 hours for causes such as key compromise or failed domain validation, and within 5 days for others such as non-compliant issuance.
  • Public TLS CAs must reissue subscriber CRLs at least every 7 days, with nextUpdate no more than 10 days after thisUpdate; letting a CRL go stale is itself a rule violation.
  • CRL anatomy: version, signature, issuer, thisUpdate, nextUpdate, revokedCertificates (serial, revocationDate, reasonCode), and extensions such as CRL Number (2.5.29.20), Delta CRL Indicator (2.5.29.27) and Issuing Distribution Point (2.5.29.28) for partitioned CRLs.
  • OCSP (RFC 6960; nonces updated by RFC 9654) answers good, revoked or unknown, and public TLS responses are valid 8 hours to 10 days. The responder learns which sites each IP visits — Let's Encrypt's main reason for ending it.
  • Firefox CRLite (Firefox 137, 2025) fetches a compact 'clubcard' encoding of all revocations for CT-logged certificates every 12 hours, about 300 KB daily. Chrome's CRLSets cover a curated subset; Chrome does no online checks by default.
  • Short-lived certificates (Let's Encrypt's 160-hour 'shortlived' profile, generally available January 2026) can carry the RFC 9608 noRevAvail extension; the BRs let sufficiently short-lived certificates omit revocation pointers entirely.
  • Enterprise systems still rely heavily on CRLs and OCSP: Windows smart-card logon, 802.1X, VPNs and AD CS all check them, so a private CA's CRL expiring (stale nextUpdate) can lock users out.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming revocation takes effect instantly everywhere — clients cache CRLs and responses, and browsers soft-fail when status is unreachable.
  • Leaving 'ssl_stapling on' and expecting Must-Staple protection with Let's Encrypt — its OCSP service no longer exists.
  • Letting a private CA's CRL pass its nextUpdate time — many enterprise clients then reject every certificate from that CA.
  • Thinking 'no OCSP URL' means 'cannot be revoked' — revocation still appears in the CRL and browser-pushed lists.

docs.title: Try it: Find revocation pointers, read a CRL, and query OCSP where it still exists
docs.text:
openssl x509 -in cert.pem -noout -ext crlDistributionPoints,authorityInfoAccess
curl -s -o ca.crl http://crl.northwind-ca.example/issuing.crl
openssl crl -inform DER -in ca.crl -noout -text | head -30
# only if the certificate still has an OCSP URL:
openssl ocsp -issuer intermediate.pem -cert cert.pem -url http://ocsp.northwind-ca.example -resp_text
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com -status </dev/null | grep -A4 'OCSP response'

docs.title: Key chips, standards, protocols, products & terms
docs.text: Name What it does Example Certificate Revocation List (CRL)RFC 5280 §5 · Format · Current · General A CA-signed list of revoked serial numbers with revocation dates and reasons, reissued before its nextUpdate time. Mozilla and Google ingest CAs' CRLs centrally, while a Windows server fetches the CRL itself from the certificate's CDP URL. Delta CRLRFC 5280 (Delta CRL Indicator 2.5.29.27) · Format · Legacy · Private PKI A small CRL listing only changes since a referenced base CRL; common in Microsoft AD CS deployments. An AD CS issuing CA publishes a weekly base CRL and a daily delta, so clients download kilobytes rather than megabytes each day. Partitioned (sharded) CRLsRFC 5280 Issuing Distribution Point; CCADB · Concept · Current · Web PKI Splitting a huge CRL into many shards, each scoped by an Issuing Distribution Point extension; public CAs disclose all shard URLs to CCADB. Let's Encrypt spreads revocations across many CRL shards; each certificate's CDP points to the shard that would list it. OCSPRFC 6960 (updated by RFC 9654) · Protocol · Legacy · General Online Certificate Status Protocol: a client asks a responder about one certificate and receives a signed good, revoked or unknown answer. A bank's internal payment gateway queries the private CA's OCSP responder before accepting a partner's client certificate. OCSP staplingRFC 6066 status_request; RFC 6961 · Protocol · Legacy · Web PKI The server fetches its own fresh OCSP response and attaches it to the TLS handshake, sparing clients a privacy-leaking lookup. With Let's Encrypt's OCSP gone since August 2025, nginx's ssl_stapling setting does nothing for its certificates and can be removed. OCSP Must-StapleRFC 7633 TLS Feature (1.3.6.1.5.5.7.1.24) · Extension · Deprecated · Web PKI A certificate extension promising the server always staples OCSP, so clients hard-fail without it; Let's Encrypt dropped support in 2025. Requests for Must-Staple certificates to Let's Encrypt began failing in 2025 as part of its OCSP shutdown plan. Soft-fail vs hard-failClient revocation policy · Concept · General Soft-fail accepts a certificate when revocation status is unavailable; hard-fail rejects it. Browsers soft-failed, so attackers could block lookups. An attacker holding a stolen key on the network path drops OCSP traffic, and a soft-failing client accepts the revoked certificate. CRLSetsGoogle Chrome · Product · Current · Web PKI Chrome's pushed list of selected high-priority revocations built from CA CRLs; Chrome does not normally perform online OCSP or CRL checks. After an intermediate is compromised, Google adds it to CRLSets and Chrome users worldwide reject it without any OCSP query. CRLiteMozilla Firefox · Product · Current · Web PKI Firefox's compact local encoding of all revocations for CT-logged certificates, updated every 12 hours and checked privately with no lookup. Since Firefox 137 desktop users receive about 300 KB of revocation data a day; Firefox 142 stopped OCSP checks for DV certificates. Short-lived certificatesCA/B Forum BRs; ACME profiles · Concept · Emerging · Web PKI Certificates valid for days, so a compromised key expires before revocation would propagate, reducing dependence on CRLs and OCSP. Let's Encrypt's 'shortlived' ACME profile, generally available since January 2026, issues 160-hour certificates renewed automatically every few days. noRevAvail extensionRFC 9608 (June 2024) · Extension · Emerging · General A non-critical extension declaring that the CA publishes no revocation information for this certificate, so validators skip revocation checks. A service mesh issuing 24-hour workload certificates adds noRevAvail, telling verifiers not to look for a CRL that never exists. Revocation reason codesRFC 5280 §5.3.1; CA/B BRs §7.2.2 · Concept · General CRL entry reasons such as keyCompromise, superseded, cessationOfOperation, affiliationChanged and privilegeWithdrawn; public TLS restricts which may be used. Ravi revokes with keyCompromise after leaking a key on GitHub; the CA then also blocks that key from future certificates. Ballot SC-063CA/Browser Forum (adopted 2023) · Standard · Current · Web PKI Made OCSP optional and CRLs mandatory for public TLS CAs from 15 March 2024, and eased revocation rules for short-lived certificates. Because of SC-063, Let's Encrypt could switch off OCSP entirely in August 2025 while publishing CRLs for every certificate. BR revocation timelinesCA/B Forum TLS BRs §4.9.1.1 · Standard · Current · Web PKI Public TLS CAs must revoke within 24 hours for causes such as key compromise and within 5 days for others, such as non-compliant issuance. When a CA finds certificates that break the rules, it has days to revoke them, so subscribers need automation to replace certificates quickly.

docs.title: 6.10 Certificate Transparency: Public Logs of Every Certificate
docs.text:
Certificate Transparency (CT) makes certificate issuance public. Before a CA issues a browser-trusted TLS certificate, it submits it to several independent append-only logs, which return signed receipts called SCTs that go inside the certificate. Browsers refuse public certificates without enough SCTs, and anyone can search the logs — so a CA cannot secretly issue a certificate for your domain without you being able to find out.

How a certificate gets its SCTs. The SCT is a promise to log; monitors close the loop by watching what was actually logged.

Think of it like…

CT is like a public land registry: every property deed must be entered in a register anyone can read, so if someone forges a deed to your house, it shows up where you — or a watchful neighbour — can spot it.

Real-world example

Harbourview Bank's security team subscribes its domains to a CT monitor. One morning it alerts on a new certificate for login-harbourview.example — a look-alike domain registered by phishers — and on another for promo.harbourview.example issued to a marketing agency nobody approved. The first goes to the takedown team; the second reveals shadow IT. Neither discovery would have been possible before CT.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The CA builds a precertificate (with a critical poison extension) and submits it to multiple CT logs.
  2. Each log returns a Signed Certificate Timestamp (SCT), promising to add the entry to its Merkle tree.
  3. The CA embeds the SCTs in the final certificate (or the server sends them via TLS extension or stapled OCSP).
  4. Browsers check SCT signatures against their list of trusted logs and count them against their CT policy.
  5. Monitors download log entries continuously and alert domain owners about unexpected certificates.

Who uses it

Security operations and threat-intelligence teams, brand-protection staff, CA compliance engineers, browser root-program staff, log operators and researchers who audit the Web PKI.

Key takeaway

CT detects mis-issuance after the fact — it does not prevent it. Pair it with CAA records (Chapter 60) to restrict which CAs may issue, and with monitoring so someone actually reads the alerts.

Going deeper

  • Chrome has required CT for public certificates issued since 30 April 2018, Apple since 15 October 2018, and Firefox desktop since version 135 (2025), which reuses Chrome's log list.
  • Chrome's policy needs 2 embedded SCTs for certificates valid 180 days or less and 3 for longer ones, from at least two different log operators.
  • Logs are Merkle trees: inclusion proofs show an entry is present and consistency proofs show the log only appended, each needing about log2(n) hashes — roughly 30 for a billion entries.
  • The static-CT API (C2SP specification) replaces RFC 6962's dynamic JSON endpoints with signed checkpoints and immutable 256-entry tiles served as plain files that CDNs cache. Implementations include Sunlight (by Filippo Valsorda, sponsored by Let's Encrypt) and Google's TesseraCT.
  • Chrome accepted static-CT logs from M134 (March 2025) if at least one SCT came from an RFC 6962 log; in November 2025 it proposed dropping that rule, effective mid-March 2026 at the earliest — check the current policy.
  • Let's Encrypt made its RFC 6962 log Oak read-only on 30 November 2025 and shut it down on 28 February 2026, keeping its static-CT logs Sycamore and Willow; other operators include Google, Cloudflare, DigiCert, Sectigo, Geomys (Tuscolo) and IPng.
  • RFC 9162 (CT version 2.0, 2021) was never adopted by browsers. CT also has a privacy cost: every public certificate's hostnames become searchable, so internal names belong on private-CA certificates.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Believing CT stops bad certificates being issued — it makes them visible; someone must monitor and react.
  • Expecting CT to show revocation status — logs record issuance only.
  • Requesting public certificates for secret internal hostnames — they become public in CT logs within minutes.

docs.title: Try it: Search CT for a domain and see the SCTs inside a certificate
docs.text:
curl -s "https://crt.sh/?q=%25.example.com&output=json" | head -c 800
openssl x509 -in cert.pem -noout -text | grep -A14 'CT Precertificate SCTs'
# open-source monitor (SSLMate): https://github.com/SSLMate/certspotter

Logs are sharded by expiry date, so a certificate expiring in 2027 goes to a shard that accepts only 2027 expiries. An iOS app's HTTPS call fails if the server certificate lacks qualifying SCTs, even though it chains to a trusted root. An enterprise exempts internal hosts with the security.pki.certificate_transparency.disable_for_hosts preference. Kenji runs the open-source certspotter tool for his domains and gets an email whenever a CA logs a new certificate.

docs.title: 6.11 TLS and Certificates Together: Handshakes, SNI and Mutual TLS
docs.text:
TLS is the protocol behind HTTPS, and it is where certificates do their daily work. During the handshake the server sends its certificate chain and then proves it holds the matching private key by signing the conversation so far. In mutual TLS (mTLS) the client does the same. The client's first message names the site it wants (SNI), so one server can pick the right certificate among many.

TLS 1.3 handshake with mutual TLS. Messages in braces are encrypted; both sides prove key possession with CertificateVerify.

Think of it like…

A TLS handshake is like meeting a courier at the door: they show an ID badge (certificate), then sign your delivery sheet in front of you (CertificateVerify) so you know the badge is theirs — and in mTLS you show your ID back before they hand over the parcel.

Real-world example

Ada's browser opens shop.lumenbikes.example. Its ClientHello carries SNI 'shop.lumenbikes.example', a hybrid X25519MLKEM768 key share and the signature algorithms it accepts. The CDN picks the shop's ECDSA certificate, sends it with one intermediate inside the encrypted part of the handshake, and signs the transcript with the matching key. The browser validates the chain and signature, and the first HTTP request goes out after a single round trip.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. ClientHello: SNI, supported groups and key shares, signature_algorithms and signature_algorithms_cert.
  2. ServerHello completes key exchange; everything after it is encrypted in TLS 1.3.
  3. Server sends EncryptedExtensions, optionally CertificateRequest (for mTLS), then Certificate (leaf first) and CertificateVerify.
  4. Server Finished; the client validates the chain, the hostname and the CertificateVerify signature.
  5. In mTLS the client sends its own Certificate and CertificateVerify, then Finished; application data follows.

Who uses it

Web, CDN and load-balancer engineers, API and service-mesh developers, network security engineers, and penetration testers analysing TLS configurations.

Key takeaway

Holding a certificate file proves nothing; CertificateVerify — a signature over the handshake transcript with the private key — is what proves identity in every connection.

Going deeper

  • TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446) encrypts the Certificate message, and each CertificateEntry can carry a stapled OCSP response or SCTs. CertificateVerify signs the whole transcript hash with a context string, so it cannot be replayed elsewhere.
  • signature_algorithms lists what the client accepts for CertificateVerify; signature_algorithms_cert (if sent) lists what it accepts inside certificates. Servers can hold both ECDSA and RSA certificates and pick per client. RSA keys must sign handshakes with RSA-PSS in TLS 1.3.
  • Size matters: a typical ECDSA chain is 2-3 KB, but TCP's initial congestion window is about 14.6 KB. Post-quantum chains of 15 KB or more add round trips, motivating certificate compression (RFC 8879) and Merkle Tree Certificates.
  • Encrypted Client Hello (RFC 9849) hides SNI and other sensitive ClientHello fields using a key published in DNS HTTPS records; observers see only the provider's public name.
  • In mTLS the server's CertificateRequest can include a certificate_authorities list to help clients choose; the server maps the validated client certificate's subject or SAN (e.g. a SPIFFE URI, Chapter 70) to an account or workload.
  • Delegated Credentials (RFC 9345) let a certificate key sign a short-lived credential (hours to days) so edge servers never hold the long-term key; the certificate must carry the DelegationUsage extension.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Believing the certificate's key encrypts the session — in TLS 1.3 it only signs; ephemeral (EC)DHE or hybrid ML-KEM keys encrypt.
  • Forgetting SNI in scripts or old clients — the server returns its default certificate and the hostname check fails.
  • Accepting any client certificate that chains to a public root for mTLS — anyone can get one; trust only your own client CA and check identity fields.

docs.title: Try it: Inspect a TLS 1.3 handshake and run a local mutual-TLS lab
docs.text:
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com -tls1_3 -brief </dev/null
# lab mTLS (your own test certificates):
openssl s_server -accept 8443 -cert server.crt -key server.key -Verify 1 -CAfile client-ca.pem -www
openssl s_client -connect localhost:8443 -cert client.crt -key client.key -CAfile server-ca.pem -brief

docs.title: Key chips, standards, protocols, products & terms
docs.text: Name What it does Example TLS 1.3IETF RFC 8446 (2018) · Protocol · Current · General The current TLS version: one-round-trip handshake, encrypted certificates, forward-secret key exchange only, and signatures over the full transcript. Ada's browser and shop.lumenbikes.example complete a TLS 1.3 handshake in one round trip before the first HTTP request. Certificate messageRFC 8446 §4.4.2 · Protocol · Current · General The handshake message carrying the sender's chain, leaf first; in TLS 1.3 each entry can carry extensions such as OCSP status or SCTs. Wireshark with logged session keys shows a Certificate message of about 3 KB holding the leaf and one intermediate. CertificateVerifyRFC 8446 §4.4.3 · Protocol · Current · General A signature with the certificate's private key over the handshake transcript hash, proving the peer holds that key right now. A stolen certificate file without its private key is useless: an impostor server cannot produce a valid CertificateVerify. signature_algorithms_certRFC 8446 §4.2.3 · Extension · Current · General ClientHello extension listing signature algorithms the client accepts inside certificates, alongside signature_algorithms for handshake signatures. A server holding ECDSA and RSA certificates sends the ECDSA chain to modern clients and the RSA chain only to older ones. Server Name Indication (SNI)RFC 6066 · Extension · Current · General The ClientHello field naming the host the client wants, so one IP address can serve many sites, each with its own certificate. A CDN edge serving 10,000 domains reads SNI to choose the right certificate before sending the Certificate message. Encrypted Client Hello (ECH)IETF RFC 9849 · Protocol · Emerging · General Encrypts the inner ClientHello, including SNI, with a key published in DNS HTTPS records, hiding which site a user visits. With ECH, a café Wi-Fi observer sees only the CDN's public name, not that Ada is visiting shop.lumenbikes.example. Mutual TLS (mTLS)RFC 8446 client authentication · Protocol · Current · Private PKI TLS in which the client also presents a certificate and CertificateVerify after the server's CertificateRequest, authenticating both ends. Bluefin's warehouse API accepts only scanners holding client certificates from its private CA; others fail during the handshake. CertificateRequestRFC 8446 §4.3.2 · Protocol · Current · General The server message asking for a client certificate, listing acceptable signature algorithms and optionally the names of acceptable CAs. Aoife's browser shows a picker listing only her certificates issued by the CAs named in the server's CertificateRequest. Certificate compressionRFC 8879 · RFC · Current · General A TLS 1.3 extension compressing the Certificate message with zlib, Brotli or zstd, saving bandwidth for large chains. Chrome supports Brotli certificate compression, shrinking typical chains so handshakes fit into fewer packets. Delegated CredentialsRFC 9345 (2023) · RFC · Emerging · Web PKI Short-lived credentials signed by a certificate's key, letting edge servers use keys valid for hours without new certificates. A CDN gives edge servers delegated credentials valid a few hours, keeping the certificate's real private key in a central HSM. X25519MLKEM768IETF TLS hybrid key-exchange design · Algorithm · Current · General Hybrid post-quantum key exchange combining X25519 and ML-KEM-768; default in major browsers and OpenSSL 3.5, independent of certificate algorithms. Ada's connection uses X25519MLKEM768 for confidentiality while the server's certificate is still plain ECDSA P-256. TLS 1.2 RSA key transportRFC 5246 (TLS 1.2) · Protocol · Deprecated · General Legacy mode where the client encrypts the premaster secret to the certificate's RSA key; no forward secrecy, and removed from TLS 1.3. Traffic recorded in 2015 using RSA key transport can be decrypted by anyone who later steals the server's private key. TLS interception proxyEnterprise security gateways · Concept · Private PKI A middlebox that terminates TLS using certificates minted on the fly from a locally trusted root, so it can inspect traffic. Bluefin's firewall re-signs websites with its inspection root, and certificate-pinned apps break until they are exempted.

docs.title: 6.12 HSTS, Pinning and DANE: Extra Locks on Certificate Trust
docs.text:
Normal certificate validation trusts any CA in the trust store for any domain. Several add-ons narrow that: HSTS forces browsers to always use HTTPS for a site; pinning tells an app to accept only specific keys; and DANE publishes the expected certificate in DNS secured by DNSSEC. Some of these worked well (HSTS, DANE for email), while browser key pinning by websites (HPKP) was abandoned because it was too easy to lock yourself out.

HSTS vs key pinning vs DANE

HSTS Key pinning DANE What it enforces HTTPS only, no click-through Only listed public keys Cert/key published in DNS Where it is set HTTP header or preload list In app code / config TLSA record + DNSSEC Failure mode Site unreachable over HTTP Lock-out if keys lost Breaks if DNSSEC breaks Status 2026 Widely used HPKP removed; apps only Strong in SMTP, not browsers

HSTS survives; website key pinning (HPKP) died; DANE thrives mainly in email.

Think of it like…

HSTS is a sign on your door saying 'never accept deliveries through the window'; pinning is telling the concierge 'only accept parcels from this one courier'; DANE is publishing the courier's ID number in the official phone book.

Real-world example

Harbourview Bank sends Strict-Transport-Security with a one-year max-age and is on the HSTS preload list, so even a first-time visitor on hostile café Wi-Fi cannot be downgraded to HTTP. Its mobile app pins two of the bank's own SPKI hashes. Its mail domain publishes DNSSEC-signed TLSA records and an MTA-STS policy, so other mail servers refuse to deliver over unauthenticated connections.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. HSTS: the site sends a Strict-Transport-Security header; the browser remembers it for max-age seconds.
  2. Preload: the domain is submitted to the HSTS preload list and shipped inside browsers.
  3. Pinning: an app stores expected SPKI hashes and rejects chains that do not contain one of them.
  4. DANE: the domain signs its zone with DNSSEC and publishes TLSA records matching its certificate or key.
  5. Clients that support each mechanism enforce it in addition to (or, for DANE-EE, instead of) normal CA validation.

Who uses it

Web security engineers, mobile app developers, email administrators, DNS operators and security auditors reviewing HTTPS and mail transport security.

Key takeaway

If you pin, pin public keys (SPKI) you control and always include a backup pin; with certificate lifetimes falling toward 47 days, pinning whole certificates guarantees outages.

Going deeper

  • HSTS (RFC 6797) directives: max-age (seconds), includeSubDomains and preload. The hstspreload.org list, used by all major browsers, requires a max-age of at least 31536000 (one year), includeSubDomains, the preload token and a valid HTTPS redirect.
  • HPKP (RFC 7469) was removed from Chrome 72 (2019) and later Firefox, because mistakes or attackers ('ransom pinning') could brick a domain for months. Expect-CT (RFC 9163) followed: deprecated in Chrome 105, removed in 107.
  • Browsers still ship a small set of built-in static pins for high-value domains; Chrome's pins helped expose the fraudulent DigiNotar google.com certificate in 2011 (the DigiNotar story is in Chapter 60).
  • TLSA fields: usage 0 PKIX-TA, 1 PKIX-EE, 2 DANE-TA, 3 DANE-EE; selector 0 full certificate, 1 SPKI; matching 0 exact, 1 SHA-256, 2 SHA-512. '3 1 1' is the usual choice for mail servers.
  • DANE for SMTP (RFC 7672) is implemented in Postfix and Exim and used by large European mail providers; MTA-STS (RFC 8461) offers a Web-PKI-based alternative for domains without DNSSEC, with TLS-RPT (RFC 8460) reporting failures.
  • Mobile pinning: Android uses Network Security Config <pin-set> with an expiration date; iOS supports NSPinnedDomains in Info.plist. Pin keys you control or your CA's intermediates with backups, and plan pin rotation before every key change.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Pinning a leaf certificate — the next renewal changes it and every installed app breaks.
  • Adding includeSubDomains and preload before every subdomain supports HTTPS — preload removal takes months to propagate.
  • Publishing TLSA records in a zone without working DNSSEC validation — DANE then provides no security, or breaks delivery when signatures expire.

docs.title: Try it: Check HSTS, compute an SPKI pin and look up a TLSA record
docs.text:
curl -sI https://example.com | grep -i strict-transport-security
# SPKI pin (base64 SHA-256) of a certificate's public key:
openssl x509 -in cert.pem -noout -pubkey | openssl pkey -pubin -outform DER \
  | openssl dgst -sha256 -binary | base64
# DANE record for a mail server (if published):
dig +dnssec TLSA _25._tcp.mail.example.org

docs.text: Name What it does Example HSTSRFC 6797 (2012) · RFC · Current · Web PKI HTTP Strict Transport Security: a header telling browsers to use only HTTPS for a domain and forbidding click-through on certificate errors. Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains makes browsers refuse plain HTTP to lumenbikes.example for a year. HSTS preload listChromium project (hstspreload.org) · Service · Current · Web PKI A list of HTTPS-only domains built into browsers, protecting even the first visit; needs one-year max-age, includeSubDomains and preload. Harbourview Bank preloads its domain so a first-time visitor on hostile Wi-Fi can never be downgraded to HTTP. HPKPRFC 7469 (2015) · RFC · Deprecated · Web PKI HTTP Public Key Pinning let websites pin SPKI hashes through a header; abandoned because mistakes or attackers could lock sites out for months. Chrome removed HPKP in version 72 (2019) after some sites locked themselves out by pinning keys they later lost. Expect-CTRFC 9163 (2022) · RFC · Deprecated · Web PKI A header letting sites demand Certificate Transparency compliance before browsers enforced CT; obsolete once CT became mandatory. Chrome deprecated Expect-CT in version 105 and removed it in 107 (2022), so sites can delete the header. Browser static pinsChromium and Firefox built-in lists · Concept · Current · Web PKI Pins compiled into browsers for a small number of high-value domains, restricting which CA keys may vouch for them. Chrome's static pins helped reveal the fraudulent DigiNotar certificate for google.com in 2011 when users hit pin violations. Application certificate pinningAndroid Network Security Config; iOS NSPinnedDomains · Concept · Current · Mobile Mobile or desktop apps accepting only specific CA or public keys for their back end, configured in code or platform settings. Lumen's app pins two SPKI hashes for keys the company controls and reuses across renewals, so frequent renewals never break logins. SPKI fingerprint (pin)Base64 SHA-256 of SubjectPublicKeyInfo · Concept · General A hash of a certificate's public-key structure; survives renewals that reuse the same key, unlike a whole-certificate fingerprint. openssl x509 -pubkey piped through openssl pkey and openssl dgst -sha256 -binary | base64 produces the pin value. DNSSECRFC 4033-4035 · Protocol · Current · General Signatures on DNS records chaining up to the DNS root key, letting resolvers detect forged answers; a prerequisite for DANE. mail.example.org's TLSA record is meaningful only because the zone is DNSSEC-signed and the sender's resolver validates it. DANERFC 6698, RFC 7671 · RFC · Current · General DNS-Based Authentication of Named Entities: publishing certificate or key hashes in DNSSEC-signed DNS so clients can authenticate TLS with or without CAs. A mail operator publishes a DANE-EE record, letting sending servers verify its self-issued certificate without any public CA. TLSA recordRFC 6698 · Format · Current · General The DNS record type for DANE: certificate usage (0-3), selector (full certificate or SPKI) and matching type (exact, SHA-256, SHA-512). _25._tcp.mail.example.org. IN TLSA 3 1 1 followed by a SHA-256 hash pins the mail server's key directly. DANE for SMTPRFC 7672 · RFC · Current · General Opportunistic DANE for mail transfer: DNSSEC-validating senders require TLS and a matching TLSA record, defeating downgrade and interception. Postfix with smtp_tls_security_level = dane refuses delivery to a DANE-protected domain if the certificate does not match. MTA-STSRFC 8461 · RFC · Current · Web PKI A Web-PKI-based alternative to DANE for email: a policy served over HTTPS tells senders to require valid TLS to the listed MX hosts. A company without DNSSEC publishes an mta-sts.txt policy in enforce mode, so major mail providers require TLS with a valid certificate.

docs.title: 6.13 Trust Stores: Who Decides Which Roots You Trust
docs.text:
A trust store is the list of root certificates a piece of software trusts as starting points. Your operating system, your browser, Java, Python and Android apps may each use a different store, maintained by a different organisation with its own rules. Whether a certificate is 'trusted' therefore depends on which software is asking.

One certificate, many trust stores. Root programs share disclosure data through CCADB, but each store is shipped and updated separately.

Think of it like…

Trust stores are like the lists of accepted foreign driving licences kept by different countries: the same licence is fine in one country and refused in another, depending on whose list the officer checks.

Real-world example

Bluefin Logistics deploys its private root through Group Policy, and Edge and Chrome on Windows immediately trust internal sites. But the Java warehouse service still fails, because it reads the JDK's cacerts; the Python reporting job fails, because requests uses certifi; and Firefox fails until IT enables enterprise roots. Kenji, the platform engineer, writes one runbook covering all five stores.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. A root program (Mozilla, Microsoft, Apple, Google Chrome, etc.) evaluates CAs against its policy and audits.
  2. Accepted roots, with trust bits and any distrust dates, are published and disclosed via CCADB.
  3. Vendors ship the store with the OS or browser and update it (Windows Update, OS releases, Chrome updates, Google Play system updates).
  4. Applications validate chains against the store they are configured to use — OS, browser or a bundled file.
  5. Administrators add private roots to the stores their software actually uses, or remove distrusted ones.

Who uses it

Platform and endpoint engineers, DevOps teams building container images, mobile developers, enterprise PKI administrators, and root-program and CA compliance staff.

Key takeaway

When a certificate is 'trusted on my laptop but not in the container', the answer is almost always a different trust store — check which store that runtime uses before anything else.

Going deeper

  • Mozilla's store (certdata.txt in NSS) has separate trust bits for websites and email and supports 'distrust after' dates; Debian/Ubuntu ca-certificates and RHEL's p11-kit-based ca-certificates are derived from it.
  • Windows downloads roots on demand: the local Cert:\LocalMachine\Root looks incomplete, while the full Microsoft list (authroot.stl) and the disallowed list (disallowedcert.stl) are fetched through Windows Update.
  • Chrome uses its own Chrome Root Store and verifier on most platforms since Chrome 105 (2022), but Apple's on iOS. Its late-2024 Entrust distrust (Chapter 60) used SCT dates to reject certificates issued after a cutoff.
  • Since Android 14 the system CA store lives in the updatable Conscrypt Mainline module, so Google can update roots via Google Play system updates; apps targeting API level 24+ ignore user-installed CAs unless their Network Security Config opts in.
  • Runtimes often bring their own stores: JDK cacerts (PKCS #12 since Java 9), Python certifi, Node.js's bundled Mozilla list, and minimal container images with stale or missing ca-certificates packages.
  • Root program policies — how roots get in, dedicated TLS hierarchies, the phase-out of multi-purpose roots and clientAuth, audits and distrust events — are covered in Chapter 60.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Adding a private root to Windows and expecting Java, Python, Node or Firefox to trust it automatically.
  • Shipping container images with an outdated ca-certificates package — new roots fail and distrusted ones stay trusted.
  • Assuming Windows' visible root list is the full Microsoft trust list — roots are fetched on demand.

docs.title: Try it: Count and list trusted roots in several stores
docs.text:
# Windows PowerShell
(Get-ChildItem Cert:\LocalMachine\Root).Count
certutil -store Root | findstr /c:"Subject:"
# Debian/Ubuntu and RHEL/Fedora
ls /etc/ssl/certs | head
trust list --filter=ca-anchors | grep -c 'label:'
# Java (press Enter at the password prompt to just list)
keytool -list -cacerts | head
# Python
python -c "import certifi; print(certifi.where())"

docs.text: Name What it does Example NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTSNode.js · Concept · Current · General A Node.js environment variable adding extra trusted roots to Node's bundled Mozilla-derived list, which ignores the OS store by default. Bluefin sets NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS=/etc/ssl/bluefin-root.pem so its Node.js services trust internal APIs signed by the private CA. Mozilla NSS root storeMozilla (certdata.txt) · Product · Current · Web PKI Mozilla's root list with separate trust bits for websites and email; used by Firefox and copied by most Linux distributions. Debian's ca-certificates package is generated from Mozilla's certdata.txt, so Mozilla decisions flow into millions of servers. Microsoft Trusted Root Program storeMicrosoft · Product · Current · Web PKI Windows' root store, updated automatically through Windows Update (authroot.stl); many roots are downloaded on demand when first needed. Get-ChildItem Cert:\LocalMachine\Root shows fewer roots than Microsoft trusts, because Windows fetches others only when a chain needs them. Apple trust storeApple Root Certificate Program · Product · Current · Web PKI The roots trusted by macOS, iOS, iPadOS, watchOS and tvOS, updated with OS releases and listed on Apple's support site. Safari and every iOS app using URLSession validate against Apple's store, which also enforces Apple's CT requirements. Chrome Root StoreGoogle Chrome Root Program · Product · Current · Web PKI Chrome's own root list and verifier, replacing OS stores on most platforms from Chrome 105 (2022); on iOS Chrome uses Apple's. When Chrome stopped trusting new Entrust certificates in late 2024, it acted through its own store, independent of Windows or macOS. CCADBCommon CA Database (Mozilla, Microsoft, Google, Apple) · Service · Current · Web PKI A shared database where public CAs disclose roots, intermediates, audits, CP/CPS documents and CRL URLs to several root programs. Firefox's intermediate preloading and CRLite both draw on CA data disclosed through CCADB. Java cacertsOpenJDK distributions · Product · Current · General The PKCS #12 trust store shipped with each JDK at lib/security/cacerts, separate from the OS store and managed with keytool. A Spring Boot service cannot call an internal API until the private root is imported into its container's cacerts. Linux ca-certificatesDebian/Ubuntu; Red Hat/Fedora with p11-kit · Software · Current · General Distribution packages building /etc/ssl/certs bundles from Mozilla's list, refreshed by update-ca-certificates (Debian) or update-ca-trust (RHEL). Kenji copies lab-root.crt into /usr/local/share/ca-certificates/ and runs update-ca-certificates so curl trusts his lab CA. Android system trust storeGoogle (Conscrypt Mainline module) · Product · Current · Mobile Android's system CA store; since Android 14 it lives in the Conscrypt module and can be updated through Google Play system updates. Apps targeting API 24 or later ignore user-installed CAs unless their Network Security Config opts in. certifiPython package (from Mozilla's list) · Library · Current · General A Python package bundling Mozilla's root list, used by requests and others instead of the OS store unless configured otherwise. A data scientist's script trusts the corporate proxy only after setting REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE or switching to the truststore package. Firefox enterprise rootsMozilla (security.enterprise_roots.enabled) · Concept · Current · Private PKI A Firefox setting, also enforceable by policy, that imports admin-added roots from the Windows or macOS store into Firefox's trust decisions. Bluefin's IT enables enterprise roots by policy so Firefox trusts the internal CA already pushed to Windows through Group Policy. Distrust-after dateMozilla NSS; Chrome Root Store · Concept · Web PKI Partial distrust where a root stays trusted only for certificates issued before a cutoff, so a CA can be phased out without breaking existing sites. NSS records a server-distrust-after date for a root; certificates issued after it fail in Firefox while older ones keep working. Trust bitsRoot store metadata · Concept · General Per-root flags limiting what a root is trusted for, such as server authentication, email protection or code signing. A root trusted by Mozilla for email but not websites cannot anchor a TLS chain in Firefox, even if its certificate looks valid.

docs.title: 6.14 Hands-On Certificate Tooling: openssl, certutil, keytool, step and crt.sh
docs.text:
A handful of tools let you inspect, create, convert and test certificates on your own machine. OpenSSL is the universal command-line toolkit; Windows has certutil; Java has keytool; cfssl and the step CLI offer friendlier output; crt.sh searches Certificate Transparency logs; and linters such as zlint check certificates against the rules. Knowing them turns certificate problems from mysteries into five-minute fixes.

The certificate toolbox. Pick the tool that matches the platform's own trust store and formats.

Think of it like…

These tools are a mechanic's diagnostic kit: a multimeter for every car (openssl), the manufacturer's own scanner (certutil, keytool), an easy-read dashboard (step, cfssl), and the national vehicle register you can search (crt.sh).

Real-world example

A Monday alert says the partner API is failing. Kenji runs openssl s_client -connect api.partner.example:443 -showcerts and sees only one certificate sent — the intermediate is missing. openssl x509 -enddate shows the leaf was renewed on Sunday. crt.sh confirms the new certificate came from a different CA hierarchy, and testssl.sh reports 'chain incomplete'. The partner adds the new intermediate and service resumes in minutes.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Fetch: openssl s_client (or step certificate inspect) shows exactly what the server sends.
  2. Read: openssl x509 -text, certutil -dump or keytool -printcert decode fields and extensions.
  3. Verify: openssl verify or certutil -verify -urlfetch walk the chain, revocation and purpose checks.
  4. Convert and package: openssl pkcs12, pkcs7, pkey and x509 -outform switch between formats.
  5. Investigate and lint: crt.sh and CT monitors show history; zlint and pkilint check rule compliance.

Who uses it

Every role that touches certificates: support engineers, SREs, sysadmins, PKI engineers, security analysts and students building home labs.

Key takeaway

Learn five OpenSSL commands by heart — x509 -text, req -new, s_client -showcerts, verify and pkcs12 — and you can handle most certificate tickets on any platform.

Going deeper

  • OpenSSL in late 2026: 3.0 and 1.1.1 are out of free support; 3.5 is the LTS line (to April 2030) with built-in ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA; 4.0 is newest. LibreSSL and BoringSSL are forks with different APIs.
  • openssl s_client sends SNI automatically from the -connect host since OpenSSL 1.1.1; add -servername to override, -showcerts for the chain, -status for a stapled OCSP response and -brief for a one-line summary.
  • Two different programs are called certutil: Microsoft's Windows tool (stores, CRLs, AD CS administration) and Mozilla NSS's certutil for NSS databases used by Firefox and some Linux services — check which one a guide means.
  • Public CAs widely run linters before signing; zlint (ZMap project, Go) covers RFC 5280, CA/B and root-program rules, and pkilint (DigiCert, Python) adds S/MIME BR and ETSI validators such as lint_cabf_smime_cert.
  • crt.sh, operated by Sectigo, exposes CT data through a web UI, JSON output and a public PostgreSQL interface; queries with % wildcards enumerate subdomains, which attackers also use, so assume public certificates reveal hostnames.
  • For labs, mkcert creates a local development CA and installs it in system and browser stores; Chapter 70 covers proper private CAs (step-ca, EJBCA, Vault) and ACME automation.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Pasting private keys or PKCS #12 files into online decoders — inspect locally; only public certificates are safe to share.
  • Trusting 'Verify return code: 20' from s_client on a machine whose OpenSSL has no CA bundle configured — point it at one with -CAfile or -CApath before concluding the site is broken.
  • Leaving a mkcert or lab root installed on a daily-use machine — anyone with that root's key can impersonate any site to you.

docs.title: Try it: A quick diagnostic toolkit session
docs.text:
openssl version   # 3.5 LTS or newer recommended
openssl x509 -in cert.pem -noout -subject -enddate -ext subjectAltName
step certificate inspect https://example.com --short
cfssl certinfo -domain example.com
certutil -verify -urlfetch server.cer          # Windows
keytool -printcert -sslserver example.com:443   # Java
zlint -pretty cert.pem

docs.title: Chapter 7: Root CAs, In Depth
docs.text: Root certificate authorities are the anchors of the web's trust: a few hundred offline keys, guarded in vaults and used in filmed ceremonies, decide which websites your browser believes. This chapter goes deep on how roots are designed, protected, audited, admitted to root stores, governed by the CA/Browser Forum and root programs, replaced, distrusted and prepared for the post-quantum era — with the 2025-2026 rule changes every PKI professional now needs to know.

docs.title: 7.1 What a Root CA Is and How CA Hierarchies Are Designed
docs.text:
A root CA is the certificate authority at the very top of a chain of certificates. Its certificate is self-signed — it vouches for itself — so nothing above it can prove it is genuine; instead, browsers and operating systems ship it pre-installed as a 'trust anchor'. Because everything below depends on it, the root's private key is kept offline and used rarely, and day-to-day signing is delegated to intermediate (issuing) CAs arranged in tiers.

A three-tier CA hierarchy. Only the bottom tier is online every day; each tier above is used less often and protected more strongly.

Think of it like…

A root CA is like a country's constitution: no higher law proves it valid, everyone simply agrees to accept it, and it is changed very rarely — ordinary laws (intermediate CAs) are made under its authority and do the daily work.

Real-world example

Amara, PKI architect at Northwind Bank (fictional), designs a two-tier hierarchy: an offline 'Northwind Root CA 2026' valid for 20 years and two online issuing CAs valid for 5 years — one for servers, one for staff smart cards. If the server issuing CA is ever compromised, she revokes only that intermediate and signs a replacement in a root ceremony; no laptop needs a new trust anchor. Public CAs such as Let's Encrypt use exactly the same pattern at internet scale.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The root generates a key pair inside an HSM and signs its own certificate (issuer = subject, cA=TRUE, keyCertSign and cRLSign).
  2. Root programs or administrators place that certificate in trust stores as a trust anchor.
  3. In a key ceremony the root signs certificates for policy or issuing CAs, optionally limited by EKU, name constraints or path length.
  4. Issuing CAs sign end-entity certificates online every day while the root goes back into the safe.
  5. A relying party builds a path from the leaf up to an anchor it already holds and checks every signature and constraint on the way.

Who uses it

PKI architects, public and private CA operators, security engineers designing enterprise or IoT PKI, and anyone debugging 'unable to get local issuer certificate' errors.

Key takeaway

Interview point: a root's self-signature proves nothing about trust — trust comes only from the decision to put it in a trust store — and public roots must never issue TLS server certificates directly.

Going deeper

  • The BR root profile is deliberately minimal: cA=TRUE and keyUsage (keyCertSign, cRLSign) both critical, a subjectKeyIdentifier, no extendedKeyUsage, and pathLenConstraint 'NOT RECOMMENDED' so future hierarchies stay flexible.
  • Every extra tier adds isolation (by policy, geography or purpose) but also adds bytes to each TLS handshake, another CRL to publish on time and more key ceremonies to run and audit.
  • Root programs now push dedicated hierarchies — one root per purpose such as TLS server, S/MIME or client authentication — because problems in one use case of a multi-purpose root force distrust of all of them.
  • Issuing CAs are rotated often: Chrome recommends sub-CAs valid for at most three years with new ones deployed yearly, and Let's Encrypt spreads issuance randomly across several intermediates so nobody hard-codes one.
  • Microsoft's root program requires a new key and a new subject name for every new root, because reusing either causes unpredictable chain building across Windows versions.
  • Private PKIs follow the same patterns with their own rules; enterprise specifics such as AD CS tiers and templates are covered in the PKI operations chapter, and X.509 field details in the PKI chapter.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Thinking a self-signed root is 'verified' by its own signature: the signature only proves the file is intact; trust comes entirely from the trust-store decision.
  • Issuing server certificates straight from the root to save effort: it forces the root online and breaks the BRs for public CAs.
  • Adding tiers 'for security' without a purpose: extra levels add handshake size, CRLs and ceremonies but no protection unless they enforce real separation.

docs.title: Try it: Inspect a root certificate from your own trust store
docs.text:
# Linux (Debian/Ubuntu)
openssl x509 -in /etc/ssl/certs/ISRG_Root_X1.pem -noout -subject -issuer -dates -ext basicConstraints,keyUsage
# Windows PowerShell
Get-ChildItem Cert:\LocalMachine\Root | Where-Object Subject -like '*ISRG*' | Format-List Subject, Issuer, NotAfter, Thumbprint

Under Chrome policy a sub-CA whose EKU excludes serverAuth needs only BR self-audits, because it cannot issue certificates Chrome trusts for TLS. Let's Encrypt's Gen Y intermediates expire on 2028-09-02, while its new Root YR is valid for twenty years. docs.title: 7.2 Offline Root Operations: Air Gaps, HSMs, Safes and M-of-N Control
docs.text:
An offline root is a root CA whose private key is never connected to a network. The key lives inside a hardware security module (HSM) — a tamper-resistant box that signs without ever revealing the key — and the HSM is locked in a safe inside a guarded room. To switch it on, several trusted people must each bring a smart card or key share, so no single person can use the root alone.

Defence in depth around a root key. An attacker must defeat every layer — and the quorum — before the HSM will sign anything.

Think of it like…

It is like a bank vault that needs two managers turning different keys at the same moment, inside a building with guards and cameras — and the vault is opened only a few times a year.

Real-world example

Harbor Trust (a fictional public CA) keeps its root HSM in a shielded room behind five layers of physical security. Activating it needs 3 of 7 smart cards, each held by a different officer and stored in its own numbered tamper-evident bag in a separate safe. A backup HSM holding the same key, protected by the same quorum, sits in another city 800 km away. The root is used about four times a year — to sign new intermediates and fresh CRLs.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Keep the root key only inside an HSM validated to FIPS 140-2/140-3 Level 3 or Common Criteria EAL 4+, marked non-exportable.
  2. Store the HSM and a dedicated network-less ceremony laptop in safes within a multi-zone secure room with logged, dual-person entry and CCTV.
  3. Split activation credentials M-of-N (for example 3 of 5 smart cards with PINs) across trusted-role holders with separated duties.
  4. Bring the root online only for scheduled ceremonies: signing intermediates, CRLs and occasional OCSP responder certificates.
  5. Keep encrypted, HSM-wrapped backups at a distant second site under the same quorum controls.
  6. Log every entry, seal number and signature; auditors review the records every year.

Who uses it

CA operations staff, HSM administrators, physical-security teams, auditors and PKI architects at public CAs, banks, governments and device manufacturers.

Key takeaway

Know the words: 'offline' means disconnected except during ceremonies, 'air-gapped' means physically and logically separated from all other systems, and BR 6.2.7 requires CA keys in FIPS 140 Level 3 or EAL 4+ hardware.

Going deeper

  • The CA/B Forum Network and Certificate System Security Requirements treat air-gapped systems separately, because patching, log shipping and monitoring work differently for systems that never touch a network.
  • HSM roles typically split into security officer (initialises and sets policy), crypto officer or user (uses keys) and auditor (reads logs); quorum card sets map onto these roles.
  • Root keys are generated with a non-exportable attribute; backups are made by wrapping under an HSM-internal key or cloning between HSMs in the same security domain — never as plaintext files.
  • Offline roots still have deadlines: BR CRLs covering CA certificates need a nextUpdate no more than 12 months after thisUpdate, and a new CRL within 24 hours of revoking a sub-CA.
  • FIPS 140-3 Level 3 adds identity-based authentication and active tamper response (zeroisation) beyond Level 2's tamper evidence; Level 4 adds environmental-attack protection and is rarely required for CAs.
  • Auditors test the physical story: they inspect access logs, CCTV retention, safe inventories and bag-number records, and sample past ceremonies end to end.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Believing 'offline' just means 'unplugged in a drawer': without quorum, logs and tamper evidence an offline key can still be stolen or misused unnoticed.
  • Keeping all M-of-N cards in one safe or with one team: the split only helps if no single person or place can reach the quorum.
  • Skipping the tested backup: one failed HSM without a quorum-protected copy means a new root and years of re-distributing trust.

With 3-of-5, two officers on holiday don't block a ceremony, but two colluding insiders still cannot activate the root. The script records bag #A1043 intact before opening and the new bag #A2217 after resealing; witnesses initial both numbers. Harbor's backup HSM in a second city can be activated only by the same 3-of-7 quorum as the primary. It boots a read-only Linux image whose SHA-256 hash is read aloud and checked against the script before every ceremony.

docs.title: 7.3 Key Ceremonies Step by Step
docs.text:
A key ceremony is a scripted, witnessed and recorded meeting in which a root CA's key is created or used. Every action — opening a safe, typing a command, signing a certificate — follows a written script, is checked off by witnesses and filmed, and an independent auditor confirms afterwards that nothing went off-script.

A root key generation ceremony. Every step is scripted, witnessed and filmed; the auditor's report is the output root programs care about.

Think of it like…

It is like a rocket-launch countdown: a checklist read aloud, each step confirmed by someone else, everything recorded — and any surprise means stopping, not improvising.

Real-world example

At 09:00 Kofi, Harbor Trust's ceremony administrator, reads step 1 of the 'Root R1 Generation' script: verify seal #A1043 on the HSM case. Two witnesses and a WebTrust auditor watch while cameras record. Over three hours the team initialises the HSM, generates an ECDSA P-384 root key, self-signs a 25-year root certificate, signs two intermediates and a first CRL, backs the key up to a second HSM and reseals everything. The auditor later issues the root key generation report that Chrome and Mozilla require for inclusion.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Prepare: write and peer-review the script, assign roles, pre-lint certificate profiles, verify software hashes and seal numbers.
  2. Open: check identities, record attendance, start video, retrieve the HSM, laptop and cards from their safes.
  3. Generate: initialise the HSM if new, generate the key pair inside it and self-sign the root certificate from the approved profile.
  4. Sign: issue intermediate CA certificates, the root CRL and any OCSP responder certificates — each linted before signing.
  5. Close: make quorum-protected backups, export only public artefacts, reseal everything and sign the log.
  6. Report: the auditor issues a key generation report; the CA publishes the new certificates and discloses them in the CCADB.

Who uses it

Ceremony administrators, security officers, HSM custodians, auditors (WebTrust practitioners and ETSI bodies), PKI architects, and teams running the DNSSEC root or enterprise roots.

Key takeaway

BR 6.1.1.1: for root keys a CA SHALL follow a key generation script, have a Qualified Auditor witness it or video the entire process, and obtain the auditor's report.

Going deeper

  • BR 6.1.1.1 also requires generation in a physically secured environment, by trusted-role staff under multiple-person control and split knowledge, inside suitable cryptographic modules, with every activity logged.
  • Chrome and Mozilla require fresh roots: inclusion requests are accepted only for root keys generated within five years, evidenced by an auditor's key generation report (Mozilla adds this rule from July 1, 2026).
  • If a root key is generated on one day but self-signed later, Chrome wants auditor evidence that the key was protected to BR section 6.2 standards for the whole gap.
  • Scripts pin the exact certificate profile — CSPRNG serial with at least 64 bits of entropy, validity, extensions — and teams lint test certificates with zlint or pkilint beforehand so the real signature holds no surprises.
  • Let's Encrypt's September 2025 ceremony generated two roots (Root YE and Root YR) and six intermediates in one session, plus cross-signatures from ISRG Root X2 and X1.
  • Good scripts expect trouble: they include branches for failed PINs, faulty media or power loss, and any unscripted action is logged as an exception for the auditor.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Improvising when something breaks: undocumented steps can invalidate the auditor's opinion and force a new ceremony with a brand-new key.
  • Treating video as optional: without a live qualified auditor or complete video, the BR evidence requirement fails and root programs will reject the key.
  • Signing unlinted profiles on the day: a wrong extension in a root or intermediate is permanent until that certificate is replaced.

docs.title: 7.4 CP, CPS (RFC 3647) and Policy OIDs
docs.text:
Every CA publishes rulebooks. The Certificate Policy (CP) states the rules certificates under it follow; the Certification Practice Statement (CPS) explains exactly how the CA carries them out, from identity checks to key protection. Both use the nine-chapter outline of RFC 3647, and certificates point to the policy they follow with an object identifier (OID).

RFC 3647: the nine sections of every CP/CPS. The BRs use the same numbering, so BR 6.1.1.1 and CPS 6.1.1.1 cover the same topic.

Think of it like…

The CP is like a national building code ('every building needs fire exits'); the CPS is one building's safety manual ('exits are at doors 3 and 7 and are tested every Monday').

Real-world example

Priya, a compliance analyst at Harbor Trust, updates CPS section 4.2.1 before March 15, 2026 so it says domain validation data is reused for at most 200 days, and bumps the version from 5.3 to 5.4 with a dated changelog entry. Auditors will test that staff really follow 5.4. When a website certificate shows policy OID 2.23.140.1.2.1, Priya knows it claims domain-validated issuance under the CA/B Forum Baseline Requirements.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Choose the governing policies (usually the CA/B Forum BRs plus the CA's own CP) and their OIDs.
  2. Write the CPS in RFC 3647's nine-section outline, mapping each requirement to a concrete practice.
  3. Publish it in the CA's repository and disclose it in the CCADB in the formats root programs ask for.
  4. Update it at least every year and whenever rules change, with a new version number and dated changelog.
  5. Assert the policy OIDs in sub-CA and subscriber certificates so relying parties and auditors can map certificates to rules.

Who uses it

CA compliance managers, PKI architects, auditors, root program reviewers and anyone writing the policy for an enterprise or government PKI.

Key takeaway

Memorise the CA/B Forum OIDs — 2.23.140.1.2.1 DV, 2.23.140.1.2.2 OV, 2.23.140.1.2.3 IV, 2.23.140.1.1 EV — and that RFC 3647 has nine sections.

Going deeper

  • The TLS BRs are themselves written in RFC 3647 format, and ballot SC-065 (2024) converted the EV Guidelines too, so section numbers line up across BRs, EV Guidelines and a CA's CPS.
  • Root programs reject CPS text that just says 'we comply with the BRs'; they expect specifics, such as which numbered domain validation methods (for example 3.2.2.4.7 DNS change or 3.2.2.4.19 ACME HTTP) the CA uses.
  • Policy OIDs matter most in government and bridge PKIs, where RFC 5280 path validation can require explicit policies and map one PKI's OIDs onto another's.
  • Version history is evidence: auditors and incident reviewers check which CPS version was in force on a given date, so CAs publish dated versions and redlines.
  • From December 1, 2025 the BRs also require CPS section 5.7.1 to assert a tested mass-revocation plan, showing how the CPS keeps absorbing new obligations.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Copying another CA's CPS: auditors test what you actually do, and every mismatch becomes a public incident.
  • Missing the annual update: BR 2.3 wants a new version within 365 days even if nothing changed.
  • Assuming an OID guarantees quality: an OV OID only claims a process was followed; trust still rests on audits and root-program oversight.

  | openssl x509 -noout -ext certificatePolicies

docs.title: 7.5 Root Programs and How a Root Gets Included
docs.text:
A root program is a browser or operating-system maker's rulebook and review team that decides which root CAs its products trust. Four dominate: Mozilla (Firefox, and indirectly most Linux systems), Apple (iOS and macOS), Microsoft (Windows) and Google's Chrome Root Program. A CA that wants a root trusted must apply, prove clean audits and good practices, survive review, and then wait for the root to reach billions of devices.

The CCADB connects CAs, auditors and root programs. One disclosure feeds four independent decisions — each program can still say no.

Think of it like…

Getting a root included is like a new airline winning landing rights: each country's aviation authority inspects its safety record separately, and losing rights in one country hurts the whole business.

Real-world example

Harbor Trust generated 'Harbor TLS Root R1' in 2026. It files a root inclusion request in the CCADB with its key generation report, audit reports, Markdown CP/CPS, test websites and ACME endpoint. Mozilla runs a public discussion; Chrome, Apple and Microsoft review separately. Approval takes over a year, and even then older phones and TVs won't know R1 — so Harbor buys a cross-signature from an established root to bridge the gap.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Generate a dedicated, fresh root (keys less than five years old when applying) in an audited ceremony.
  2. Operate under audit — readiness first, then period-of-time WebTrust or ETSI reports — with a published CP/CPS.
  3. Submit a Root Inclusion Request through the CCADB with audits, policies, test sites and automation evidence.
  4. Each program reviews independently; Mozilla adds a public discussion and every program examines incident history.
  5. Approved roots ship in trust-store updates: NSS, the Chrome Root Store, Apple OS updates and Microsoft's root list.
  6. Staying in means annual audits, CCADB disclosures, self-assessments and prompt public incident reports.

Who uses it

CA compliance teams, root program managers at Google, Mozilla, Apple and Microsoft, auditors, and researchers who watch CA behaviour in public forums.

Key takeaway

Since Chrome launched its own Chrome Root Store (2022, on Android since Chrome 114-115), 'trusted by Windows' no longer means 'trusted by Chrome' — check each program separately.

Going deeper

  • Chrome announced its root program in September 2022; Policy v1.8 (February 5, 2026) added 'one in, one out' replacements, a two-roots-per-owner cap from September 15, 2027, and automation duties for all existing CAs.
  • Mozilla is the most transparent program: inclusions, incident reports and distrust debates happen on public mailing lists and Bugzilla, which is one reason many downstream stores copy Mozilla's decisions.
  • Apple and Microsoft ship roots with OS updates; Windows also downloads roots on demand from Microsoft's certificate trust list and can mark certificates as disallowed or limit trust by date.
  • Root programs reward automation: Mozilla requires new TLS roots to demonstrate automated issuance with test certificates renewed at least every 30 days, and Chrome extends that to all included CAs from March 15, 2027.
  • Programs act independently: Chrome distrusted Chunghwa Telecom's new certificates in 2025, while Firefox adjusted trust only for an older Chunghwa root — outcomes can differ by browser.
  • Inclusion is slow, often more than a year from application to broad trust, which is why new CAs buy cross-signs or acquire existing root keys while they wait.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming one decision covers every browser: each program decides independently, and Chrome no longer relies on the operating system's store for TLS.
  • Thinking inclusion is permanent: roots are removed for age limits, policy changes or misbehaviour, often via an SCT-based cut-off.
  • Forgetting non-browser clients: Java, Android, embedded and IoT stores can lag browsers by years.

docs.title: 7.6 Root Program Rules 2025-2027: Dedicated Hierarchies, Term Limits and the End of clientAuth
docs.text:
Between 2025 and 2027 the big root programs rewrote the rules for public roots. Roots must now serve one purpose only (for example TLS servers or email, not both), can stay trusted for only about 15 years after their key was created, and public website certificates are losing the 'client authentication' purpose. CAs must also prove they can issue certificates automatically.

Root program changes, 2025-2028. Most deadlines fall on the 15th of a month, matching CA/B Forum habits — put them in your calendar.

Think of it like…

It is like a city ruling that every building has one purpose (homes or factories, never both), that buildings are rebuilt after 15 years, and that all deliveries must be automated.

Real-world example

Lena's company VPN authenticates laptops with public TLS certificates that include the clientAuth EKU. Her CA warns that Chrome's rules end clientAuth in public TLS hierarchies, and Let's Encrypt stopped issuing clientAuth certificates on July 8, 2026. Lena moves the VPN to a private CA. Meanwhile her web certificates move from USERTrust-chained roots to Sectigo Public Server Authentication Root R46 because Chrome set a June 15, 2026 cut-off for the older multi-purpose roots.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Dedicated hierarchies: new roots must serve a single purpose (Mozilla from March 15, 2025; Chrome for all applicants; Apple from August 1, 2026).
  2. EKU tightening in Chrome: sub-CAs disclosed from June 15, 2026 must be serverAuth-only; leaf certificates issued from March 15, 2027 must be serverAuth-only.
  3. Term limits: Chrome and Mozilla withdraw TLS trust from roots whose key material is over 15 years old, phased in from April 15, 2026.
  4. Fresh keys: new inclusion requests need root keys generated within the previous five years.
  5. Automation: by March 15, 2027 every TLS profile of a Chrome-trusted CA must be issuable through ACME or equivalent automation.
  6. Consolidation: from September 15, 2027 Chrome keeps at most two roots per CA owner.

Who uses it

CA product and compliance teams, engineers running VPN, Wi-Fi or mTLS on public certificates, IT admins handling root migrations, and security architects.

Key takeaway

If anything you run uses public TLS certificates for client authentication (mTLS, VPN, 802.1X), move it to a private CA — Chrome's rules remove clientAuth from public TLS hierarchies by March 15, 2027.

Going deeper

  • Chrome measures root age from the earlier of an auditor's key generation report or the first certificate containing that public key, so re-issuing a root certificate with a new date does not reset the clock.
  • Chrome's phase-in schedule: keys created 2006-2007 removed around April 15, 2026; 2008-2009 on April 15, 2027; 2010-2011 on April 15, 2028; January 2012-April 14, 2014 on April 15, 2029; later keys 15 years after generation.
  • The dedicated-hierarchy test is strict: a sub-CA must not share its public key with any other unexpired certificate asserting different EKUs, closing the trick of re-certifying one key for several purposes.
  • Chrome may keep a multi-purpose root without an SCTNotAfter case by case, but only if the CA owner had already requested inclusion of a replacement root before June 15, 2026.
  • Mozilla allowed dual-purpose roots to stay trusted past April 15, 2026 only if the CA filed a transition plan to dedicated hierarchies by that date, with completion by December 31, 2028.
  • For organisations the outcome is a clean split: public CAs for browser-facing TLS, private CAs for client authentication, Wi-Fi, VPN and device identity (see the PKI operations chapter).

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Treating a root's notAfter date as its trusted lifetime: term limits and distrust decisions can end trust years earlier.
  • Pinning a specific public root or intermediate in apps or devices: forced migrations such as G1 to G2 then break them.
  • Keeping public TLS certificates for client authentication: it relied on a side-effect root programs are deliberately removing.

docs.title: 7.7 The CA/Browser Forum and the Baseline Requirements
docs.text:
The CA/Browser Forum (CA/B Forum) is where certificate authorities and browser makers agree on common rules for public certificates. Its main rulebook, the TLS Baseline Requirements (BRs), says how CAs must check domains, what certificates must contain, how fast they must revoke and how they protect keys. Rules change through numbered 'ballots' that both CAs and browsers vote on.

How a CA/B Forum ballot becomes a rule. Many ballots carry future effective dates, so the BRs always contain a list of upcoming changes.

Think of it like…

It is like an international aviation body where airlines and airport operators vote on shared safety rules — while each country's regulator (the root programs) can still demand more and ground anyone.

Real-world example

Tomás, a junior engineer at a CA, is told 'we must implement SC-085 by March 15, 2026'. He looks it up: ballot SC-085 requires DNSSEC validation for CAA and domain-validation lookups. He reads BR section 1.2.2 'Relevant Dates', updates the resolver configuration, adds tests for SERVFAIL handling, and the compliance team updates CPS section 3.2.2.4. Much CA engineering work begins exactly like this — with a ballot number and an effective date.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. A member proposes a ballot with a redline against the BRs on GitHub and finds at least two endorsers.
  2. A discussion period of at least seven days is followed by a seven-day vote.
  3. It passes with at least two-thirds of voting certificate issuers (CAs) and more than half of voting certificate consumers (browsers), with quorum.
  4. After an intellectual-property review period the change takes effect, often with later compliance dates.
  5. Root programs enforce the BRs through audits and their own policies; any violation is a public incident.

Who uses it

CA engineers and compliance staff, browser root program teams, auditors, and engineers whose systems depend on certificate rules such as validation methods and lifetimes.

Key takeaway

Learn to read BR section 1.2.2 'Relevant Dates' — it lists every upcoming deadline — and know the key ballots: SC-081 (lifetimes), SC-067 (MPIC), SC-075 (linting), SC-085 (DNSSEC).

Going deeper

  • Voting has two classes — certificate issuers (CAs) and certificate consumers (browsers such as Apple, Google, Microsoft, Mozilla and Opera) — so browsers can block a change even if most CAs want it, and vice versa.
  • Landmark ballots: SC-062 (strict profiles, 2023), SC-063 (OCSP optional, CRLs required), SC-075 (linting), SC-067 (MPIC), SC-081 (lifetimes), SC-085 (DNSSEC), SC-089 (mass-revocation plans) and SC-097 (SHA-1 sunset from September 15, 2026).
  • Browsers can and do require more than the BRs: Chrome's automation, CT-before-issuance and dedicated-hierarchy rules are not in the BRs at all.
  • The BRs live on GitHub (cabforum/servercert), so every change is a pull request you can diff; BR 1.2.1 lists each ballot with its adoption and effective dates.
  • Linting is layered: mandatory pre-issuance linting of the tbsCertificate since March 15, 2025, plus recommended re-linting of the quarterly self-audit sample (at least 3% of issued certificates).
  • Short-lived subscriber certificates — at most 7 days for those issued from March 15, 2026 — are exempt from some revocation obligations, a deliberate incentive towards automation.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Thinking the CA/B Forum is a regulator: it has no enforcement power — root programs enforce the BRs by restricting or distrusting CAs.
  • Treating the BRs as best-practice advice: any deviation is misissuance or non-compliance and must be reported publicly.
  • Working from an old copy: the BRs change many times a year; always check the latest version and its 'Relevant Dates' table.

docs.title: 7.8 Issuance Rules for 2026-2029: SC-081 Lifetimes, DCV Reuse, MPIC and DNSSEC
docs.text:
Certificate lifetimes and domain checks are tightening on a fixed schedule. Ballot SC-081 cuts the maximum public TLS certificate lifetime from 398 days to 200 days (March 2026), 100 days (2027) and 47 days (2029), and limits how long a CA may reuse an earlier domain check. CAs must also confirm every domain check from several places on the internet (MPIC) and validate DNSSEC, making hijack-based mis-issuance much harder.

Maximum public TLS certificate lifetime over time. Each step forced more automation; the last bar is Let's Encrypt's optional short-lived profile.

Think of it like…

It is like airport security tightening: boarding passes expire sooner, your ID is re-checked more often, and officers in different terminals must all agree it is really you.

Real-world example

Kenji manages 400 certificates for an online retailer. On March 15, 2026 his CA's maximum dropped to 200 days, ending his yearly manual renewals, so he moved everything to ACME with ACME Renewal Information. Now, when he requests a certificate, the CA checks his DNS TXT record from its primary data centre and from remote perspectives in other regions at least 500 km apart; if too many disagree, issuance stops. By 2029 he expects renewals every month without anyone noticing.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Until March 14, 2026: maximum 398 days validity and up to 398 days of domain-validation reuse.
  2. From March 15, 2026: maximum 200 days; domain and IP validation reuse 200 days; organisation identity reuse 398 days.
  3. From March 15, 2027: maximum 100 days and 100 days of domain validation reuse.
  4. From March 15, 2029: maximum 47 days, and domain validation may be reused for only 10 days.
  5. MPIC: every domain validation and CAA check is corroborated by remote perspectives; too many disagreements block issuance.
  6. DNSSEC: from March 15, 2026 the primary perspective validates DNSSEC on validation and CAA lookups.

Who uses it

SREs, platform engineers, certificate-lifecycle owners, CA validation engineers, and anyone who owns certificates in production.

Key takeaway

Memorise '200/100/47 days on March 15 of 2026/2027/2029, with DCV reuse 200/100/10' — ballot SC-081v3, passed April 11, 2025.

Going deeper

  • SC-081v3 passed with 25 CAs in favour, none against, and all four major browser vendors voting yes — remarkable consensus after earlier lifetime ballots (such as SC-22 in 2019) failed.
  • Shorter lifetimes shrink the window in which a mis-issued certificate or stolen key is useful, because revocation checking is unreliable; they also force automation, which makes future algorithm changes such as post-quantum migration practical.
  • MPIC targets equally-specific BGP prefix hijacks: briefly hijacking the route to a server can fool one vantage point but not several in different regions; DNS resolvers used by a perspective must sit in its RIR region.
  • CAA corroboration evidence may be reused for up to 398 days, and the MPIC systems themselves sit outside audit scope, though the BRs list hardening expectations such as RPKI-validating networks.
  • Further dated changes: SHA-1 fully sunset in certificates and CRLs from September 15, 2026 (SC-097), and CAA accounturi/validationmethods processing from March 15, 2027 (SC-098).
  • Let's Encrypt made 160-hour certificates and IP-address certificates generally available in January 2026, selected through the 'shortlived' ACME profile.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Believing existing certificates break on the deadline: limits apply only to newly issued certificates.
  • Treating 47 days as a 2029 problem: DCV reuse falls to 10 days then, so any manual validation step must be automated well before.
  • Assuming MPIC makes DNS security irrelevant: an attacker who controls your authoritative DNS or registrar account fools every perspective — lock those accounts and use CAA with accounturi.
