docs.title: 9.3 IETF RFCs: The Protocols of PKI and Attestation
docs.text:
The IETF writes the RFCs that define how certificates, revocation, transparency, enrolment and attestation actually work on the internet. If NIST says what cryptography to use, the IETF says how to speak it over the wire.

The core PKI and attestation RFCs. A small set of RFCs underpins almost everything in this guide.

Think of it like…

If NIST writes the dictionary of approved words, the IETF writes the grammar and the postal rules: how to format a certificate, how to ask if one is revoked, and how to request a new one, so independent software can hold a conversation.

Real-world example

A developer building a certificate tool keeps a shelf of RFCs open: RFC 5280 for what a valid X.509 certificate looks like, RFC 6960 for OCSP revocation checks, RFC 8555 for ACME issuance, and RFC 9334 for the attestation architecture their device-health feature uses.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. An idea becomes an internet-draft in a working group (e.g. LAMPS for PKI, RATS for attestation).
  2. The group refines it through review and running-code interoperability.
  3. The IESG approves it and it is published as a numbered RFC.
  4. Implementers build to the RFC; later RFCs update or obsolete earlier ones.
  5. Reading the exact RFC is how you resolve disputes about correct behaviour.

Who uses it

Protocol and PKI engineers, security-tool developers, and anyone who must implement certificate or attestation behaviour correctly.

Key takeaway

Learn the headline numbers: 5280 (X.509 profile), 6960 (OCSP), 6962 and 9162 (Certificate Transparency), 8555 (ACME), 9334 (RATS attestation) and 3647 (CP/CPS format). They recur in interviews and documentation.

Going deeper

  • RFC 5280 is the internet profile of X.509: it defines which fields and extensions are valid and the path-validation algorithm every certificate verifier implements.
  • Revocation and transparency: RFC 6960 defines OCSP, while Certificate Transparency runs on RFC 6962; RFC 9162 (CT 2.0, 2021) was published but browsers never adopted it, and logs now also use the static-CT API (Sunlight, Tessera).
  • Enrolment lives in several RFCs: 8555 (ACME) and 9773 (ACME Renewal Information), 7030 (EST), 8894 (SCEP) and 9810/9811 (the updated CMP), covering web and device issuance.
  • The RATS working group produced RFC 9334 (the remote attestation architecture of attester, verifier and relying party) and RFC 9711 (Entity Attestation Token), the backbone of modern attestation.
  • Post-quantum PKI is arriving as RFCs too: RFC 9881 (2025) defines ML-DSA in certificates and RFC 9935 (2026) defines ML-KEM in certificates, from the LAMPS working group.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Citing an obsoleted RFC: CMP's current core is RFC 9810, not RFC 4210, and Certificate Transparency's modern spec is RFC 9162 alongside 6962.
  • Assuming an RFC describes a law or a product; it describes a protocol, and real deployments add their own policy on top.
  • Reading summaries instead of the RFC when behaviour is disputed — the normative 'MUST/SHOULD' wording in the document is what counts.

docs.title: 9.4 ISO/IEC, Common Criteria and ETSI
docs.text:
Outside the US-centric NIST world, international and European bodies write the standards that let products be certified and trusted across borders. ISO/IEC publishes global standards, Common Criteria evaluates security products, and ETSI writes the European rules behind electronic signatures and trust services.

Who writes what, and the US equivalent

Covers US counterpart ISO/IEC 11889 TPM 2.0 library TCG spec ISO/IEC 19790 crypto modules FIPS 140-3 ISO/IEC 15408 product evaluation Common Criteria ETSI EN 319 411 trust-service policy WebTrust (analogous)

International and European standards often mirror NIST documents.

Think of it like…

These are like international safety-rating schemes for cars: ISO sets the global specifications, Common Criteria is the independent crash-test lab, and ETSI writes the European road rules that say which rated cars are allowed on the motorway.

Real-world example

A European trust-service provider, Aegis TSP, must meet ETSI EN 319 411 to issue qualified certificates recognised across the EU. Its HSMs carry Common Criteria certificates, and it points to ISO/IEC 19790 and 11889 to show its modules and TPMs meet global baselines.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. ISO/IEC JTC 1 publishes global standards (e.g. 11889 for TPM, 19790 for crypto modules, 15408 for evaluation).
  2. Common Criteria (ISO/IEC 15408) evaluates products against protection profiles at assurance levels (EAL1-7).
  3. ETSI writes European standards for trust services, signatures and their formats.
  4. Auditors and certification bodies assess products and services against these.
  5. Regulators (like eIDAS) reference them to grant legal recognition.

Who uses it

Product-security and certification engineers, HSM and smart-card vendors, qualified trust-service providers and EU-market compliance teams.

Key takeaway

Map the equivalents: ISO/IEC 19790 is the international sibling of FIPS 140-3, ISO/IEC 11889 is the TPM 2.0 library, and ISO/IEC 15408 is Common Criteria — knowing the number-to-name mapping impresses interviewers.

Going deeper

  • ISO/IEC 15408 (Common Criteria) evaluates products against a Protection Profile at Evaluation Assurance Levels EAL1-7; TPMs, smart cards and HSMs commonly carry CC certificates, and the EU's EUCC scheme is replacing national schemes.
  • ISO/IEC 19790:2025 (third edition) is the international standard for cryptographic-module security that FIPS 140-3 is harmonised with, so a module can map one evaluation to both worlds.
  • ISO/IEC 11889 is simply the TPM 2.0 library specification published as an international standard, which is why government procurements can require 'ISO/IEC 11889 TPMs'.
  • ETSI's EN 319 4xx series governs European trust-service providers: EN 319 411 sets policy requirements for issuing certificates, and the EN 319 1xx series defines the AdES signature formats (PAdES, XAdES, CAdES).
  • ETSI standards are the technical backbone of eIDAS: a qualified trust-service provider is audited against them, which is what gives a qualified electronic signature its legal weight across the EU.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming a high EAL number means 'more secure' in general; it means more thoroughly evaluated against a specific protection profile, which is not the same thing.
  • Treating FIPS 140-3 and ISO/IEC 19790 as unrelated; they are deliberately harmonised, so a module is often evaluated once for both.
  • Confusing ETSI (European technical standards) with eIDAS (the EU law that references them) — the standards are the 'how', the regulation is the 'must'.

docs.title: 9.5 Industry Bodies: DMTF SPDM, OCP, GlobalPlatform, CA/B Forum
docs.text:
Beyond the big standards agencies, industry consortia solve specific problems: how components attest to each other inside a server, how data-centre hardware is secured, how secure elements run applets, and what rules public CAs must follow. These bodies shape day-to-day practice.

Industry bodies and their domains. Each consortium owns a practical slice of the trust landscape.

Think of it like…

If NIST and ISO are the national governments, these are the trade associations: the one that agrees how car parts plug together, the one that sets rules for the taxi trade, each solving a practical problem the big bodies leave open.

Real-world example

A server maker, Cindermoor Systems, uses DMTF SPDM so its BMC can verify each component's firmware, follows OCP security guidelines for the chassis design, builds its secure element to GlobalPlatform specs, and ships TLS certificates that comply with the CA/Browser Forum Baseline Requirements.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. DMTF defines SPDM, the protocol components use to authenticate and measure each other.
  2. The Open Compute Project (OCP) publishes open hardware and security specifications for data-centre gear.
  3. GlobalPlatform standardises secure elements, TEEs and how applets are managed on them.
  4. The CA/Browser Forum writes the Baseline Requirements that public CAs must follow.
  5. Vendors implement these so parts, platforms and certificates interoperate and are trusted.

Who uses it

Hardware and firmware security engineers, data-centre and server designers, secure-element developers and public-CA compliance teams.

Key takeaway

Know each body's one job: DMTF = SPDM (component attestation), OCP = open data-centre hardware security, GlobalPlatform = secure elements and TEEs, CA/Browser Forum = public-TLS rules. One line each is enough for interviews.

Going deeper

  • DMTF's SPDM (Security Protocol and Data Model, DSP0274) lets a device like a BMC authenticate a component, retrieve its certificates and read firmware measurements; version 1.4 arrived in 2025, extending session and attestation features.
  • The Open Compute Project drives open server security: Project Cerberus (a hardware root of trust for firmware), DC-SCM modular management, and Caliptra, an open silicon RoT block adopted across the industry.
  • GlobalPlatform standardises how secure elements and TEEs are structured and how applications are loaded and managed, underpinning SIMs, payment chips and mobile trusted applications.
  • The CA/Browser Forum is not a government but its Baseline Requirements are effectively mandatory, because browser root programs require compliance; it is where ballots like the SC-081 lifetime reduction and CSC-31 code-signing change are decided.
  • The Connectivity Standards Alliance (Matter) and FIDO Alliance (passkeys, device onboarding) are further industry bodies whose specifications define device and authentication trust at consumer scale.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Thinking the CA/Browser Forum can force a CA to comply; its leverage is indirect — browser root programs enforce the rules by threatening removal from trust stores.
  • Confusing SPDM (how components attest inside a platform) with RATS (the IETF architecture for remote attestation); they operate at different layers.
  • Assuming OCP is only about cheap hardware; its security projects (Cerberus, Caliptra) are serious roots of trust used by hyperscalers.

docs.title: 9.6 Regulations Driving Roots of Trust and PKI
docs.text:
Increasingly, the law requires the things this guide describes. New regulations demand secure-by-design products, post-quantum readiness, digital identity wallets and PKI for whole industries. Knowing them tells you why organisations suddenly care about trust.

Regulatory deadlines shaping trust. A cluster of mandates land across 2026-2030.

Think of it like…

Regulations are like seatbelt and emissions laws for software: once optional good practice, now legally required, with deadlines and penalties that turn 'we should' into 'we must by this date'.

Real-world example

A European IoT maker, Voltaire Devices, must meet the EU Cyber Resilience Act: from September 2026 it reports exploited vulnerabilities within 24 hours, and from December 2027 its products need secure-by-design features, an SBOM and CE marking. Separately, US federal buyers now expect post-quantum-ready products under Executive Order 14306.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. A regulator identifies a risk (insecure products, quantum threat, weak digital identity).
  2. It publishes a law with scope, requirements and staged deadlines.
  3. Standards bodies' specifications become the practical way to comply.
  4. Vendors and operators implement roots of trust, PKI or attestation to meet them.
  5. Audits, market surveillance or procurement rules enforce compliance.

Who uses it

Product-security leads, compliance and legal teams, PKI architects and anyone selling into the EU, US federal or regulated markets.

Key takeaway

Have two or three dates ready: EU CRA reporting from 11 September 2026 and full application 11 December 2027; EU member states must offer an EUDI Wallet by late 2026; US EO 14306 pushes TLS 1.3 and PQC readiness. Dates show you follow the field.

Going deeper

  • The EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) mandates secure-by-design for products with digital elements: vulnerability-reporting obligations apply from 11 September 2026 and the full requirements (SBOMs, update support, CE marking) from 11 December 2027, pushing hardware roots of trust and signed updates into mainstream products.
  • eIDAS 2.0 (Regulation (EU) 2024/1183) creates the European Digital Identity Wallet; member states must make a certified EUDI Wallet available to citizens by late 2026, built on PKI and qualified trust services.
  • US Executive Order 14306 (June 2025) directed CISA to publish PQC-ready product categories (released January 2026) and agencies to support TLS 1.3 by January 2030, while CNSA 2.0 sets the deeper national-security PQC timeline.
  • Sector rules add PKI requirements: PCI DSS v4 tightens key and certificate management for payments, UNECE R155 with ISO/SAE 21434 mandates cybersecurity management (and effectively PKI) for new vehicles, and FDA guidance requires an SBOM and secure updates for medical devices.
  • National PKIs are legally anchored too: India's CCA under the IT Act licenses certifying authorities, and government bridge PKIs (US Federal PKI, DoD PKI) set requirements for anyone transacting with them.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Treating the CRA as only about reporting: the heavier secure-by-design and SBOM obligations arrive in December 2027 and need design changes started now.
  • Assuming post-quantum mandates are far off; US procurement already references PQC readiness, so products specified today may be rejected tomorrow if they cannot migrate.
  • Thinking regulations and standards are the same thing — the regulation sets the legal 'must', while an ETSI or NIST standard is the practical 'how' you point to for compliance.

docs.title: 9.7 A Timeline of Trust: Incidents That Shaped the Field
docs.text:
The rules we follow today were written in the ashes of real failures. Understanding the big incidents in hardware trust and PKI explains why offline roots, transparency logs and firmware resiliency exist, and gives you concrete stories to tell in interviews.

Milestone incidents in trust. Each entry changed a rule or created a new defence.

Think of it like…

It is like learning aviation safety through famous crashes: each disaster led to a new rule, and knowing the crash explains why the rule exists far better than memorising the rule alone.

Real-world example

In an interview, Jordan is asked why Certificate Transparency exists. Instead of reciting the spec, he tells the DigiNotar story: in 2011 a Dutch CA was breached and issued a fraudulent Google certificate used to spy on Iranian users. The industry's answer, over time, was public logs so no certificate is issued in secret.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. A trust component fails: a CA is breached, a key leaks, or firmware is subverted.
  2. Real harm follows: interception, mass device compromise, or loss of trust.
  3. Investigators trace the root cause and the industry debates a fix.
  4. A new control emerges: transparency, distrust, resiliency requirements.
  5. The lesson is baked into standards so the same failure is harder to repeat.

Who uses it

Everyone in the field; these stories are the shared memory of platform-security and PKI professionals and common interview fodder.

Key takeaway

Have one incident ready per theme: DigiNotar for CA breach and CT, Symantec for mis-issuance and distrust, Heartbleed for key exposure, BlackLotus for secure-boot bypass, and the Infineon ROCA flaw for weak key generation.

Going deeper

  • DigiNotar (2011): a compromised Dutch CA issued fraudulent certificates for Google and others, used to intercept Iranian users; the CA was distrusted and went bankrupt, and the episode drove Certificate Transparency.
  • The Symantec distrust (2017-2018): years of mis-issuance led browsers to progressively distrust Symantec's huge certificate estate, forcing mass reissuance and ultimately the sale of that business to DigiCert.
  • Heartbleed (2014): an OpenSSL bug let attackers read server memory, potentially leaking private keys, triggering a global wave of certificate revocation and reissuance and hardening how keys are handled.
  • ROCA (2017): a flaw in Infineon's RSA key generation weakened keys in TPMs, smart cards and ID documents, showing that even hardware-generated keys can be systematically broken and must be scrutinised.
  • Firmware and boot incidents (LoJax 2018, BootHole 2020, BlackLotus 2023, LogoFAIL and PKfail 2024) repeatedly bypassed or undermined secure boot, driving dbx updates, the Secure Boot certificate refresh of 2026 and NIST SP 800-193 resiliency.
  • More recent CA distrusts (Entrust's TLS business exiting the public trust story in 2024, with its public-certificate operations moving to Sectigo) show the root-program enforcement model still bites in the 2020s.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Memorising incident names without the lesson; the point is why each one changed practice, not the trivia.
  • Assuming these are ancient history — firmware bootkits and CA distrusts kept happening into the mid-2020s, so the field is still learning.
  • Blaming only the breached organisation; most incidents expose a systemic weakness the whole ecosystem then has to fix.

docs.title: 9.8 Careers in Platform Security and PKI
docs.text:
The skills in this guide map to real, well-paid jobs. From firmware security to PKI architecture to CA compliance, organisations need people who understand how trust is built and protected. This section describes the main roles and what each actually does day to day.

A career map in trust. Common entry points lead into three deepening specialist tracks.

Think of it like…

Think of a cathedral: some people quarry and shape the foundation stones (firmware/silicon security), some design the arches that carry the load (PKI architects), and some inspect that it was all built to code (CA auditors). The building needs all of them.

Real-world example

After studying this guide, Amina applies for a PKI engineer role. The job is exactly what she learned: run the internal CA, automate certificate renewal with ACME, keep keys in the HSM, and help teams migrate off expiring certificates. A firmware-security role her classmate takes instead focuses on secure boot and chip RoTs.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Entry roles (SOC analyst, junior sysadmin, IT security) build the fundamentals.
  2. Specialise toward a track: firmware/platform, PKI/crypto, or product security.
  3. Deepen with hands-on work: run a CA, break and fix a boot chain, operate an HSM.
  4. Grow into architect or lead roles designing trust across an organisation.
  5. Or move into assurance: CA compliance, auditing, and standards work.

Who uses it

Students and career-changers planning a path, and managers mapping skills to roles in security teams.

Key takeaway

PKI and platform-security skills are scarce and sticky: few people understand them deeply, the work is foundational, and the knowledge transfers across employers, which makes these durable, recession-resistant careers.

Going deeper

  • A PKI engineer runs the certificate machinery: operating CAs, automating issuance and renewal, managing HSMs and keeping services from expiring; a PKI architect designs the hierarchies, policies and lifecycle strategy across the organisation.
  • Firmware and platform-security engineers work close to the metal: secure and measured boot, TPM and RoT integration, firmware signing and resiliency, often in C and assembly with vendor toolchains.
  • HSM and cryptography engineers specialise in key management, PKCS #11/KMIP integration, FIPS 140-3 compliance and increasingly post-quantum migration.
  • Product-security engineers embed trust into products: threat modelling, secure boot, device identity and attestation, now shaped heavily by regulations like the EU CRA.
  • CA compliance and audit roles ensure a CA meets WebTrust/ETSI and root-program rules; this assurance track blends deep PKI knowledge with policy and audit skills and is in short supply.
  • Demand is driven by shrinking certificate lifetimes, machine-identity growth, confidential computing and the post-quantum migration, all of which need people who understand trust end to end.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Chasing job titles over substance; 'security engineer' means very different things, so read what the role actually does with trust and certificates.
  • Believing you must start in cryptography research — most trust jobs are engineering and operations, reachable from a sysadmin or SOC background.
  • Neglecting the soft skills: PKI and firmware work means writing policy, explaining risk to non-experts, and careful change control, not just code.

docs.title: 9.9 Certifications Worth Your Time
docs.text:
Certifications can open doors, prove a baseline, and structure your learning. Some are broad security credentials employers recognise everywhere; others are specialist PKI, HSM or cloud certificates that signal deep expertise. Choose by career stage and goal.

Certifications by stage and focus

Broad Specialist Entry CompTIA Security+ vendor fundamentals Mid CISSP, CCSP GIAC (GSEC/GPEN) Deep CISM (management) HSM/PKI vendor courses Proof degree/apprenticeship homelab + open source

Match the credential to where you are and where you want to go.

Think of it like…

Certifications are like belts in martial arts: a white belt (Security+) shows you have started properly, higher belts (CISSP, GIAC) show breadth and depth, and specialist badges (vendor PKI/HSM courses) show you have trained in one discipline.

Real-world example

Starting out, Sam earns CompTIA Security+ to get past HR filters and prove the fundamentals. A year into a PKI role, Sam takes a vendor certificate-management course and a cloud security credential, which together signal the specific skills employers in that niche actually want.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Early career: a broad foundation like CompTIA Security+ gets you shortlisted.
  2. Mid career: CISSP or GIAC credentials prove breadth and seniority.
  3. Specialise: vendor PKI, HSM and cloud-security certificates show depth.
  4. Keep them current: most require continuing education or renewal.
  5. Pair certs with hands-on proof (a lab, a homelab CA, open-source contributions).

Who uses it

Students, career-changers and professionals deciding where to spend limited study time and money.

Key takeaway

A current detail: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 has been the live exam since 2023, with SY0-801 launching around November 2026 adding AI and LLM content, so check which version you are studying before you book.

Going deeper

  • CompTIA Security+ is the common entry credential: vendor-neutral, HR-recognised, and a structured way to learn fundamentals; SY0-701 is current, with SY0-801 arriving around November 2026 and adding AI/LLM security topics.
  • (ISC)²'s CISSP is the broad senior benchmark (requiring experience), and CCSP its cloud-security equivalent; CISM (ISACA) targets security management rather than hands-on work.
  • GIAC certifications (from SANS) are respected, hands-on and specialised (GSEC foundational, GPEN for testing, GDSA for defence) but are expensive, so they often suit those with employer sponsorship.
  • Vendor and product training is where PKI depth lives: Keyfactor, DigiCert and Idira (formerly CyberArk/Venafi) run certificate-management courses, Thales and Entrust run HSM training, and Microsoft learning paths cover AD CS and Intune Cloud PKI.
  • Cloud providers' security certifications (AWS, Azure, Google) increasingly include KMS, HSM and private-CA content, which is valuable given how much PKI now runs as cloud services.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Collecting certificates with no hands-on experience; employers quickly spot a 'paper' candidate who has never operated a CA or HSM.
  • Booking the wrong exam version — Security+ is mid-transition from SY0-701 to SY0-801 around 2026, so confirm the objectives you are studying.
  • Assuming CISSP is an entry cert; it requires several years of experience, so it is a mid-career goal, not a starting point.

docs.title: 9.10 Learning Resources: Books, Specs, Blogs and Courses
docs.text:
You do not have to learn this field alone or only from specifications. A handful of books, free courses, well-run blogs and the primary specs themselves will take you a long way. This section points you to the resources practitioners actually recommend.

How to layer your learning. Build the model, make it hands-on, then go to the source.

Think of it like…

It is like a reading list from a trusted mentor: not every book ever written, but the few that repay the time, plus where to go when you need the authoritative answer and who to follow to stay current.

Real-world example

Priya builds her knowledge in layers: she reads 'Bulletproof TLS and PKI' for the big picture, keeps 'A Practical Guide to TPM 2.0' open while coding against a TPM, takes the free OST2 TPM course for hands-on practice, and follows a few CA and firmware blogs to track the fast-moving changes.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Start with a readable book to build the mental model.
  2. Use a hands-on course to turn reading into skill.
  3. Keep the primary specs nearby for authoritative detail.
  4. Follow a few high-signal blogs and mailing lists to stay current.
  5. Practise in a lab as you go, because trust is learned by doing.

Who uses it

Self-learners, students and professionals assembling a study path that mixes theory, practice and current awareness.

Key takeaway

Two books anchor the field: Ivan Ristić's 'Bulletproof TLS and PKI' for certificates and TLS, and 'A Practical Guide to TPM 2.0' (free from Apress) for TPMs. Start there before diving into specs.

Going deeper

  • 'Bulletproof TLS and PKI' (Ivan Ristić) is the standard practical reference for TLS and certificates, updated regularly, and pairs well with the author's SSL Labs test tooling.
  • 'A Practical Guide to TPM 2.0' (Arthur, Challener, Goldman) is a free, approachable book on TPM concepts and programming, ideal alongside tpm2-tools experimentation.
  • OpenSecurityTraining2 (OST2), a non-profit, offers free hands-on courses, and with the TCG runs a Trusted Computing track (TC1101 introductory TPM usage, TC1103 advanced/FAPI, TC2202 Python with tpm2-pytss).
  • Primary specs are worth reading directly: the RFCs for PKI, the TCG TPM documents, the CA/Browser Forum Baseline Requirements, and NIST FIPS/SP publications, all freely available.
  • High-signal blogs and lists track the fast-moving parts: the mozilla.dev.security.policy forum for CA incidents, root-program announcements from Google/Mozilla/Apple/Microsoft, and firmware-security researchers' write-ups keep you current on distrusts and vulnerabilities.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Reading only specifications first; they are precise but dense, and a book or course builds the model that makes the specs make sense.
  • Trusting outdated material in such a fast field — certificate lifetimes, CMP RFC numbers and product names have all changed recently, so check the date on everything.
  • Consuming passively without a lab; trust concepts stick only when you have actually broken and fixed a boot chain or issued a certificate.

docs.title: 9.11 A Hands-On Lab Plan You Can Build at Home
docs.text:
Trust is learned by doing. With a laptop, some free software and virtual machines, you can simulate a TPM, build your own CA, enrol secure-boot keys, run an attestation service and issue real certificates. This is the single best way to become job-ready.

The home-lab journey. Each lab maps to a chapter and builds on the last.

Think of it like…

Reading about swimming teaches you nothing until you get in the pool. These labs are your pool: safe, repeatable, and the fastest route from understanding trust to actually being able to operate it.

Real-world example

Over a few weekends, Diego works the plan on his laptop: he runs a software TPM with swtpm and reads PCRs with tpm2-tools, builds a two-tier CA with step-ca, enrols Secure Boot keys in a QEMU VM, runs Keylime for attestation, issues ACME certificates, and inspects real certificates in CT logs. Each lab makes a chapter of this guide concrete.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Set up a Linux VM or spare machine as your lab, with virtualisation enabled.
  2. Simulate a TPM with swtpm and explore it using tpm2-tools.
  3. Build a two-tier CA with OpenSSL or step-ca and issue certificates.
  4. Experiment with Secure Boot keys (PK/KEK/db) in a throwaway VM.
  5. Run an attestation service (Keylime) and issue certificates over ACME.
  6. Inspect real-world certificates and CT logs to connect lab to reality.

Who uses it

Students and self-learners turning this guide into demonstrable skills, and anyone preparing for interviews.

Key takeaway

Everything here is free and runs on a laptop; do it in VMs so mistakes cost nothing. A homelab you can talk through in detail beats another certificate on your CV.

Going deeper

  • swtpm plus libtpms gives a full software TPM 2.0 you can attach to QEMU/KVM VMs, so you can practise sealing, quotes and PCR policies without any hardware; tpm2-tools and tpm2-pytss drive it.
  • Building a two-tier CA by hand with OpenSSL teaches the mechanics (key generation, CSRs, extensions, signing, CRLs), while step-ca shows the automated, ACME-driven way the same thing is done in production.
  • A QEMU/OVMF VM lets you enrol your own Secure Boot PK, KEK and db keys with tools like sbctl and efitools, sign a kernel, and watch boot succeed or fail, making secure boot tangible and reversible.
  • Keylime provides a real remote-attestation lab: a verifier checks a VM's TPM quote against expected PCRs and the event log, demonstrating the RATS attester/verifier/relying-party model end to end.
  • Finishing with ACME issuance (certbot or step against a local CA) and CT-log inspection on crt.sh ties the labs back to the live internet you use every day.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Doing Secure Boot experiments on your real machine; use a VM, because enrolling the wrong keys on bare metal can stop it booting.
  • Skipping the manual OpenSSL CA and jumping straight to a tool, so you never learn what the tool is actually doing underneath.
  • Treating labs as one-and-done; rebuild them from scratch until the commands are second nature, because that fluency is what interviews probe.

docs.title: Try it: Start a software TPM and read its PCRs
docs.text:
# Start a simulated TPM:
swtpm socket --tpm2 --tpmstate dir=/tmp/mytpm \
  --ctrl type=tcp,port=2322 --server type=tcp,port=2321 &
# Point tpm2-tools at it and read PCR banks:
export TPM2TOOLS_TCTI="swtpm:port=2321"
tpm2_pcrread sha256:0,7

docs.title: 9.12 Interview Questions With Model Answers
docs.text:
Interviews for trust and PKI roles return to a core set of concepts again and again. If you can answer these clearly, in plain language, with a real example, you will stand out. Here are common questions and the shape of a strong answer.

How to answer a trust interview question. A repeatable structure that works for nearly every concept question.

Think of it like…

It is like knowing the scales before a music audition: the examiners will ask you to play them in some form, and fluency frees you to show the musicality — here, the judgement and clarity that mark a good engineer.

Real-world example

Asked 'what is the difference between secure boot and measured boot?', Maya answers crisply: secure boot refuses to run unsigned code, measured boot records a hash of each stage into TPM PCRs so a verifier can later check what ran. She adds that they are complementary and often used together, which earns a nod.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Listen for which concept the question targets and answer that directly first.
  2. Give the one-sentence definition in plain language.
  3. Add a concrete example or the 'why it matters'.
  4. Mention a real detail (a standard, an incident) to show depth.
  5. Stop; a tight answer beats rambling, and invites a good follow-up.

Who uses it

Anyone preparing for platform-security, PKI, firmware or product-security interviews, and mentors coaching them.

Key takeaway

For almost every question, the winning structure is: plain definition, then why it matters, then one real example. Interviewers are testing whether you understand, not whether you can recite.

Going deeper

  • 'Why keep a root CA offline?' Because its key is the ultimate trust anchor; if stolen, every certificate it ever signed is suspect. It lives in an HSM, offline, used only in witnessed ceremonies to sign intermediates, which do the daily work.
  • 'How does a TPM protect a disk-encryption key?' It seals the key to expected PCR values; the key only unseals if the measured boot state matches, so tampering with firmware or the boot chain leaves the disk locked.
  • 'What is Certificate Transparency and why does it exist?' Public append-only logs of issued certificates, with SCTs proving inclusion, created after CA breaches like DigiNotar so mis-issuance can be detected rather than hidden.
  • 'How does ACME prove you control a domain?' The client answers a challenge: serving a file (HTTP-01), publishing a DNS TXT record (DNS-01) or a TLS-ALPN response, validated by the CA from multiple vantage points before issuing.
  • 'Why are certificate lifetimes shrinking?' Shorter lifetimes limit the damage from a compromised or mis-issued certificate and reduce reliance on revocation; the public TLS ceiling drops to 47 days by 2029, which forces automation.
  • 'What changes with post-quantum?' Classical RSA/ECC become breakable by future quantum computers; we migrate to ML-KEM (key exchange) and ML-DSA (signatures), starting with hybrids, because long-lived data and roots must be protected now.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Over-answering: reciting everything you know about a topic signals insecurity; a precise answer with one example signals mastery.
  • Using jargon without meaning it; if you say 'attestation' you must be able to explain attester, verifier and evidence in plain words.
  • Guessing confidently when unsure — saying 'I'd check the spec/RFC for the exact detail' is a stronger answer than a wrong fact stated boldly.

docs.title: 9.13 A Twelve-Week Study Plan to Job-Ready
docs.text:
This final section turns the whole guide into a schedule. Twelve weeks of focused study, a few hours a week, moving from foundations to hands-on labs to interview practice, will take a motivated beginner to genuinely job-ready in platform security and PKI.

The twelve-week arc. Foundations, then hands-on depth, then interview readiness.

Think of it like…

It is like a couch-to-5k plan: you do not run the race on day one, you build up in planned stages, and by following the schedule you arrive at the finish line almost without noticing how far you have come.

Real-world example

Lena follows the plan alongside her job. Weeks 1-3 she reads the foundations and crypto chapters and sets up her lab. Weeks 4-8 she works through TPMs, boot, TEEs and PKI with labs each week. Weeks 9-11 she builds a CA end to end and runs attestation. Week 12 she drills interview questions and applies. She lands a junior PKI role.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Weeks 1-3: foundations, crypto refresher and roots of trust; set up the lab.
  2. Weeks 4-6: TPMs and boot/firmware trust, with swtpm and Secure Boot labs.
  3. Weeks 7-8: TEEs, confidential computing and attestation, with a Keylime lab.
  4. Weeks 9-11: X.509, root CAs and PKI operations; build a CA and automate issuance.
  5. Week 12: standards, careers, interview drills and applications.

Who uses it

Motivated beginners and career-changers who want a concrete, time-boxed path rather than open-ended study.

Key takeaway

Consistency beats intensity: a few hours every week for twelve weeks, always paired with a lab, will take you further than occasional marathon sessions, and the homelab you build is your portfolio.

Going deeper

  • Weeks 1-3 build the mental model: read the foundations and crypto-refresher material, understand the chain-of-trust idea, and set up a Linux lab VM so later weeks are hands-on from day one.
  • Weeks 4-6 go deep on the hardware-and-boot core: simulate a TPM with swtpm, practise PCRs, sealing and quotes, then enrol Secure Boot keys and sign a kernel in a VM, mapping each exercise to the relevant chapter.
  • Weeks 7-8 cover trusted execution and attestation: read the TEE and RATS material and run Keylime so you have seen evidence produced and verified, which many candidates have only read about.
  • Weeks 9-11 are the PKI heart: read the X.509, root-CA and operations chapters, build a two-tier CA by hand and with step-ca, issue certificates over ACME, and practise revocation and monitoring.
  • Week 12 converts knowledge to offers: skim the standards and careers material, drill the interview questions out loud, write up your homelab as a portfolio, and start applying to entry roles that match your strongest labs.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Front-loading all the reading and leaving labs for 'later' — later never comes, and employers hire for demonstrable skill, so lab every week.
  • Trying to master everything to expert depth in twelve weeks; aim for job-ready breadth plus two or three areas you can discuss deeply.
  • Studying in isolation; share your lab write-ups, ask questions in communities, and get feedback, because that accelerates learning and builds a network.

docs.title: Ten Things Every Student of Trust Should Master
docs.text: If you can explain these ten ideas, you understand how computers decide what to trust better than most engineers — and you are ready for platform-security, PKI or security-engineering work.

docs.title: 1. Trust has to start somewhere
docs.text: A root of trust is the small, well-protected component that everything else is checked against. If it is wrong or stolen, nothing built on it can be trusted.

docs.title: 2. Know the chain of trust
docs.text: Each stage of boot or each certificate in a chain is verified by the one before it, all the way back to an anchor that is trusted by design, not by proof.

docs.title: 3. Secure boot blocks, measured boot records
docs.text: Secure boot refuses to run unsigned code; measured boot hashes every stage into TPM PCRs so a verifier can later check exactly what ran.

docs.title: 4. Understand the TPM's three jobs
docs.text: Store keys that never leave the chip, record measurements in PCRs, and report them in signed quotes — and seal secrets so they only unlock in a known-good state.

docs.title: 5. Attestation is evidence, not a promise
docs.text: A device proves its state by signing measurements with a key rooted in hardware; a verifier compares that evidence with reference values and decides.

docs.title: 6. Keep the root CA offline
docs.text: Root keys live in an HSM, used only in witnessed key ceremonies to sign intermediates; day-to-day certificates come from online issuing CAs.

docs.title: 7. Read a certificate like a pro
docs.text: Subject, issuer, validity, public key, SAN, Basic Constraints, Key Usage, EKU and the signature — and know how path validation checks each one.

docs.title: 8. Revocation and transparency matter
docs.text: CRLs, OCSP and Certificate Transparency logs let the world spot and stop bad certificates; short-lived certificates reduce how much revocation must do.

docs.title: 9. Automate the certificate lifecycle
docs.text: Public TLS lifetimes fall to 200 days in 2026, 100 in 2027 and 47 in 2029 — ACME and certificate-lifecycle tools are now essential, and expired certificates still cause outages.

docs.title: 10. Plan for crypto agility and post-quantum
docs.text: Inventory keys and certificates, prefer algorithm-agile hardware and software, and prepare for ML-DSA and ML-KEM in boot chains, TPMs and PKI.

docs.title: Chapter 3: The Trusted Platform Module, In Depth
docs.text: The Trusted Platform Module is the security chip — or protected firmware — inside almost every modern PC and server. This chapter opens it up: TPM 1.2 versus 2.0 and the 2026 post-quantum update, form factors from discrete chips to cloud vTPMs, hierarchies, sessions and policies, the special keys, PCRs and the extend operation, sealing, quotes and remote attestation. It then shows how Windows and Linux use the TPM, who makes TPM chips, how TPMs have been attacked and defended, and how to program and test TPMs safely with simulators.

docs.title: 3.1 What a TPM Is — and What It Is Not
docs.text:
A Trusted Platform Module (TPM) is a small, standardised security component — a separate chip or protected firmware — built into almost every modern PC and server and many other devices. It creates and guards keys that never leave it, keeps tamper-evident records of what software started, and signs reports about those records. It is not a fast encryption engine, not a place to run your own code, and not a shield against malware that is already running.

What lives inside a TPM. A TPM is a small toolbox of protected functions, not a general-purpose processor.

Think of it like…

A TPM is like a notary's sealed strongbox with a ledger whose pages cannot be torn out: the notary's stamp never leaves the box, every visitor is written into the ledger, and the notary will stamp a certified copy of the ledger on request — but the notary does not guard the rest of the building.

Real-world example

Priya, an IT engineer at the fictional Harbor Clinics, rolls out 400 laptops. Each laptop's TPM holds the key that unlocks the disk, sealed so it is only released when the boot measurements look normal. When a laptop is stolen and the thief boots a different operating system from USB, the measurements differ and the TPM refuses to release the key. Meanwhile, the clinic's compliance service checks TPM-signed health reports before letting any laptop reach patient records.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. At power-on the firmware sends TPM2_Startup; from then on the TPM answers commands over a bus (SPI, I2C or legacy LPC) or a memory-mapped buffer.
  2. Each boot stage hashes the next stage and 'extends' that hash into the TPM's Platform Configuration Registers (PCRs).
  3. Software asks the TPM to create keys inside protected hierarchies; private keys can be used only inside the TPM.
  4. Secrets can be sealed to a policy (PCR values, a PIN, a time window) and are released only when that policy is satisfied.
  5. A remote verifier can request a quote: a TPM-signed copy of selected PCRs plus a fresh random challenge, proving the boot state.

Who uses it

Platform-security engineers, Windows and Linux endpoint administrators, firmware developers, cloud infrastructure teams, and anyone deploying disk encryption, device identity or attestation meets the TPM.

Key takeaway

Say it in one breath for interviews: a TPM protects keys, records measurements and reports them — it is the Root of Trust for Storage and for Reporting, while the first firmware code that measures (the CRTM) is the Root of Trust for Measurement.

Going deeper

  • The TCG treats the TPM as the Root of Trust for Storage and for Reporting; the Root of Trust for Measurement is the first firmware code (the CRTM), so the TPM only records what that code tells it.
  • Inside a TPM you find an I/O buffer, a command parser, engines for RSA, ECC, SHA-2, HMAC and AES, a hardware random number generator, seed-based key derivation, a few kilobytes of non-volatile memory, monotonic counters and a clock.
  • TPMs are deliberately small and slow: an RSA-2048 private-key operation on a discrete chip takes tens to hundreds of milliseconds, so the TPM protects a few root keys while bulk encryption (BitLocker, LUKS) runs on the CPU.
  • Because internal memory is tiny, most keys live outside the TPM as encrypted blobs wrapped by a parent key; they are loaded when needed and flushed afterwards, and only a handful of keys are kept at persistent handles.
  • Dictionary-attack protection counts failed authorisations and locks the TPM out for a period, which is why a short TPM PIN can be acceptable where a short password protecting a file would be trivially brute-forced.
  • Localities (0-4) tell the TPM which tier sent a command: ordinary OS software uses locality 0, while CPU microcode performing a dynamic launch uses locality 4 — so some PCRs can be reset only by that trusted hardware path.
  • Platform profiles such as the TCG PC Client Platform TPM Profile (PTP) say which algorithms, interfaces and PCR counts a TPM must offer on a given device class, so Windows and Linux tools can rely on the same baseline.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Thinking the TPM encrypts your whole disk: BitLocker or LUKS do the bulk AES work on the CPU; the TPM only protects the small key that unlocks it.
  • Assuming a TPM stops malware: it records and reports state; a compromised running OS can still misuse TPM keys it is authorised to use.
  • Confusing a TPM with a TEE or an HSM: it runs no custom code and is far slower than an HSM, but it is cheap and present in almost every PC.

docs.title: Try it: Check whether your machine has a TPM and which kind
docs.text:
# Windows PowerShell (admin)
Get-Tpm

# Linux
ls -l /dev/tpm*
cat /sys/class/tpm/tpm0/tpm_version_major      # 2 = TPM 2.0
tpm2_getcap properties-fixed | grep -A2 -E 'TPM2_PT_FAMILY_INDICATOR|TPM2_PT_MANUFACTURER'

docs.title: Key chips, standards, protocols, products & terms
docs.text: Name What it does Example TPM2_Startup / TPM2_ShutdownTCG TPM 2.0 Library, Part 3 · Command · Current · Firmware & boot Commands that start the TPM after reset or resume and save its state cleanly before power-off or sleep. Firmware sends TPM2_Startup(CLEAR) at cold boot; before S3 sleep the OS sends TPM2_Shutdown(STATE) so TPM2_Startup(STATE) can restore sessions on resume. TPM2_GetCapabilityTCG TPM 2.0 Library, Part 3 · Command · Current · Platform & OS Reads what the TPM supports and its current state: algorithms, PCR banks, handles, manufacturer, firmware version and lockout settings. tpm2_getcap algorithms lists every algorithm the chip supports; tpm2_getcap pcrs shows which PCR banks are active. TPM2_GetRandomTCG TPM 2.0 Library, Part 3 · Command · Current · Platform & OS Returns bytes from the TPM's hardware random number generator, which the OS may use as an extra entropy source. tpm2_getrandom --hex 16 prints 16 random bytes; Linux can also feed TPM randomness into its kernel entropy pool via the hwrng framework. Non-volatile (NV) indicesTCG TPM 2.0 Library · Concept · Platform & OS Small named storage areas inside the TPM with their own access rules: ordinary data, counters, bit fields, or extend-only types. An IoT gateway keeps a firmware security-version counter in an NV index so updates can refuse rollback to older, vulnerable images. Dictionary-attack lockoutTCG TPM 2.0 Library · Concept · Platform & OS TPM anti-hammering: failed authorisations are counted and, past a threshold, the TPM refuses further tries for a recovery period. After repeated wrong startup PINs, the TPM pauses attempts; an admin with lockout authorisation can reset it with tpm2_dictionarylockout --clear-lockout. LocalitiesTCG PC Client Platform TPM Profile · Concept · Firmware & boot Hardware-signalled levels (0-4) identifying which software tier sent a command, so policies and PCRs can trust firmware or DRTM over the OS. PCR 17 can be reset only from locality 4, which only the CPU's dynamic-launch microcode can use, so an OS cannot fake a late launch. Monotonic clock and reset countersTCG TPM 2.0 Library · Concept · Platform & OS A clock that only moves forward plus reset/restart counters, included in quotes and usable in time-limited policies. A verifier sees resetCount increase between two quotes and knows the server rebooted, so it re-checks the new boot log. TIS / FIFO and CRB interfacesTCG PC Client Platform TPM Profile (PTP) · Protocol · Current · Platform & OS Standard ways the CPU talks to a TPM: FIFO/TIS registers for discrete chips and the Command Response Buffer (CRB) for most firmware TPMs. Linux's tpm_tis_spi driver serves an Infineon SPI chip while tpm_crb serves an Intel PTT firmware TPM — both appear as /dev/tpm0. Platform-specific TPM profilesTCG PC Client PTP, Mobile and Automotive Thin profiles · Specification · Current · General Profiles that state which optional TPM features, algorithms, PCR counts and interfaces a TPM must provide for a device class. The PC Client profile requires at least 24 PCRs per bank, so Windows and Linux tools can rely on PCRs 0-23 existing. TPM crypto commandsTCG TPM 2.0 Library: TPM2_Sign, TPM2_RSA_Decrypt, TPM2_HMAC, TPM2_EncryptDecrypt2 · Command · Current · Platform & OS General-purpose operations using TPM-held keys; correct but slow, so used for small values like keys and hashes, not bulk data. A VPN client signs its TLS handshake hash with TPM2_Sign, so the private key never leaves the laptop's TPM. TPM response codes (TPM_RC)TCG TPM 2.0 Library, Part 2 · Format · Current · General Every TPM response carries a code: 0 means success; others such as TPM_RC_LOCKOUT (0x921) or TPM_RC_POLICY_FAIL explain failures. When unsealing fails, tpm2_rc_decode 0x99d translates the code into 'a policy check failed', pointing to changed PCRs. What a TPM is notScope boundary · Concept · General A TPM does not run application code, isolate memory, scan for malware or replace an HSM; TEEs and HSMs (other chapters) do those jobs. A team wanting AI inference in protected memory needs Intel TDX or AMD SEV-SNP, not a TPM — though those technologies borrow similar attestation ideas.

docs.title: 3.2 TPM 1.2 vs TPM 2.0: Versions, Algorithm Agility & ISO/IEC 11889
docs.text:
There are two TPM families. TPM 1.2 (finished in 2011) had its algorithms hard-wired — SHA-1 and RSA — with one owner and one storage key. TPM 2.0 (first published in 2014) is a redesign with 'algorithm agility' (it can use SHA-256, elliptic curves and, from 2026, post-quantum algorithms), several hierarchies and flexible policies. The two are not compatible: software is written for one or the other.

TPM specification history. TPM 2.0 has been revised many times; post-quantum support arrived in 2026.

Think of it like…

TPM 1.2 is a padlock with one fixed key shape; TPM 2.0 is a lock with a swappable cylinder, so when one key design becomes easy to pick you change the cylinder instead of the whole door.

Real-world example

Marco runs IT for a fictional school district with 2012-era desktops. Their TPM 1.2 chips only do SHA-1, so they fail Windows 11's check even though a TPM is present. New laptops arrive with TPM 2.0 firmware supporting SHA-256 and ECC P-256. When the TCG published library v1.85 with ML-KEM and ML-DSA in 2026, Marco noted that post-quantum TPM keys will need new hardware or firmware — not the TPMs already on his desks.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. 2003-2011: the TCG publishes TPM 1.1b and then TPM 1.2, whose final revision (116) appears in March 2011; ISO/IEC 11889:2009 adopts TPM 1.2.
  2. 2014: TPM 2.0 Library revision 1.16 is published and becomes ISO/IEC 11889:2015 (four parts).
  3. 2016-2019: revisions 1.38 and 1.59 add commands and fixes; many shipping PC TPMs implement one of these.
  4. 2024-2025: revision 1.83 and then Version 184 (March 2025) roll up errata and enhancements.
  5. 2026: library v1.85 (announced March 2026) adds ML-KEM, ML-DSA, Curve25519 and Curve448; TCG names PC Client PTP 1.07 as the PQC-ready baseline.
  6. 2026: draft ISO/IEC 11889 parts intended to replace the 2015 edition enter the ISO enquiry (DIS) stage.

Who uses it

Hardware procurement teams, firmware developers, Windows and Linux platform teams, and every TPM software developer must know which TPM version and revision a device implements.

Key takeaway

Memorise: TPM 2.0 = algorithm agility + multiple hierarchies + enhanced authorisation; ISO/IEC 11889:2015 is TPM 2.0 revision 1.16; v1.85 (2026) brings ML-KEM and ML-DSA.

Going deeper

  • TPM 1.2 fixed its algorithms (SHA-1, RSA up to 2048 bits, HMAC-SHA1), had a single owner password and one Storage Root Key, and proved identity with AIKs certified by a privacy CA or Direct Anonymous Attestation.
  • TPM 2.0 names every algorithm with a TPM_ALG_ID, so PCR banks, key types and hashes are chosen per object; typical PC TPMs offer SHA-1 and SHA-256 PCR banks, RSA-2048, ECC NIST P-256 and AES-128, with SHA-384 and P-384 on newer parts.
  • The library specification is split into parts covering architecture, structures, commands and supporting routines; the command and routine parts include C code from which the TCG/Microsoft reference implementation is built.
  • v1.85 adds ML-KEM (FIPS 203) for decryption-type keys including Endorsement Keys and ML-DSA (FIPS 204) for signing keys including Attestation Keys, with eight new commands such as TPM2_Encapsulate, TPM2_Decapsulate, TPM2_SignDigest and TPM2_SignSequenceStart/Complete.
  • TCG guidance published in 2026 says a 'PQC-ready' PC TPM is one implementing the PC Client Platform TPM Profile (PTP) 1.07, which selects the PQC parts of library v1.85; early PQC silicon and open-source firmware TPMs appeared during 2026.
  • Before PQC keys existed, Infineon's OPTIGA TPM SLB 9672 (2022) already verified its own firmware updates with XMSS hash-based signatures, so the chip can be updated even if RSA/ECC become untrustworthy.
  • ISO/IEC 11889:2015 was reconfirmed in 2021; in 2026 Draft International Standards for a new edition entered the ISO enquiry stage to bring the ISO text closer to current TCG releases.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming any TPM satisfies Windows 11: it requires TPM 2.0, so an enabled TPM 1.2 chip still fails the check.
  • Expecting every TPM 1.2 to be upgradable: only some chips received vendor 1.2-to-2.0 firmware upgrades through PC makers; many cannot change.
  • Expecting today's TPMs to do post-quantum crypto: PQC needs v1.85-capable hardware or firmware; installed TPMs remain RSA/ECC-only.
  • Following TPM 1.2 tutorials (TrouSerS, tpm_takeownership) on a TPM 2.0 machine: the command sets are incompatible; use tpm2-tss and tpm2-tools.

tpm2_getcap algorithms | grep -E '^[a-z]'
tpm2_getcap pcrs

Get-CimInstance -Namespace root/cimv2/Security/MicrosoftTpm -ClassName Win32_Tpm |

An outdated how-to telling you to run tpm_takeownership fails on a modern laptop because that command is TPM 1.2 only.

docs.title: 3.3 TPM Form Factors: Discrete, Integrated, Firmware, Pluton & Virtual
docs.text:
The TPM is a specification, so it can be built in several ways. A discrete TPM is its own chip; an integrated TPM is a separate hardware block inside a bigger chip; a firmware TPM (fTPM) runs as protected code inside the CPU's security processor; Microsoft Pluton can act as the TPM; and a virtual TPM (vTPM) is software that gives each virtual machine its own TPM. All understand the same commands, but each resists different attacks.

Discrete vs firmware vs virtual TPM

Discrete TPM Firmware TPM Virtual TPM Runs in Separate chip CPU security engine Hypervisor software Interface SPI / I2C / LPC CRB memory buffer Emulated device Bus sniffing Possible if TPM-only No external bus Host sees everything Shares CPU flaws No Yes (e.g. faulTPM) Yes, plus host risks Certification Often CC EAL4+ and FIPS Varies by vendor Cloud provider reports Examples Infineon SLB 9672, Nuvoton NPCT75x Intel PTT, AMD fTPM Hyper-V, NitroTPM, swtpm

Same commands, different attack surfaces.

Think of it like…

Think of safes: a free-standing safe bolted to the floor (discrete), a safe built into the wall (integrated or firmware), or a safety-deposit box the bank rents to each customer inside its own vault (virtual).

Real-world example

The fictional Tidewater Bank owns three kinds of machine. Its servers use plug-in Nuvoton discrete TPM modules, its laptops use AMD's firmware TPM, and its cloud VMs get Azure Trusted Launch vTPMs. The security team writes one attestation policy using the same TPM 2.0 commands everywhere. Their risk notes differ, though: discrete chips have a bus that can be sniffed, fTPMs share the CPU's weaknesses, and vTPMs trust the cloud host.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Discrete: a separately certified chip (Infineon, Nuvoton, STMicroelectronics) soldered on the board or on a header, connected over SPI, I2C or legacy LPC.
  2. Integrated: TPM logic as a dedicated hardware block inside a larger SoC or chipset, with no external TPM bus.
  3. Firmware: TPM code runs in a CPU security engine — Intel PTT in the CSME, AMD fTPM on the Platform Security Processor, or a TrustZone trusted application on Arm.
  4. Pluton: Microsoft's on-die security processor (in AMD, Qualcomm and some Intel chips) can be selected in firmware as the system TPM.
  5. Virtual: the hypervisor emulates a TPM for each VM and stores its state encrypted, ideally anchored to the host's own hardware.

Who uses it

Hardware buyers, BIOS and firmware engineers, virtualisation and cloud teams, and threat modellers deciding which attacks their TPM must resist.

Key takeaway

One-line trade-off: discrete = separately certified but bus-exposed; firmware = no external bus but shares CPU flaws; virtual = convenient but trusts the hypervisor.

Going deeper

  • The PC Client profile defines the FIFO/TIS register interface over LPC, SPI or I2C for discrete chips and the Command Response Buffer (CRB) used by most firmware TPMs; Linux drivers are tpm_tis, tpm_tis_spi, tpm_tis_i2c, tpm_crb and tpm_ftpm_tee.
  • Intel Platform Trust Technology (PTT) runs inside the Converged Security and Management Engine; AMD's fTPM runs on the Platform Security Processor; firmware TPMs keep their state in SPI flash, encrypted and integrity-protected with chip-unique keys.
  • Pluton-as-TPM is offered on AMD Ryzen 6000 and later, Qualcomm Snapdragon and some Intel Core Ultra platforms; Get-Tpm then reports manufacturer 'MSFT', and Pluton firmware can be updated through Windows Update.
  • Virtual TPMs: Hyper-V Generation 2 VMs, VMware vSphere vTPM (requires a key provider), QEMU/KVM with swtpm, Azure Trusted Launch, Google Shielded VM and AWS NitroTPM (generally available since May 2022).
  • A vTPM's EK is created by the cloud or hypervisor, not a chip vendor, so verifiers must trust that provider's EK certificate CA or fetch the EK through a cloud API such as Google's get-shielded-identity.
  • Single-board computers add TPMs through SPI add-on modules; on a Raspberry Pi a device-tree line such as dtoverlay=tpm-slb9670 in config.txt enables an Infineon TPM board.
  • Discrete TPMs are usually evaluated against a Common Criteria TPM protection profile at EAL4 augmented and often hold FIPS 140 certificates; firmware-TPM certification varies by vendor, which matters for government procurement.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming an fTPM is 'not a real TPM': it implements the same TPM 2.0 specification and Windows 11 accepts it; its threat model differs, not its API.
  • Treating a vTPM as hardware-protected by default: unless the host anchors vTPM state in its own TPM or confidential-VM hardware, a hypervisor admin can read it.
  • Switching between fTPM, discrete TPM or Pluton in firmware setup without preparation: it changes the TPM, so sealed BitLocker keys and enrolled identities stop working.

docs.title: Try it: Find out which kind of TPM you have
docs.text:
# Windows PowerShell (admin)
Get-Tpm | Select-Object ManufacturerIdTxt, ManufacturerVersion
# INTC = Intel PTT, AMD = AMD fTPM, MSFT = Pluton or Hyper-V vTPM, IFX/NTC/STM = discrete chip

# Linux
sudo dmesg | grep -i tpm
readlink /sys/class/tpm/tpm0/device/driver     # tpm_tis, tpm_tis_spi, tpm_crb, tpm_ftpm_tee

docs.title: 3.4 Hierarchies, Seeds & Handles
docs.text:
TPM 2.0 organises its keys into four hierarchies, each with its own owner and authorisation. The platform hierarchy belongs to the firmware, the storage (owner) hierarchy to the device owner and operating system, the endorsement hierarchy to privacy-sensitive identity keys, and the null hierarchy to temporary work erased at every reboot. Each hierarchy has a secret seed from which its top-level ('primary') keys are recalculated whenever needed.

Seeds, hierarchies and keys. Each hierarchy grows from its own secret seed; clearing a seed kills everything beneath it.

Think of it like…

Picture four key cabinets in a building: one for the landlord (platform), one for the tenant (storage), one holding the tenant's passport (endorsement), and a scratch drawer that is emptied every night (null).

Real-world example

Aisha, a Linux admin at the fictional Northwind Labs, runs tpm2_createprimary -C o. The TPM derives the same primary key from the storage seed and the same template every time, so nothing needs storing. When she repurposes the server and clears the TPM, the storage seed is replaced and every key under the owner hierarchy becomes useless. The endorsement seed — and the TPM's identity — survives the clear.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. During manufacturing the TPM creates its Endorsement Primary Seed; platform and storage seeds also exist inside the TPM, and the null seed is regenerated at every reset.
  2. At boot, firmware typically sets platformAuth to a random value it then forgets, so the operating system cannot use the platform hierarchy.
  3. The owner may set ownerAuth, endorsementAuth and lockoutAuth; Windows by default does not keep a full owner password.
  4. Primary keys are created with TPM2_CreatePrimary from a hierarchy seed plus a public template: same seed and template always give the same key.
  5. Child keys are created under a primary with TPM2_Create and stored outside as wrapped blobs, or made persistent inside the TPM with TPM2_EvictControl.
  6. TPM2_Clear replaces the storage seed and wipes the owner hierarchy; the endorsement identity is only destroyed by the rarely used TPM2_ChangeEPS.

Who uses it

TPM software developers, platform engineers provisioning fleets, and anyone debugging 'key not found', 'hierarchy disabled' or 'authorisation failed' errors.

Key takeaway

Learn the handle map: 0x40000001 owner, 0x4000000B endorsement, 0x4000000C platform, 0x40000007 null, 0x4000000A lockout; transient objects start 0x80, persistent 0x81, NV indices 0x01.

Going deeper

  • Each hierarchy has an authorisation value (ownerAuth, endorsementAuth, platformAuth) and optionally a policy; the separate lockoutAuth controls dictionary-attack reset and, with platformAuth, TPM2_Clear.
  • Primary keys are derived with KDFa — an HMAC-based counter-mode KDF from NIST SP 800-108 — from the seed and the hashed public template, so standard templates (for example the TCG EK templates) reproduce identical keys.
  • Handle ranges: PCRs 0x00000000-0x00000017, NV indices 0x01xxxxxx, HMAC sessions 0x02xxxxxx, policy sessions 0x03xxxxxx, permanent handles 0x40xxxxxx, transient objects 0x80xxxxxx and persistent objects 0x81xxxxxx.
  • TCG provisioning guidance reserves persistent handle 0x81000001 for the SRK and 0x81010001 for the RSA EK; owner persistent handles span 0x81000000-0x817FFFFF and platform ones 0x81800000-0x81FFFFFF.
  • TPM2_HierarchyControl can disable a hierarchy until the next reset; some firmware disables the endorsement hierarchy for privacy, which breaks attestation tools expecting to use the EK.
  • Every object has a Name — its name algorithm ID plus a hash of its public area — and sessions and policies bind to Names, so an attacker cannot substitute a different key with the same handle.
  • TPM2_ContextSave and TPM2_ContextLoad swap objects and sessions out of the TPM's few internal slots as encrypted blobs; the Linux kernel resource manager behind /dev/tpmrm0 does this automatically per process.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Clearing the TPM 'to fix errors': it irreversibly destroys every owner-hierarchy key — BitLocker protectors, Windows Hello keys, enrolled credentials. Escrow recovery keys first.
  • Expecting primary keys to be stored somewhere: they are recalculated, so the template must be byte-for-byte identical, including attributes and the unique field.
  • Assuming the owner controls everything: the endorsement hierarchy has its own authorisation and can be disabled separately, so EK operations may fail even for the owner.

docs.title: Try it: Inspect hierarchies and create a primary key
docs.text:
tpm2_getcap properties-variable | grep -E 'ownerAuthSet|endorsementAuthSet|lockoutAuthSet|shEnable|ehEnable|phEnable|inLockout'
tpm2_getcap handles-persistent          # e.g. 0x81000001 (SRK), 0x81010001 (EK)
tpm2_createprimary -C o -g sha256 -G ecc -c primary.ctx
tpm2_readpublic -c primary.ctx | head -20
tpm2_flushcontext -t                    # free transient slots

UEFI firmware defines a platform NV index for its own settings, then sets a random platformAuth so Windows cannot alter it. Storage (owner) hierarchy (SH)TCG TPM 2.0 Library · Concept · Platform & OS Hierarchy for the device owner and OS; holds the Storage Root Key and almost all application keys and sealed data. systemd-cryptenroll creates the sealed object protecting a LUKS key under the owner hierarchy's storage root. Endorsement hierarchy (EH)TCG TPM 2.0 Library · Concept · Platform & OS Privacy-sensitive hierarchy rooted in the manufacturer-created endorsement seed; it holds the EK that identifies a genuine TPM. An attestation server requests the EK public key and certificate, both from the endorsement hierarchy, to confirm a genuine TPM. Null hierarchyTCG TPM 2.0 Library · Concept · Platform & OS Temporary hierarchy whose seed changes at every TPM reset; keys and tickets under it vanish at reboot. Software needing a throwaway key for one session creates it under TPM_RH_NULL so nothing about it survives a restart. Primary seeds (EPS, SPS, PPS)TCG TPM 2.0 Library · Key · Silicon Large secret values that never leave the TPM; every primary key of a hierarchy is derived deterministically from its seed. Replacing the storage seed with TPM2_Clear instantly invalidates every SRK-wrapped key blob on disk, although the files still exist. TPM2_CreatePrimaryTCG TPM 2.0 Library, Part 3 · Command · Current · Platform & OS Derives a primary key from a hierarchy seed and a public template and loads it at a transient handle. tpm2_createprimary -C o -G ecc -c srk.ctx returns the identical ECC primary every time it runs with the same template. TPM2_EvictControlTCG TPM 2.0 Library, Part 3 · Command · Current · Platform & OS Makes a loaded object persistent at a 0x81xxxxxx handle, or deletes a persistent object, so keys survive reboots. tpm2_evictcontrol -C o -c srk.ctx 0x81000001 stores the SRK at its conventional handle for other tools to use. TPM2_ClearTCG TPM 2.0 Library, Part 3 · Command · Current · Platform & OS Resets the owner hierarchy: new storage seed, owner authorisations removed, owner NV and persistent objects deleted; the EK survives. Before recycling a laptop, IT clears the TPM from firmware setup so keys belonging to the previous user can never be used again. lockoutAuthTCG TPM 2.0 Library · Concept · Platform & OS The authorisation that resets dictionary-attack lockout and authorises TPM2_Clear; protect it like a master admin password. tpm2_changeauth -c lockout sets a lockout password so malware cannot simply clear the TPM to cause disruption. Handles and NamesTCG TPM 2.0 Library, Part 1 · Concept · Platform & OS Handles are 32-bit references such as 0x81000001; a Name is an object's algorithm-tagged public-area hash used to bind authorisations. tpm2_readpublic -c 0x81000001 prints the key's Name, which a policy can reference to approve exactly that key. TPM2_ContextSave / TPM2_ContextLoadTCG TPM 2.0 Library, Part 3 · Command · Current · Platform & OS Swap objects and sessions out of the TPM's few internal slots as encrypted contexts and bring them back later. A resource manager serving twenty processes saves idle sessions' contexts so the TPM never runs out of session slots. A privacy BIOS option disables the endorsement hierarchy, so attestation enrolment fails with TPM_RC_HIERARCHY on that machine.

docs.title: 3.5 Authorisation: Passwords, HMAC Sessions & Policies
docs.text:
Every TPM object can demand proof before it is used. The simplest proof is a password (the authValue). An HMAC session proves you know the password without sending it, and can encrypt sensitive values on their way to and from the TPM. Enhanced authorisation — policies — lets you require combinations of conditions: specific PCR values, a PIN, a signature from an administrator, a time window or a particular command.

How a policy session unlocks an object. Each assertion is hashed into the session digest; order matters.

Think of it like…

A password is a door key; an HMAC session is proving you hold the key by describing its shape through a frosted window so no one can copy it; a policy is a bank-vault rule such as 'two managers, during business hours, with the alarm switched off'.

Real-world example

The fictional Orion Health stores a database key in a TPM. Its policy says: PCRs 0 and 7 must match the approved boot AND the request must be signed by the security team's key — OR a recovery password may be used, but only for TPM2_Unseal. As the software runs each policy command, the TPM hashes it into a running policy digest. The key opens only if that digest exactly equals the authPolicy stored with the key.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Each object gets an authValue and/or an authPolicy (the digest of its required policy) when it is created.
  2. Password sessions (reserved handle TPM_RS_PW) send the authValue in clear — simple but visible to anyone sniffing the bus.
  3. HMAC sessions start with TPM2_StartAuthSession; nonces and a session key let every command carry an HMAC proving knowledge of the authValue.
  4. Policy sessions run assertions such as TPM2_PolicyPCR, TPM2_PolicyAuthValue, TPM2_PolicySigned or TPM2_PolicyOR, each extending the session's policy digest.
  5. When the object is used, the TPM compares the session's policy digest with the object's authPolicy; a match authorises the command.
  6. Session attributes 'decrypt' and 'encrypt' switch on parameter encryption (AES-CFB or XOR) for the first command or response parameter.

Who uses it

TPM application developers, Linux and Windows security engineers designing unlock policies, and attestation architects.

Key takeaway

Know the three session types — password, HMAC, policy — and that TPM2_PolicyAuthorize answers the classic question 'how do you change PCR policies without re-sealing everything?'.

Going deeper

  • Policy digests chain like PCRs: new digest = H(old digest ‖ command code of the assertion ‖ its arguments), so an authPolicy can be computed offline in a trial session or entirely in software.
  • TPM2_PolicyOR accepts up to eight alternative branch digests; TPM2_PolicyAuthorize lets a named authority key approve new policies later, removing the brittleness of locking secrets to exact PCR hashes.
  • Further assertions include PolicySecret (prove another object's auth), PolicySigned (fresh external signature), PolicyNV (compare NV contents), PolicyCounterTimer (time windows), PolicyLocality, PolicyCpHash, PolicyNameHash, PolicyDuplicationSelect and PolicyPassword.
  • Salted sessions encrypt a random salt to a TPM key (often the SRK or EK) so a bus observer who even knows the authValue cannot derive the session key; bound sessions additionally mix in a bound object's authValue.
  • Parameter encryption protects only the first parameter of a command or response, and only if it is a sized buffer — enough for sealed data, PINs and key material in TPM2_Unseal, TPM2_Create or TPM2_Import.
  • Objects marked noDA are exempt from dictionary-attack counting; that suits high-entropy secrets, but human-chosen PINs must stay under lockout protection.
  • Windows and Linux keep most system keys' authValues in software or empty and rely on policies and lockout; a TPM PIN's strength comes from the TPM refusing rapid guesses, not from its length.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Using plain password sessions over a discrete TPM bus: the authValue travels in clear; use salted HMAC sessions with parameter encryption.
  • Sealing to exact PCR 0 or 2 values with no PolicyAuthorize or recovery path: the next firmware update locks you out.
  • Assuming policy steps can be run in any order: the digest is a hash chain, so PolicyPCR then PolicyAuthValue differs from the reverse order.

docs.title: Try it: Compute a policy digest for 'PCR 0 and 7 plus the object's PIN' in a trial session
docs.text:
tpm2_startauthsession -S session.ctx                  # trial session by default
tpm2_policypcr -S session.ctx -l sha256:0,7
tpm2_policyauthvalue -S session.ctx -L pcr-pin.policy
tpm2_flushcontext session.ctx
xxd -p pcr-pin.policy        # use this digest as the object's authPolicy

docs.text: Name What it does Example authValueTCG TPM 2.0 Library · Concept · Platform & OS An object's or hierarchy's password-like secret, set at creation and proved through a password or HMAC session. When Leo types his six-digit startup PIN, it becomes an authorisation the TPM checks, under lockout protection, before releasing his disk key. authPolicyTCG TPM 2.0 Library · Concept · Platform & OS The digest of the policy an object requires; it is fixed when the object is created and cannot be changed later. tpm2_readpublic on a sealed LUKS object shows its authPolicy, the digest of a PolicyPCR assertion over PCR 7. Password session (TPM_RS_PW)TCG TPM 2.0 Library · Protocol · Current · Platform & OS The simplest authorisation: the plaintext authValue accompanies the command under the reserved handle 0x40000009. tpm2_unseal -c key.ctx -p mypass uses a password session, readable by anyone sniffing a discrete TPM's SPI bus. HMAC sessionTCG TPM 2.0 Library · Protocol · Current · Platform & OS A session where caller and TPM exchange nonces and prove knowledge of the authValue with an HMAC over each command, never sending it. The Linux kernel option CONFIG_TCG_TPM2_HMAC wraps kernel TPM traffic in salted HMAC sessions to resist bus interposers. Salted and bound sessionsTCG TPM 2.0 Library · Concept · Platform & OS Ways to strengthen a session key: a salt encrypted to a TPM key, or binding to an object's authValue, hides it from bus observers. tpm2_startauthsession --hmac-session -c 0x81000001 salts the session with the SRK so session secrets stay hidden. Parameter encryptionTCG TPM 2.0 Library · Concept · Platform & OS Session attributes that encrypt the first parameter of a command or response, protecting secrets as they cross the TPM bus. With parameter encryption on, a sniffed TPM2_Unseal response shows only ciphertext instead of the disk-encryption key. TPM2_StartAuthSessionTCG TPM 2.0 Library, Part 3 · Command · Current · Platform & OS Starts an HMAC, policy or trial session, optionally salted with a TPM key and bound to an object. Every tpm2-tools policy script begins with tpm2_startauthsession, as a trial session to compute a digest or a real one to use it. TPM2_PolicyPCRTCG TPM 2.0 Library, Part 3 · Command · Current · Platform & OS Policy assertion requiring selected PCRs to hold specific values; extends the policy digest with the selection and their combined digest. tpm2_policypcr -S s.ctx -l sha256:7 ties unsealing to the current Secure Boot configuration recorded in PCR 7. TPM2_PolicyAuthorizeTCG TPM 2.0 Library, Part 3 · Command · Current · Platform & OS Accepts any policy that a named authority key has signed, so policies can change without re-creating protected objects. systemd-cryptenroll --tpm2-public-key uses it so vendor-signed PCR 11 predictions unlock disks after kernel updates. TPM2_PolicyORTCG TPM 2.0 Library, Part 3 · Command · Current · Platform & OS Lets an object accept any one of up to eight alternative policy digests, such as normal boot or recovery. A server key unseals if PCRs match either the old firmware or the newly approved firmware during a rolling update. TPM2_PolicySigned / TPM2_PolicySecretTCG TPM 2.0 Library, Part 3 · Command · Current · Platform & OS Assertions requiring a fresh signature from an external key, or proof of another TPM object's authorisation. A data-centre key unlocks only with a short-lived ticket signed by the operations team's hardware security key via PolicySigned. TPM2_PolicyCommandCodeTCG TPM 2.0 Library, Part 3 · Command · Current · Platform & OS Restricts a policy session to one specific command so a satisfied policy cannot be reused for something else. Adding PolicyCommandCode for TPM2_Unseal means the recovery branch can only unseal, not duplicate or re-authorise the object.
