A licence key works only while an NV 'revoked' flag stays zero; setting the flag on that device disables the key instantly.

docs.title: 3.6 TPM Keys: EK, SRK, AK & Device Identities
docs.text:
A TPM uses a few special keys. The Endorsement Key (EK) is a unique identity derived from the manufacturer's seed, usually with a certificate from the TPM maker proving it is genuine. The Storage Root Key (SRK) is the parent that wraps other keys. Attestation Keys (AKs) sign reports about the TPM's state. Device identity keys (IDevID and LDevID) let a device prove 'I am serial number X from manufacturer Y' on a network.

Where TPM keys come from. Manufacturer certificates anchor identity; owner-created keys do the daily work.

Think of it like…

The EK is the chip's birth certificate, the SRK the master key to a filing cabinet, the AK a notary's stamp used only on official reports, and a DevID the staff badge you show at the door.

Real-world example

The fictional Quanta Grid deploys 2,000 smart-meter gateways. At the factory each TPM's EK certificate is checked against the TPM vendor's CA, an AK is created and proven via credential activation, and an LDevID key with a certificate from Quanta's private CA is generated inside the TPM. In the field, gateways use the LDevID for mutual TLS and the AK to sign quotes — never the EK itself.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. EK: created with TPM2_CreatePrimary in the endorsement hierarchy from a standard TCG template; its certificate usually sits in NV (RSA at 0x01C00002, ECC P-256 at 0x01C0000A).
  2. SRK: a restricted decryption primary key in the storage hierarchy, conventionally at 0x81000001, that wraps child keys.
  3. AK: a restricted signing key that signs only TPM-generated data such as quotes, proven to share a TPM with the EK through credential activation.
  4. DevIDs: IDevID installed by the manufacturer and LDevID by the owner — signing keys with X.509 certificates for TLS or 802.1X.
  5. Ordinary keys: signing, decryption, HMAC or symmetric keys created under the SRK and stored outside as wrapped blobs.

Who uses it

Attestation and device-identity engineers, PKI teams issuing device certificates, IoT manufacturers, and enterprise Windows teams using TPM key attestation.

Key takeaway

The EK is a decryption key, not a signing key — which is exactly why attestation needs a separate AK and credential activation to link the two.

Going deeper

  • The TCG EK Credential Profile defines standard EK templates — RSA-2048 and ECC NIST P-256 in the 'low range' plus 'high range' templates for stronger keys such as RSA-3072 and P-384 — so verifiers can recreate the EK and match its certificate.
  • EK certificates are X.509 certificates chaining to TPM vendor CAs; for firmware TPMs they may be issued by Intel, AMD or Microsoft services and downloaded rather than stored in NV.
  • Key attributes fixedTPM, fixedParent, sensitiveDataOrigin, userWithAuth, adminWithPolicy, restricted, sign and decrypt decide what a key may do and whether it can ever leave the TPM.
  • A restricted signing key refuses to sign external data that begins with TPM_GENERATED_VALUE (0xFF544347), and every TPM attestation structure begins with it — so a stolen AK authorisation still cannot forge a quote.
  • TCG's 'TPM 2.0 Keys for Device Identity and Attestation' specification describes creating IDevID/LDevID and IAK/LAK keys inside the TPM and certifying them during manufacturing or onboarding, aligned with IEEE 802.1AR.
  • Windows AD CS key attestation can require proof that a certificate's private key is TPM-protected, with trust based on the EK certificate, a pre-registered EK public key, or the user's credentials, recorded as issuance-policy OIDs.
  • Keys created without fixedTPM can be wrapped for another TPM with TPM2_Duplicate and brought in with TPM2_Import, enabling controlled backup or migration under a duplication policy.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Using the EK as a login identity: it is privacy-sensitive and decryption-only; use an AK for attestation and a DevID for authentication.
  • Trusting an EK without validating its certificate chain to a TPM vendor CA: software TPMs can produce EKs too.
  • Assuming every TPM ships an EK certificate in NV: many firmware TPMs require downloading it, and vTPMs may provide it through a cloud API.

docs.title: Try it: Create an EK and AK and read the EK certificate (Linux)
docs.text:
tpm2_createek -c ek.ctx -G rsa -u ek.pub
tpm2_getekcertificate -o ek_cert.der        # some fTPMs need an online fetch (see man page)
openssl x509 -inform DER -in ek_cert.der -noout -issuer -subject -dates
tpm2_createak -C ek.ctx -c ak.ctx -G rsa -g sha256 -s rsassa -u ak.pub -n ak.name
tpm2_flushcontext -t

docs.title: 3.7 PCRs, the Extend Operation & PCR 0-23
docs.text:
Platform Configuration Registers (PCRs) are special registers inside the TPM that record what happened during boot. You cannot write a PCR directly — you can only 'extend' it, which mixes a new measurement into the old value with a hash. The final value therefore proves the exact sequence of measurements; change any one and the result changes. A separate event log lists each measurement so a verifier can replay it.

PCR 0-23 allocation (PC Client). Firmware owns 0-7, OS loaders and the OS use 8-15, DRTM uses 17-22.

Think of it like…

A PCR is like a blender that never empties: every ingredient you add changes the flavour, and the final taste can only be reproduced by adding exactly the same ingredients in exactly the same order.

Real-world example

On Sam's laptop, firmware measures itself into PCR 0, the Windows Boot Manager into PCR 4 and the Secure Boot settings into PCR 7. Each step computes PCR = SHA-256(old PCR ‖ new hash). If malware swaps the boot manager, PCR 4 ends up completely different. A verifier replaying the event log sees exactly which entry changed and pinpoints the tampered file.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. At TPM reset, PCRs 0-16 and 23 start as all zeros; DRTM PCRs 17-22 start as all ones until a dynamic launch resets them to zero.
  2. A measuring component hashes the next piece of code or configuration.
  3. It calls TPM2_PCR_Extend: PCR_new = H(PCR_old ‖ digest), once for each active PCR bank.
  4. It appends an event record (PCR index, event type, digests, data) to the TCG event log in memory.
  5. The OS exposes the log (Linux securityfs, Windows MeasuredBoot logs) and anyone can read PCR values without authorisation.
  6. A verifier replays the log; if the recomputed values equal the quoted PCRs, the log is authentic and can be checked entry by entry.

Who uses it

Measured-boot and attestation engineers, disk-encryption admins choosing PCR profiles, Linux distribution developers and incident responders verifying boot integrity.

Key takeaway

Memorise PCR 0 (firmware code), 2 (option ROMs), 4 (boot manager), 7 (Secure Boot policy), 10 (Linux IMA) and 11 (BitLocker on Windows, UKI on systemd) — they come up constantly.

Going deeper

  • With a SHA-256 bank each PCR holds 32 bytes; PC Client TPMs provide at least 24 PCRs per active bank, and firmware chooses which banks (SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-384) are active using TPM2_PCR_Allocate.
  • The TCG PC Client Platform Firmware Profile assigns PCR 0 to firmware code, 1 to its configuration, 2-3 to option-ROM/driver code and data, 4 to boot-manager code, 5 to boot configuration and GPT, 6 to manufacturer events, 7 to Secure Boot policy.
  • Windows uses PCR 11 for BitLocker access control and 12-14 for data events, boot modules and boot authorities; Linux uses 8-9 (GRUB), 10 (IMA), 11 (UKI), 12 (command line), 13 (sysext), 14 (shim MOK) and 15 (LUKS keys, machine-id).
  • PCRs 17-22 belong to the Dynamic Root of Trust for Measurement (Intel TXT, AMD SKINIT, Windows System Guard): they are reset only by a late launch from locality 4, giving a fresh chain independent of earlier firmware (details in the boot chapter).
  • PCR 16 (debug) and PCR 23 (application) can be reset by software with TPM2_PCR_Reset, so they are useful for experiments and never valid as security evidence.
  • The event log itself is unprotected data; its trustworthiness comes from replaying it against quoted PCRs. The modern crypto-agile format records one digest per active bank for every event.
  • Measuring identical bits always gives identical PCRs, so verifiers keep 'golden' values or vendor Reference Integrity Manifests; a firmware setting or even a different option-ROM version produces a new value.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Thinking PCRs can be set or rolled back: they can only be extended or reset at reboot, which is precisely what makes them trustworthy.
  • Treating the event log as trusted on its own: always verify it by replaying it against PCR values from a signed quote.
  • Comparing SHA-1 bank values with SHA-256 golden values: each bank is computed separately with its own algorithm; check which banks are active.
  • Expecting identical PCR 0 across a fleet: different firmware versions and settings produce different values, so group reference values by model and version.

docs.title: Try it: Read PCRs, decode the boot log and practise an extend on the debug PCR
docs.text:
tpm2_pcrread sha256:0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7
sudo tpm2_eventlog /sys/kernel/security/tpm0/binary_bios_measurements | less
# Windows: per-boot TCG logs are in C:\Windows\Logs\MeasuredBoot\

# Practise on PCR 16 (debug, resettable) - best on a test VM
tpm2_pcrextend 16:sha256=$(printf 'hello' | sha256sum | cut -d' ' -f1)
tpm2_pcrread sha256:16
tpm2_pcrreset 16

Extend operationTCG TPM 2.0 Library · Algorithm · Current · Firmware & boot PCR_new = Hash(PCR_old ‖ measurement): order-sensitive, one-way and impossible to undo without a reset. Measuring A then B gives a different PCR than B then A, so a verifier also notices reordered boot steps. TPM2_PCR_ExtendTCG TPM 2.0 Library, Part 3 · Command · Current · Firmware & boot Extends a supplied digest into a PCR for each specified bank; the workhorse of measured boot. GRUB's TPM module calls TPM2_PCR_Extend for every command and file it loads, into PCRs 8 and 9. TPM2_PCR_EventTCG TPM 2.0 Library, Part 3 · Command · Current · Firmware & boot Has the TPM hash up to 1,024 bytes of event data itself and extend the result into every active bank. Firmware recording a short configuration string uses TPM2_PCR_Event so each bank's digest is computed inside the TPM. PCR banksTCG TPM 2.0 Library; PC Client PTP · Concept · Current · Firmware & boot Parallel sets of PCRs, one per hash algorithm (SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-384), each extended separately with that algorithm. A firmware option such as 'PCR bank: SHA-256 only' uses TPM2_PCR_Allocate so the SHA-1 bank disappears from the next boot. PCR 0-1: firmware code and configurationTCG PC Client Platform Firmware Profile · Concept · Current · Firmware & boot PCR 0 records core firmware code and embedded option ROMs; PCR 1 records firmware configuration such as settings and SMBIOS data. After a vendor BIOS update, PCR 0 changes on every laptop, so secrets sealed to PCR 0 must be resealed first. PCR 2-3: option ROMs and UEFI driversTCG PC Client Platform Firmware Profile · Concept · Current · Firmware & boot PCR 2 records code from add-in cards and UEFI drivers; PCR 3 records their configuration and data. Swapping a server's RAID card changes PCR 2 because the new card's option ROM is measured at boot. PCR 4-6: boot manager, GPT and platform eventsTCG PC Client Platform Firmware Profile · Concept · Current · Firmware & boot PCR 4 records boot-manager code and boot attempts; PCR 5 boot configuration and the GPT; PCR 6 manufacturer-specific events. Replacing Windows Boot Manager with a malicious EFI binary changes PCR 4, so a key sealed to PCRs 0, 2, 4 and 11 stays locked. PCR 7: Secure Boot policyTCG PC Client Platform Firmware Profile · Concept · Current · Firmware & boot Records Secure Boot state, the PK, KEK, db and dbx contents, and which db certificate authorised each loaded image. BitLocker's default profile binds to PCRs 7 and 11, so firmware updates rarely trigger recovery but Secure Boot key changes do. PCR 8-9: OS loaderGRUB, Linux kernel; UAPI Linux TPM PCR Registry · Concept · Current · Platform & OS Used by boot loaders: GRUB measures commands and the kernel command line into 8 and loaded files into 9; Linux measures its initrd into 9. Editing the GRUB kernel line to add init=/bin/bash changes PCR 8, so automatic TPM disk unlock refuses. PCR 10: Linux IMALinux kernel IMA · Concept · Current · Platform & OS The Integrity Measurement Architecture extends a hash for each measured file at runtime; the IMA log replays to this PCR. A Keylime verifier replays the IMA log against PCR 10 and spots an unexpected binary executed on a web server. PCR 11-15: operating-system useMicrosoft; UAPI Linux TPM PCR Registry (systemd) · Concept · Current · Platform & OS OS-defined PCRs: Windows uses 11-14 for BitLocker control and boot details; systemd uses 11 (UKI) through 15 (LUKS keys, machine-id). systemd-measure predicts PCR 11 for a signed Unified Kernel Image so disks unlock only with that vendor-signed kernel. PCR 16 and 23: debug and applicationTCG PC Client Platform Firmware Profile · Concept · Current · Platform & OS Software-resettable PCRs — 16 for debugging, 23 for applications — useful for experiments but worthless as security evidence. Students practise extends on PCR 16 with tpm2_pcrextend, knowing nothing trusts that PCR and real boot measurements stay untouched. PCR 17-22: dynamic root of trustTCG PC Client profiles; Intel TXT, AMD DRTM · Concept · Current · Firmware & boot Start at all ones, are reset to zero only by a hardware late launch, then record the measured launch environment. With Windows System Guard Secure Launch, quotes include PCRs 17-22 showing the hypervisor started through a DRTM launch. TCG event logTCG PC Client Platform Firmware Profile · Format · Current · Firmware & boot List of each measurement — PCR index, event type, digests and description — kept by firmware and OS, verifiable by replay. tpm2_eventlog decodes Linux's binary_bios_measurements, showing an EV_EFI_BOOT_SERVICES_APPLICATION entry for each EFI binary loaded.

docs.title: 3.8 Sealing, Unsealing & PCR-Bound Secrets
docs.text:
Sealing means encrypting a small secret with the TPM so that only the same TPM can decrypt ('unseal') it, and only when a policy is met — usually that certain PCRs show a known-good boot. It is how disk-encryption keys unlock automatically on a healthy machine but stay locked if someone boots another operating system or tampers with the boot loader.

Automatic disk unlock with a sealed key. The secret leaves the TPM only if PCR 7 still matches the sealing policy.

Think of it like…

Sealing is like a time-capsule lock that opens only for the same person, in the same room, with the furniture arranged exactly as before — move one chair and it stays shut.

Real-world example

Ben enrols his Fedora laptop's encrypted volume with systemd-cryptenroll --tpm2-device=auto --tpm2-pcrs=7. A key slot is now protected by a TPM-sealed secret bound to PCR 7. Each normal boot, the Secure Boot state matches and the disk unlocks silently. When a thief disables Secure Boot to start a USB stick, PCR 7 changes, the TPM refuses to unseal, and the thief is left facing a passphrase prompt.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Choose PCRs and compute the expected policy digest — for example TPM2_PolicyPCR over sha256:7, optionally plus TPM2_PolicyAuthValue for a PIN.
  2. Create a sealed data object with TPM2_Create under the SRK: secret up to 128 bytes, authPolicy set to the digest.
  3. Store the returned public and private blobs on disk, for example in a LUKS2 header token.
  4. At boot, load the blobs with TPM2_Load, start a policy session and replay the same policy commands against the current PCRs.
  5. Call TPM2_Unseal in that session; the TPM releases the secret only if the session digest equals the object's authPolicy.
  6. Plan for change: use signed policies, reseal before planned updates and always keep a recovery key.

Who uses it

Disk-encryption and endpoint admins, Linux distribution engineers, embedded developers protecting device secrets, and teams automating unattended server unlock.

Key takeaway

Sealing ties a secret to TPM + state; binding (encrypting to a TPM key) ties it to the TPM only — interviewers like to ask the difference.

Going deeper

  • A sealed object is a keyedHash object whose sensitive area holds up to 128 bytes of data, encrypted by its parent (usually the SRK); TPM2_Unseal returns the data, ideally protected by parameter encryption.
  • BitLocker's default PCR profiles are 7 and 11 when Secure Boot is in use, or 0, 2, 4 and 11 otherwise; Windows Boot Manager extends PCR 11 after unlocking, so the key cannot be unsealed again later in that boot.
  • Brittleness fixes: TPM2_PolicyAuthorize with vendor-signed policies (systemd-measure and --tpm2-public-key), systemd-pcrlock predicting future PCR values from the event log, and Suspend-BitLocker -RebootCount before firmware updates.
  • Clevis combines a tpm2 pin with network-bound Tang servers through Shamir secret sharing ('sss'), e.g. unlock only if the TPM state is good AND the machine can reach the corporate Tang server.
  • Adding PolicyAuthValue makes unsealing require both a healthy boot and something the user knows; the TPM's dictionary-attack lockout limits PIN guessing.
  • TPM-only automatic unlock still hands the key to software on every boot; anyone who can run code after unlock, or sniff an unprotected bus, can capture it — sealing defeats offline and boot-tampering attacks, not a live compromised OS.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Sealing to PCR 0 or 2 without an update plan: every firmware or option-ROM update triggers recovery. Prefer PCR 7 or signed policies and suspend protection during updates.
  • Losing the recovery key: if PCRs change, the TPM is cleared or the motherboard is replaced, the recovery key or passphrase is the only way back in.
  • Assuming sealing protects a running, logged-in system: once unsealed, the key lives in RAM, beyond the TPM's protection.

docs.title: Try it: Seal and unseal a secret bound to PCR 7 (try it on swtpm or a test VM)
docs.text:
echo -n 'my-secret' > secret.txt
tpm2_createprimary -C o -c prim.ctx
tpm2_pcrread -o pcr7.bin sha256:7
tpm2_createpolicy --policy-pcr -l sha256:7 -f pcr7.bin -L pcr7.policy
tpm2_create -C prim.ctx -L pcr7.policy -i secret.txt -u seal.pub -r seal.priv
tpm2_load -C prim.ctx -u seal.pub -r seal.priv -c seal.ctx
tpm2_unseal -c seal.ctx -p pcr:sha256:7      # prints my-secret while PCR 7 is unchanged

A kiosk stores the seal.pub and seal.priv blobs of its database password on disk; copied to another machine, they decrypt nothing. A backup agent binds each file key to the server's TPM key, so restores work on that server even after a firmware update. At each boot the initrd runs TPM2_Load on the sealed blobs from the LUKS2 header before attempting to unseal. TPM2_UnsealTCG TPM 2.0 Library, Part 3 · Command · Current · Platform & OS Returns a sealed object's data when the session's authorisation — password or policy digest — matches the object. tpm2_unseal -c seal.ctx -p pcr:sha256:7 prints the secret while PCR 7 is unchanged and fails after Secure Boot is turned off. Bluefin Insurance keeps the default 7+11 profile so monthly firmware updates rarely push 3,000 laptops into recovery. After a kernel update, a laptop enrolled with --tpm2-public-key still unlocks because the new UKI ships a fresh signed PCR prediction. systemd-pcrlocksystemd (v255 and later) · Tool · Emerging · Platform & OS Predicts valid future PCR values from known boot components and stores a matching policy, so disks survive planned updates. An admin registers the next firmware version's measurements with systemd-pcrlock before rollout, avoiding recovery prompts. Policy brittlenessIndustry term · Concept · General The problem that exact-PCR policies break after legitimate changes such as firmware, bootloader or kernel updates. A fleet sealed to PCR 0 hits 900 recovery prompts after one BIOS update — the textbook brittleness failure. docs.title: 3.9 TPM Quotes & Remote Attestation
docs.text:
Remote attestation lets a server ask a device 'prove what you booted'. The device's TPM produces a quote: a signature, made with an Attestation Key, over selected PCR values and a random number (nonce) chosen by the verifier. The verifier checks the signature, checks the key really belongs to a genuine TPM, replays the event logs, and compares the results with known-good values.

Enrolment and quote with credential activation. Credential activation trusts the AK once; each quote then proves fresh state.

Think of it like…

It is like a health inspector phoning a restaurant with a random code word; the manager must send back a signed, stamped checklist containing that word — proving it is fresh, genuine and from the right restaurant.

Real-world example

The fictional Cobalt Cloud runs Keylime on 5,000 Linux hosts. Each host's agent registers its EK and AK, and credential activation proves the AK lives in that TPM. Every few seconds the verifier sends a nonce; the agent returns a TPM2_Quote plus boot and IMA logs, which are checked against policy. When one host's IMA log shows an unknown binary, Keylime marks it failed and triggers actions that remove it from the cluster.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Enrol: the device sends its EK certificate and AK public key; the verifier checks the EK chain up to the TPM vendor CA.
  2. Credential activation: the verifier encrypts a secret to the EK, bound to the AK's Name; only a TPM holding both recovers it with TPM2_ActivateCredential.
  3. Challenge: the verifier sends a fresh nonce and the PCR selection it wants.
  4. Quote: TPM2_Quote returns a TPMS_ATTEST structure (magic value, signer, nonce, clock information, PCR digest) signed by the AK.
  5. Verify: check signature and nonce, replay the event logs to reproduce the PCR digest, then compare events with reference values.
  6. Decide: grant access, issue a certificate or quarantine — and repeat periodically.

Who uses it

Zero-trust and attestation engineers, cloud and edge platform teams, device-management and compliance services, and confidential-computing architects who build on the same ideas.

Key takeaway

A quote = AK signature over (PCR digest + verifier nonce + clock and reset counters); the nonce gives freshness and credential activation links the AK to a genuine EK.

Going deeper

  • A quote's TPMS_ATTEST holds the magic TPM_GENERATED_VALUE, type TPM_ST_ATTEST_QUOTE, the signer's qualified name, extraData (the nonce), clockInfo (clock, resetCount, restartCount, safe), firmwareVersion, and the PCR selection plus a digest of those PCRs.
  • In credential activation the verifier encrypts a seed to the EK and derives keys from it and the AK's Name; TPM2_ActivateCredential succeeds only if that EK and the named AK share one TPM — the EK never signs.
  • TPM 1.2 relied on a privacy CA to issue AIK certificates after this check; TPM 2.0 can do the same with AK certificates, or use ECDAA for anonymous attestation, although DAA is rarely deployed.
  • Keylime, a CNCF project that began at MIT Lincoln Laboratory, has a registrar, verifier, tenant CLI and Rust agent; it checks measured-boot and IMA policies and has added an agent-driven 'push' mode for devices behind firewalls.
  • Other TPM evidence commands: TPM2_Certify (a key lives in this TPM), TPM2_GetTime (signed clock), TPM2_NV_Certify (signed NV contents) and TPM2_GetSessionAuditDigest (signed record of a command sequence).
  • In IETF RATS terms (RFC 9334, covered in the TEE and attestation chapter) the TPM plus its agent is the Attester, Keylime's verifier the Verifier, and the scheduler or access gateway the Relying Party.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Skipping or reusing the nonce: without fresh challenge data an attacker can replay an old, good quote recorded before the compromise.
  • Verifying the signature but not replaying the log against policy: a perfectly valid quote can still describe a bad boot.
  • Trusting an AK just because the device says it is TPM-resident: insist on credential activation or a trusted AK certificate.
  • Treating attestation as runtime protection: quotes describe what was measured; unmeasured attacks such as in-memory exploits stay invisible.

docs.title: Try it: Make and verify a quote end to end (Linux, ideally on swtpm)
docs.text:
tpm2_createek -c ek.ctx -G rsa -u ek.pub
tpm2_createak -C ek.ctx -c ak.ctx -G ecc -g sha256 -s ecdsa -u ak.pem -f pem -n ak.name
tpm2_quote -c ak.ctx -l sha256:0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7 -q 0123456789abcdef \
  -m quote.msg -s quote.sig -o quote.pcrs -g sha256
tpm2_checkquote -u ak.pem -m quote.msg -s quote.sig -f quote.pcrs -g sha256 -q 0123456789abcdef

docs.text: Name What it does Example Remote attestation (TPM-based)TCG; IETF RATS architecture · Concept · General A verifier checks a TPM-signed report of a device's measurements to decide whether its software state is acceptable. A VPN gateway admits laptops only after a fresh quote shows Secure Boot on and an approved boot manager in PCR 4. TPM2_QuoteTCG TPM 2.0 Library, Part 3 · Command · Current · Platform & OS Signs a structure containing selected PCRs' digest, the verifier's nonce and TPM clock data with a restricted signing key. tpm2_quote -c ak.ctx -l sha256:0,7 -q abc123 returns quote.msg and quote.sig for the verifier to check. A verifier decodes TPMS_ATTEST to confirm extraData equals its nonce and to notice resetCount rising after a reboot. A verifier asks a gateway to NV_Certify its security-version counter, proving its firmware is version 12 or later.

docs.title: 3.10 The TPM in Windows
docs.text:
Windows uses the TPM more than any other operating system. BitLocker seals disk keys to it, Windows Hello keeps sign-in keys in it, Credential Guard uses it to protect secrets, and Microsoft's attestation services read its measurements to check device health. Windows 11 requires TPM 2.0, and Windows prepares ('provisions') the TPM automatically.

What Windows uses the TPM for. One TPM underpins disk encryption, sign-in, credential isolation and compliance.

Think of it like…

For Windows the TPM is like a hotel's front-desk safe that the hotel manages itself: guests (apps) use it every day without ever learning the combination.

Real-world example

When Nadia unboxes her company laptop, Windows Autopilot uses TPM attestation to prove the device is genuine, BitLocker seals its key to PCRs 7 and 11 and escrows the recovery password to Entra ID, and Windows Hello for Business creates a sign-in key in the TPM. Intune then checks the health report — BitLocker on, Secure Boot on, code integrity enabled — before allowing access to company email.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. TPM Base Services (TBS) shares the TPM between applications; Windows provisions the TPM automatically during setup.
  2. BitLocker seals the Volume Master Key with a TPM protector, optionally adding a PIN or USB startup key.
  3. Windows Hello and Hello for Business create non-exportable keys through the Microsoft Platform Crypto Provider; the PIN unlocks them under TPM anti-hammering.
  4. Measured-boot logs plus a TPM quote go to Microsoft's health attestation service, whose verdict feeds Intune compliance.
  5. Admins inspect and manage everything with Get-Tpm, tpm.msc, tpmtool, manage-bde and the BitLocker PowerShell cmdlets.

Who uses it

Windows and endpoint administrators, Intune and Entra ID engineers, desktop support, and security architects designing Windows device trust.

Key takeaway

Know BitLocker's protector types — TPM-only, TPM+PIN, TPM+startup key, TPM+PIN+startup key — and why TPM+PIN defeats bus-sniffing attacks.

Going deeper

  • Windows 11 (October 2021) requires TPM 2.0; in December 2024 Microsoft publicly called the requirement 'non-negotiable', ahead of Windows 10's end of support on 14 October 2025.
  • BitLocker's default profile with UEFI Secure Boot is PCRs 7 and 11; otherwise 0, 2, 4 and 11. Suspend-BitLocker -RebootCount N lets firmware updates install without recovery prompts.
  • Windows Hello for Business keys live in the Microsoft Platform Crypto Provider, a CNG key storage provider backed by the TPM; the PIN never leaves the device and is protected by TPM lockout.
  • Credential Guard isolates NTLM hashes and Kerberos secrets in the virtualisation-based security process LSAIso; where a TPM exists it protects the VBS keys, binding secrets to the device. It is enabled by default on eligible Windows 11 22H2+ enterprise devices.
  • Intune's Windows health attestation (BitLocker, Secure Boot, code integrity) uses the Device Health Attestation service; Microsoft announced in September 2026 that evaluation will move to Microsoft Azure Attestation, targeted for the end of Q1 2027.
  • Windows stores each boot's TCG log under C:\Windows\Logs\MeasuredBoot; developers reach the TPM through the TBS API (Tbsi_Context_Create, Tbsip_Submit_Command) or Microsoft's TSS.MSR libraries.
  • TPM virtual smart cards (tpmvscmgr) emulate a smart card with a TPM-protected key and PIN; Microsoft steers new deployments to Windows Hello for Business or FIDO2 security keys instead.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Clearing the TPM in tpm.msc to 'fix' a Hello error: it destroys BitLocker TPM protectors and Hello keys; make sure recovery keys are escrowed first.
  • Relying on TPM-only BitLocker for high-risk laptops: bus sniffing and boot-manager downgrade attacks such as bitpixie (CVE-2023-21563) can recover the key; add a pre-boot PIN.
  • Bypassing the Windows 11 TPM check with registry tweaks: the device becomes unsupported and loses the TPM-based protections the requirement exists for.

docs.title: 3.11 The TPM in Linux
docs.text:
On Linux the kernel provides TPM device files and uses the TPM itself for runtime measurement (IMA) and TPM-sealed 'trusted keys'. User-space libraries and tools — the tpm2-software stack — let you create keys, seal secrets and attest. Modern distributions can unlock encrypted disks through the TPM using systemd-cryptenroll or Clevis.

The Linux TPM software stack. Applications call high-level APIs; TCTI decides whether commands reach real hardware or a simulator.

Think of it like…

The kernel is the building receptionist who queues visitors for the safe, and tpm2-tools are the request forms anyone can fill in to ask the safe for a job.

Real-world example

Elena, a DevOps engineer at the fictional Fernleaf Analytics, provisions Linux servers. She binds each data volume to PCR 7 with systemd-cryptenroll for unattended reboots, enables IMA so executables are measured into PCR 10, and installs the Keylime agent to send quotes. For an older fleet she uses Clevis with tpm2 and Tang pins. Before touching production she tests everything in a VM backed by swtpm.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Kernel drivers (tpm_tis, tpm_tis_spi, tpm_tis_i2c, tpm_crb, tpm_ftpm_tee) expose /dev/tpm0 (raw) and /dev/tpmrm0 (with the in-kernel resource manager).
  2. tpm2-tss provides the TCG Software Stack APIs (FAPI, ESAPI, SAPI) and TCTI transports to the device, a simulator or a broker daemon.
  3. tpm2-tools wraps those APIs in commands such as tpm2_pcrread, tpm2_createprimary and tpm2_quote.
  4. systemd-cryptenroll or Clevis seals LUKS2 keys to the TPM; the initrd unseals them at boot.
  5. IMA and EVM measure and appraise files at runtime; kernel trusted keys are generated and sealed by the TPM.
  6. Attestation agents such as Keylime quote PCRs and send logs to a verifier.

Who uses it

Linux sysadmins and SREs, embedded Linux and distribution developers, and security engineers building attestation or disk-encryption automation.

Key takeaway

Point applications at /dev/tpmrm0, not /dev/tpm0, and remember the one-liner systemd-cryptenroll --tpm2-device=auto --tpm2-pcrs=7 for TPM disk unlock.

Going deeper

  • tpm2-tss implements the TCG TSS 2.0 specifications: FAPI (high-level, JSON policies and key paths such as /HS/SRK/mykey), ESAPI (sessions and parameter encryption), SAPI (low-level) and MU (marshalling), with TCTI modules for device, tabrmd, swtpm, mssim and libtpms.
  • The in-kernel resource manager behind /dev/tpmrm0 (since Linux 4.12) swaps contexts per process; tpm2-abrmd is an older user-space broker still found on some systems.
  • Kernel trusted keys: keyctl add trusted kmk "new 32 keyhandle=0x81000001" @u makes the TPM generate and seal a 32-byte key; encrypted keys, dm-crypt and EVM can build on it.
  • Linux 6.10 added HMAC-protected, encrypted kernel TPM sessions (CONFIG_TCG_TPM2_HMAC) to resist bus interposers; because of boot-time and PCR-extend overhead it was later made default-off upstream, with backports to 6.10+.
  • IMA measures files into PCR 10 according to policy (for example ima_policy=tcb), exposes /sys/kernel/security/ima/ascii_runtime_measurements, and can appraise file signatures; EVM protects security metadata with an HMAC or signature.
  • systemd uses the TPM widely: systemd-cryptenroll (LUKS2), systemd-pcrphase and systemd-pcrextend (boot-phase and identity measurements into PCRs 11 and 15), systemd-measure (signed UKI policies), systemd-pcrlock and systemd-creds (TPM-encrypted service credentials).
  • Clevis is a pluggable decryption framework; clevis luks bind -d /dev/sda3 tpm2 '{"pcr_ids":"7"}' adds a TPM-sealed LUKS slot, and the sss pin combines TPM with Tang network unlock.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Letting several programs use /dev/tpm0 directly: without a resource manager they collide over handles and sessions; use /dev/tpmrm0.
  • Enrolling a TPM key slot and deleting the passphrase: if PCRs change or the board fails, the data is gone. Keep a recovery key (systemd-cryptenroll --recovery-key).
  • Following TPM 1.2 guides (tcsd, tpm-tools) on modern systems: those commands do not work with TPM 2.0.

docs.title: Try it: Explore the Linux TPM stack (keep your LUKS passphrase slot!)
docs.text:
ls -l /dev/tpm*
cat /sys/class/tpm/tpm0/tpm_version_major
systemd-cryptenroll --tpm2-device=list
# On a test machine: add a TPM-bound key slot alongside your passphrase
sudo systemd-cryptenroll /dev/nvme0n1p3 --tpm2-device=auto --tpm2-pcrs=7
sudo head -5 /sys/kernel/security/ima/ascii_runtime_measurements

A high-security distribution enables CONFIG_TCG_TPM2_HMAC, accepting slower boots in exchange for protection against TPM bus sniffing.

docs.title: 3.12 TPM Vendors, Chips & Certification
docs.text:
Only a handful of companies make discrete TPM chips — mainly Infineon, Nuvoton and STMicroelectronics — while Intel, AMD and Microsoft supply firmware or on-die TPMs. Good TPMs are tested against TCG compliance suites and certified under Common Criteria and often FIPS 140, which matters for governments and regulated industries.

Who supplies TPMs. Three big discrete-chip vendors plus CPU and platform makers' firmware TPMs.

Think of it like…

Like door locks: many brands look alike, but the one with an independent burglary-resistance certificate is what insurers ask for.

Real-world example

Rahul is choosing a TPM for a fictional medical-device line. He shortlists an Infineon OPTIGA TPM SLB 9672 and an STMicroelectronics ST33 TPM, checks each is TCG-certified with Common Criteria and FIPS 140 certificates, compares temperature ranges and lifetime, and confirms signed firmware updates are available. He also checks the vendors publish their EK CA certificates so his factory can verify each chip.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Choose form factor and interface: SPI is most common in PCs, I2C in embedded designs, LPC is legacy.
  2. Check the specification level (library revision, PC Client PTP version) and algorithms (SHA-256/384, RSA-3072, ECC P-384, PQC roadmap).
  3. Verify certifications: TCG certified, Common Criteria TPM protection profile, FIPS 140-2/140-3, and automotive qualification (AEC-Q100) if needed.
  4. Check the firmware-update path and the vendor's security-advisory history.
  5. Plan EK-certificate verification and any device-identity provisioning on the production line.

Who uses it

Hardware engineers, procurement and supply-chain security teams, OEM/ODM firmware teams and compliance officers.

Key takeaway

Manufacturer IDs appear in Get-Tpm and tpm2_getcap: IFX (Infineon), NTC (Nuvoton), STM (STMicroelectronics), INTC (Intel PTT), AMD (AMD fTPM), MSFT (Pluton or Hyper-V vTPM).

Going deeper

  • Infineon's OPTIGA TPM range includes the SLB 9670 (SPI), SLB 9672 (SPI, with XMSS-protected firmware updates and NIST SP 800-193-style recovery) and SLB 9673 (I2C), plus industrial and automotive variants.
  • Nuvoton's NPCT75x TPM 2.0 chips and STMicroelectronics' ST33-based TPMs are widely used in business PCs and servers; ST also offers automotive-grade ST33 TPMs.
  • TCG's certification programme combines functional compliance testing with a Common Criteria evaluation against the TCG PC Client TPM protection profile, typically EAL4 augmented; many discrete TPMs also hold FIPS 140-2 or 140-3 certificates.
  • Vendor flaws matter: Infineon's 2017 ROCA bug (CVE-2017-15361) made on-chip RSA keys factorable, forcing firmware updates and key replacement in TPMs and national ID cards.
  • TPM 2.0 defines algorithm IDs for China's SM2, SM3 and SM4; Chinese platforms may use domestic TPM 2.0 or TCM/TPCM designs to meet national cryptography rules.
  • PQC roadmap: SEALSQ's QVault TPM implementing v1.85 ML-KEM and ML-DSA was sampling in 2026 with CC, FIPS 140-3 and TCG certification targeted, and wolfSSL released an open-source firmware TPM with v1.85 PQC support.
  • Google's Titan chips act as the TPM on Chromebooks, and Microsoft's Pluton can be the TPM on Windows PCs — their wider security-processor roles are covered in the hardware roots-of-trust chapter.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Choosing a TPM only on price: check certifications, firmware-update path and EK-certificate availability — retrofitting these later is expensive.
  • Ignoring TPM firmware updates: serious bugs such as ROCA, TPM-Fail and CVE-2023-1017 were fixed only by vendor firmware.
  • Assuming 'TPM 2.0' means government-grade: Common Criteria and FIPS certificates name specific firmware versions, and updates can change certified status.

tpm2_getcap properties-fixed | grep -A3 -E 'TPM2_PT_MANUFACTURER|TPM2_PT_VENDOR_STRING_1|TPM2_PT_FIRMWARE_VERSION_1'

# Windows PowerShell (admin)
Get-Tpm | Select-Object ManufacturerIdTxt, ManufacturerVersion, ManufacturerVersionFull20

docs.title: 3.13 TPM Attacks, Limits & Mitigations
docs.text:
TPMs are strong but not magic. Attackers with physical access can sniff the wires between a discrete TPM and the CPU, glitch firmware TPMs, exploit timing leaks or software bugs, or trick the platform into resetting PCRs. Most attacks need hands-on access and target 'TPM-only' setups; simple mitigations — a pre-boot PIN, encrypted TPM sessions and firmware updates — block most of them.

Notable TPM attacks. Almost every attack needs physical access or a firmware bug — and most have simple mitigations.

Think of it like…

A TPM is an excellent safe, but if it hands the cash to the cashier through an open window (an unencrypted bus), a thief only has to stand at the window.

Real-world example

A red team hired by the fictional Larkspur Legal tests a laptop using TPM-only BitLocker with a discrete TPM. With authorisation, they clip a cheap logic probe onto the TPM bus, boot the machine and capture the Volume Master Key in under a minute. The firm responds by requiring TPM+PIN through Intune and preferring firmware-TPM models; the repeated test yields nothing usable.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Define the threat model: remote attacker, malicious insider, thief with minutes, or a lab with hours and equipment.
  2. Find where secrets leave the TPM (bus traffic, RAM after unsealing) and where firmware or measuring code could lie.
  3. Apply mitigations: pre-boot PIN, salted and encrypted sessions, DRTM, PIN-including policies and firmware updates.
  4. Track advisories from TCG, Intel, AMD, Microsoft and TPM vendors, and patch TPM firmware like any other firmware.
  5. Test with authorised physical red-team exercises on representative hardware.

Who uses it

Authorised penetration testers and red teams, platform-security engineers, endpoint architects and auditors assessing disk-encryption risk.

Key takeaway

The one sentence to remember: TPM-only BitLocker is vulnerable to physical attacks, and TPM+PIN closes most of them.

Going deeper

  • Bus sniffing works because TPM-only BitLocker unseals the key in plaintext over LPC, SPI or I2C; public demonstrations ran from 2019 onwards, including a 2024 Raspberry Pi Pico capture in about 43 seconds. TPM+PIN, firmware TPMs or parameter encryption defeat it.
  • TPM-Fail (2019) recovered ECDSA and ECSchnorr keys through timing leaks in Intel PTT (CVE-2019-11090) and an STMicroelectronics ST33 TPM (CVE-2019-16863), including a remote attack on a VPN server; vendors shipped constant-time fixes.
  • faulTPM (TU Berlin, 2023) used about $200 of equipment to glitch the voltage of AMD's Secure Processor on Zen 2 and Zen 3 chips, extracting all fTPM secrets after hours of physical access — bypassing anti-hammering, so short PINs could then be brute-forced offline.
  • Reset attacks: Bernhard Kauer (2007) showed that resetting a discrete TPM independently of the CPU returns PCRs to zero; the 2018 'A Bad Dream' work (CVE-2018-6622) abused S3 sleep handling so software could replay fake measurements.
  • Reference-code bugs spread widely because most TPMs derive from the TCG code: CVE-2023-1017/1018 (Quarkslab) were out-of-bounds write/read in parameter decryption, and CVE-2025-2884 an out-of-bounds read in CryptHmacSign, fixed via TCG errata and vendor updates.
  • Some attacks avoid the TPM entirely: 'bitpixie' (CVE-2023-21563) boots an older, still-trusted Windows Boot Manager over the network so the key is left in memory — again blocked by a pre-boot PIN.
  • Inherent limits: the TPM only knows what it is told; compromised early firmware or a broken CRTM can report false measurements, and secrets already unsealed into RAM are outside its protection.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Believing firmware TPMs are immune to physical attack: they avoid bus sniffing but inherit security-processor flaws such as faulTPM.
  • Assuming any PIN is enough: if the TPM itself is broken, short PINs can be brute-forced offline — use longer enhanced PINs for high-risk users.
  • Treating TPM attacks as remote threats: almost all need physical access or local admin rights, so prioritise by who can touch your devices.

docs.title: 3.14 Programming & Testing TPMs
docs.text:
You do not need special hardware to learn the TPM. Software simulators such as swtpm and the IBM and Microsoft/TCG reference simulators behave like real TPMs, so you can script tpm2-tools, write Python, Go, C or C# code, and even give a test virtual machine its own TPM. Libraries handle the complex byte formats and sessions for you.

A safe path from simulator to hardware. Learn and test on software TPMs; confirm on real chips last.

Think of it like…

A TPM simulator is like a flight simulator: you practise every manoeuvre safely before touching the real aircraft.

Real-world example

Kofi, a student, starts swtpm in a terminal, points tpm2-tools at it with TPM2TOOLS_TCTI and practises sealing and quoting. He then writes a short Python script using tpm2-pytss to create a primary key and sign data, and a Go service with go-tpm that verifies quotes. Finally he runs a QEMU virtual machine with an swtpm-backed vTPM to test systemd-cryptenroll before touching his real laptop.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Start a simulator (swtpm, IBM's ibmswtpm2 or the TCG/Microsoft reference simulator) on a TCP port or socket.
  2. Point your stack at it with a TCTI string such as swtpm:port=2321 or mssim:host=localhost,port=2321.
  3. Send TPM2_Startup(CLEAR) with tpm2_startup -c if the simulator does not do it automatically.
  4. Script tasks with tpm2-tools, then move to a library: tpm2-pytss, go-tpm, TSS.MSR, IBM TSS or wolfTPM.
  5. Run simulators in CI, then verify on real hardware, where timing, algorithms and EK certificates differ.

Who uses it

Students, firmware and OS developers, attestation and product engineers, and QA teams building CI pipelines for TPM-dependent software.

Key takeaway

Always prototype against a simulator first — a mistaken TPM2_Clear or lockout costs nothing there, but on your laptop it can cost your BitLocker and Windows Hello keys.

Going deeper

  • swtpm, maintained by Stefan Berger and built on the libtpms library, emulates TPM 1.2 and 2.0 and is the backend libvirt/QEMU use for VM vTPMs, e.g. <tpm model='tpm-crb'><backend type='emulator' version='2.0'/></tpm>.
  • IBM's TPM 2.0 simulator (ibmswtpm2) and IBM TSS, by Ken Goldman, are long-standing C references; the TCG/Microsoft reference implementation (ms-tpm-20-ref, also published under the TrustedComputingGroup GitHub organisation) builds the official simulator and underpins many firmware TPMs.
  • Language bindings: tpm2-pytss (Python ESAPI and FAPI), go-tpm and go-tpm-tools (Go, by Google), TSS.MSR (Microsoft: C#, C++, Java, JavaScript, Python), the Rust tss-esapi crate (used by Keylime's agent and Parsec) and wolfTPM (embedded C).
  • tpm2-pytss exposes ESAPI calls such as create_primary, create, load, sign and unseal as Python methods, plus FAPI's path-based API (keys under /HS/SRK/), with a TCTI string choosing device or simulator.
  • Simulators start without vendor EK certificates; swtpm_setup --create-ek-cert with swtpm_localca issues test EK certificates from a local CA so attestation code can be exercised end to end.
  • Debugging: TSS2_LOG=all+debug traces tpm2-tss calls, and tpm2_rc_decode explains response codes — for example 0x921 is TPM_RC_LOCKOUT.
  • Learning resources: Google's tpm-js runs a TPM simulator in the browser, the tpm2-software community publishes tutorials, and 'A Practical Guide to TPM 2.0' (Arthur, Challener, Goldman; Apress 2015, open access) remains the standard book.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming simulator behaviour equals hardware: real TPMs are slower, may lack algorithms, enforce lockout and carry vendor EK certificates.
  • Experimenting on your laptop's real TPM: a clear or lockout can wipe BitLocker and Hello keys; use swtpm or a VM.
  • Leaving transient objects and sessions loaded in scripts: TPMs have few slots; flush with tpm2_flushcontext -t and -s, or use /dev/tpmrm0.

docs.title: Try it: Run a software TPM and talk to it with tpm2-tools
docs.text:
mkdir -p /tmp/mytpm
swtpm socket --tpm2 --tpmstate dir=/tmp/mytpm \
  --server type=tcp,port=2321 --ctrl type=tcp,port=2322 \
  --flags not-need-init,startup-clear &
export TPM2TOOLS_TCTI="swtpm:port=2321"
tpm2_getcap properties-fixed | head -20
tpm2_getrandom --hex 16

docs.title: Chapter 1: Trust Foundations
docs.text: Before learning chips, TPMs and certificate authorities, you need the core ideas they all share: what trust means, what roots and chains of trust are, the bits of cryptography that make them work and the threats they defend against. This chapter gives you those foundations and a map of how hardware roots of trust, TPMs, boot security, trusted execution and PKI fit together — each later chapter fills in one part of the map.

docs.title: 1.1 What "Trust" Means in Computing
docs.text:
In security, to trust a component means you rely on it to behave correctly — if it misbehaves, your protection fails and you may not even notice. "Trusted" describes that dependence; "trustworthy" means there is good evidence the component deserves it. Good security design keeps the list of trusted things short and works hard to make each one trustworthy.

What one web login silently trusts. Every layer relies on the layers beneath it, so the bottom of the stack matters most.

Think of it like…

Giving a neighbour your spare house key makes them trusted whether or not they are honest — if they misuse it, you are burgled. You would pick someone with a track record (trustworthy) and hand over only the front-door key, not the safe combination.

Real-world example

Maya, the new IT lead at the fictional Harbour Credit Union, lists everything a member's online-banking login silently depends on: the laptop's firmware, the operating system, the browser, the root certificates inside it, DNS and the bank's TLS server key. She notices that tampered firmware could quietly undermine every other item on the list. That insight drives her next purchase: laptops with a hardware root of trust, measured boot and a TPM, so the bottom of the stack can be checked rather than just assumed.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Name the asset you are protecting (money, patient records, a signing key).
  2. List every component that could break that protection if it misbehaved — these are your trust dependencies.
  3. Draw trust boundaries where data or control passes between parts you trust differently.
  4. Remove or shrink dependencies you do not need, so less has to be trusted.
  5. Gather evidence for what remains: certification, audits, open review, signatures and attestation.
  6. Re-check over time — keys leak, vendors change and bugs are found, so trust decays.

Who uses it

Security architects, threat modellers, platform and PKI engineers, auditors and anyone who writes a security design document starts from this list of trust assumptions.

Key takeaway

Memorise the classic definition: a trusted component is one whose failure can break your security — so 'trusted' is a warning label, not a compliment.

Going deeper

  • A useful exercise is the 'trust inventory': for one asset, list every hardware, firmware, software, person and organisation that could defeat its protection. Most inventories reveal dozens of entries nobody consciously chose.
  • Trust is directional and scoped: a CA trusted to vouch for web servers is not automatically trusted to sign code. Certificates express this with Extended Key Usage, and roots of trust with separate keys per purpose.
  • Evidence for trustworthiness comes in several forms — formal verification (e.g. the seL4 microkernel), independent certification (Common Criteria, FIPS 140-3), transparency (open source, Certificate Transparency logs) and runtime evidence (attestation).
  • Trust has a time dimension: keys expire, algorithms weaken (SHA-1, RSA-1024), and vendors stop patching. Good designs plan for rotating keys, revoking certificates and updating trusted code.
  • Insiders and suppliers are trust dependencies too. Supply-chain security frameworks such as NIST SP 800-161 and SLSA treat the people and build systems that produce code as part of what you trust.
  • Reducing trust is often cheaper than proving trustworthiness: removing an unneeded admin account or driver eliminates a dependency, whereas evaluating it can take months.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Treating 'trusted' as meaning 'safe'. It only means 'relied upon'; a trusted component that is compromised is the worst kind of failure.
  • Listing only software in a trust inventory. Firmware, hardware, manufacturers, administrators and certificate authorities belong on the list too.
  • Assuming trust once granted stays valid forever. Revisit trust decisions when keys leak, vendors change or new attacks appear.

# Linux (Debian/Ubuntu)

# macOS

docs.title: Key chips, standards, protocols, products & terms
docs.text: Name What it does Example TrustGeneral security engineering · Concept · General Relying on a component to behave as expected, accepting that its failure or betrayal would break your security goals. A web browser trusts about 150 root CAs; any one of them could issue a certificate the browser would accept. Trusted vs trustworthySecurity engineering literature · Concept · General Trusted means you depend on it; trustworthy means evidence shows it deserves that dependence. Aim for components that are both. An unvetted USB driver running in the kernel is trusted (it can do anything) but not shown to be trustworthy. Trust boundaryThreat modelling (e.g. Microsoft STRIDE) · Concept · General A line in a design where data or control crosses between parts trusted to different degrees; checks belong there. Data entering a TPM from the operating system crosses a trust boundary, so the TPM validates every command. Trust assumptionSecurity design practice · Concept · General Something a design takes for granted without proof, such as 'the boot ROM has no bugs' or 'the CA checked identity'. A secure-boot design assumes the vendor's signing key never leaks; the 2023 MSI key leak broke exactly that assumption. Threat modelOWASP, Microsoft STRIDE, MITRE ATT&CK · Concept · General A structured description of what you protect, from whom, how attackers could act and which risks you accept. Harbour Credit Union's laptop threat model includes theft in taxis but excludes nation-state chip decapping. Trust anchorRFC 5280, RFC 5914 · Concept · General A key or certificate accepted directly, without further proof, at the top of a verification chain. A browser's root store and a CPU's fused public-key hash are both trust anchors for different chains. Transitive trustTCG architecture · Concept · General Trusting B because trusted A vouched for it — the basis of boot chains and certificate chains, and weaker with every hop. Firmware trusts the bootloader because its signature verifies; the bootloader then vouches for the kernel. Least privilegeSaltzer & Schroeder design principles (1975) · Concept · General Give each component only the access it needs, so a trusted part that fails can do limited damage. A firmware-update service can write the flash region but cannot read the disk-encryption key. Defence in depthSecurity architecture practice · Concept · General Layering independent protections so one broken layer does not lose everything. Secure boot blocks unsigned bootloaders; measured boot plus attestation catches anything that slips past. AssuranceISO/IEC 15408 Common Criteria, FIPS 140-3 · Concept · General The level of confidence, gained through evaluation, testing and review, that a component really meets its security claims. A smart-card chip evaluated at EAL6+ offers more assurance than an unevaluated microcontroller. Zero trustNIST SP 800-207 (2020) · Concept · Current · General An architecture that never trusts by network location; every request is authenticated and checked against device and user state. Before opening the payroll app, the gateway checks Maya's identity plus her laptop's attested health. Relying partyRFC 5280, IETF RATS RFC 9334 · Role · General Whoever depends on a certificate or attestation result to make a decision, and therefore bears the risk if it is wrong. The bank's login server is the relying party when it checks a laptop's device certificate.

docs.title: 1.2 The Trusted Computing Base (TCB)
docs.text:
The trusted computing base is the complete set of hardware, firmware and software that must work correctly for a system's security rules to hold. Anything outside the TCB can misbehave without breaking those rules; anything inside it cannot. Security engineers try to keep the TCB as small and simple as possible, because every extra line of trusted code is another place for a fatal bug.

Big TCB vs small TCB for one secret key

Key in an ordinary app Key inside a secure element Trusted code size Tens of millions of lines Thousands of lines Who can read the key Kernel, drivers, admins, malware Only the chip's own firmware Attack surface Hundreds of system calls, drivers A small command set Evidence of quality Usually none independent Certified (e.g. CC EAL5+) Cost and flexibility Free, flexible Extra chip, limited features

Moving a key into a dedicated security chip removes millions of lines from what must be trusted.

Think of it like…

In a bank, the TCB is the vault door, the guards and the alarm system — not the carpets or the coffee machine. If the coffee machine breaks, the money is still safe; if the vault door fails, it is not.

Real-world example

Leon, a student at the fictional Ridgeway Polytechnic, compares two designs for a password manager. In design A the decryption key lives in an ordinary process, so the whole operating system kernel, every driver and the app itself are in the TCB — tens of millions of lines of code. In design B the key never leaves a secure element that runs a few thousand lines of evaluated code. Design B's TCB for the key is thousands of times smaller, so there is far less that can go wrong.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Pick the security property you care about, such as 'only Ana can read this file'.
  2. Trace every component that enforces or could bypass that property — kernel, firmware, hypervisor, CPU microcode, security chip.
  3. Everything on that trace is in the TCB; everything else is untrusted and must be checked at the boundary.
  4. Shrink the TCB by moving secrets into smaller isolated components (TPM, secure element, enclave).
  5. Harden and verify what remains: code review, formal methods, certification, measured and signed updates.

Who uses it

Operating-system and hypervisor designers, platform security engineers, evaluators writing Common Criteria security targets and confidential-computing architects all reason in TCB terms.

Key takeaway

In interviews, describe the TCB as 'the parts that must be correct for security to hold' and explain why smaller is better — fewer lines, fewer bugs, easier to verify.

Going deeper

  • The TCSEC (Orange Book) defined the TCB in the early 1980s and graded systems D, C1, C2, B1, B2, B3 and A1; Common Criteria (ISO/IEC 15408) replaced it internationally from 1999 with EAL1-EAL7.
  • A reference monitor's three classic properties — complete mediation, tamper-proofness and verifiability — still guide TPM, hypervisor and enclave design today.
  • Modern TCBs include things people forget: CPU microcode, the management engine, BMC firmware in servers, peripheral firmware with DMA access and the compilers that built trusted code.
  • Confidential computing explicitly shrinks the TCB by removing the hypervisor and host OS; the remaining TCB is the CPU, its security firmware and the guest itself — which is why CPU firmware bugs matter so much there.
  • TCB size is measured loosely in lines of code: seL4's verified kernel is around 10,000 lines of C, compared with tens of millions for a general-purpose OS kernel plus drivers.
  • TCB recovery is a related idea: after a vulnerability in trusted firmware is fixed, a platform must prove (for example via a new security version in attestation) that it now runs the patched TCB.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Thinking the TCB is just the security software you installed. It includes the kernel, firmware, hardware and anything with DMA or privileged access.
  • Adding features to trusted components for convenience. Every feature in the TCB enlarges what must be correct; push non-essential code outside it.
  • Assuming a small TCB is automatically secure. Small helps, but it still needs review, testing, patching and protection from physical attack.

docs.title: Try it: See how big part of your own TCB is — count loaded kernel modules and drivers
docs.text:
# Linux: every loaded module runs with full kernel privilege
lsmod | wc -l
# Windows PowerShell: running kernel drivers
(Get-CimInstance Win32_SystemDriver | Where-Object State -eq 'Running').Count

docs.title: Key chips, standards, protocols, products & terms
docs.text: Name What it does Example Trusted computing base (TCB)US DoD TCSEC 'Orange Book' (DoD 5200.28-STD, 1985) · Concept · General All hardware, firmware and software whose correct behaviour is required to enforce a system's security policy. For BitLocker, the TCB includes the TPM, UEFI firmware, Windows Boot Manager and the Windows kernel. Orange Book (TCSEC)US Department of Defense, 1983/1985 · Standard · Legacy · General The early US evaluation criteria that defined the TCB and rated systems from D to A1; replaced by Common Criteria. 1980s secure operating systems were sold as 'B2' or 'A1' rated under the Orange Book. Reference monitorAnderson Report, US Air Force (1972) · Concept · General A component that checks every access; it must be always invoked, tamper-proof and small enough to verify. An operating system's access-control check on every file open is meant to behave as a reference monitor. Attack surfaceSecurity engineering practice · Concept · General All the interfaces an attacker can reach — commands, ports, files, buses — that lead into trusted code. A TPM's attack surface is its command interface; a full OS kernel exposes hundreds of system calls. Privilege levels (rings)x86 rings 0-3, Arm exception levels EL0-EL3 · Concept · Platform & OS Hardware-enforced levels that stop less-privileged code from touching more-privileged code and data. Apps run at EL0, the Linux kernel at EL1, a hypervisor at EL2 and secure monitor firmware at EL3 on Arm. MicrokernelDesigns such as seL4, QNX, MINIX 3 · Concept · Platform & OS A kernel that keeps only essentials in privileged mode and runs drivers outside it, shrinking the TCB. A medical-device maker picks a microkernel so a buggy USB driver cannot crash the insulin-dosing logic. seL4seL4 Foundation (Linux Foundation) · Software · Current · Platform & OS A microkernel with machine-checked mathematical proof that its C code matches its specification — a rare, fully verified TCB component. Defence and aviation projects choose seL4 when they need strong evidence the kernel cannot be subverted. IsolationHardware MMU, IOMMU, TrustZone, enclaves · Concept · General Keeping components in separate protected compartments so one cannot read or change another's memory. A TPM, a secure enclave and a confidential VM each isolate secrets from the main operating system. Separation of privilegeSaltzer & Schroeder (1975) · Concept · General Requiring two independent conditions or parties for a sensitive action, so one failure is not enough. Unsealing a disk key needs both correct boot measurements and the user's PIN. Formal verificationProof assistants such as Isabelle/HOL, Coq/Rocq · Concept · General Mathematically proving code or hardware meets a specification, giving the strongest evidence for a small TCB. Parts of the OpenTitan and Caliptra projects use formal property checking to verify security-critical hardware blocks. Security targetISO/IEC 15408 Common Criteria · Concept · General A document defining exactly what a product's TCB (the 'TOE security functionality') protects, against which threats, for evaluation. A smart-card vendor's security target lists the threats its chip resists, such as fault injection. Confidential computing TCBConfidential Computing Consortium (Linux Foundation) · Concept · Current · Trusted execution In confidential VMs and enclaves, the cloud host is removed from the TCB, leaving the CPU and a little firmware. A hospital's analytics VM no longer has to trust the cloud provider's hypervisor administrators.

docs.title: 1.3 Threats That Roots of Trust Defend Against
docs.text:
Roots of trust exist because some attacks hide below the operating system or happen before it starts, where antivirus cannot see them. Typical threats are malicious firmware (rootkits and bootkits), tampering in the supply chain, someone with brief physical access (the 'evil maid'), stolen laptops and disks, devices pretending to be something they are not, and attackers rolling software back to an old, buggy version.

Threat versus the defence that counters it

Threat Main hardware-rooted defence Firmware rootkit Persists in flash Silicon RoT verifies firmware Bootkit Replaces bootloader UEFI Secure Boot Evil maid Brief physical access Measured boot + TPM PIN Stolen disk Offline reading TPM-sealed encryption Impersonation Fake device or server Hardware-bound keys + PKI Rollback Old signed firmware Anti-rollback counters Supply chain Factory or transit change Attestation vs reference values

Each defence relies on something trusted that runs before, or beneath, the attacker.

Think of it like…

Antivirus is a security guard inside the building; firmware attacks are like someone who rewired the building before the guard arrived. You need a check that runs first, from something the attacker could not rewire.

Real-world example

Tomás, a journalist working for the fictional Lantern News, leaves his laptop in a hotel room. An intruder could boot it from USB, copy the disk or flash modified firmware that logs his password. Full-disk encryption sealed to the TPM defeats the disk copy; secure boot stops the USB bootkit; measured boot plus attestation would let Lantern's IT team notice changed firmware. Each defence relies on something trusted that runs before the attacker's code.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Attackers aim for persistence and stealth: code that survives OS reinstall and runs before security tools.
  2. Firmware, bootloaders and peripheral controllers are attractive because they start first and are rarely inspected.
  3. Physical access enables disk theft, booting other media, flashing chips or sniffing buses.
  4. Supply-chain attacks insert changes before the device reaches you — at the factory, distributor or update server.
  5. Roots of trust counter these by verifying code before it runs, recording what ran, and protecting keys in hardware.

Who uses it

Threat-intelligence analysts, firmware security researchers, endpoint-security teams and procurement officers buying hardware for high-risk staff all reason about these threats.

Key takeaway

Remember the pairing: secure boot mainly stops bootkits, measured boot plus attestation detects tampering, TPM-sealed encryption protects stolen disks, and hardware identity stops impersonation.

Going deeper

  • MITRE ATT&CK lists pre-OS persistence under techniques such as T1542 (Pre-OS Boot) with sub-techniques for system firmware, component firmware and bootkits — useful vocabulary for threat reports.
  • Firmware threats are attractive because the code runs with the highest privilege, before endpoint tools load, and is rarely scanned; NIST SP 800-193 therefore asks platforms to protect, detect and recover firmware.
  • Physical-access threats come in tiers: minutes (evil maid, booting USB), hours (opening the case, flashing SPI chips, sniffing the TPM bus) and lab-grade (decapping, fault injection). Defences are chosen per tier.
  • Supply-chain defences combine signed firmware, manufacturer device certificates, platform certificates (TCG) that describe the as-built configuration, and attestation compared against reference values.
  • Rollback attacks are subtle because the old image is genuinely signed; only a monotonic security version stored in fuses, a TPM NV counter or replay-protected memory can refuse it.
  • Leaked signing keys turn verification against you: firmware or bootloaders signed with a leaked key pass every check until the key is revoked in fuses, dbx or a certificate revocation list.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Believing reinstalling the OS removes all malware. Firmware rootkits survive reinstalls; only reflashing from a trusted source, ideally verified by a root of trust, does.
  • Assuming disk encryption alone stops an evil maid. Without secure or measured boot, an attacker can trojan the unlock screen and capture the passphrase.
  • Treating physical security as 'out of scope' for laptops and IoT. These devices are lost, stolen and handled by strangers every day.

# Linux

docs.text: Name What it does Example Firmware rootkitDocumented by ESET, Kaspersky and others since 2018 · Attack · Firmware & boot Malware implanted in UEFI or other firmware so it survives disk wipes and OS reinstalls. LoJax (2018) was the first UEFI rootkit found in the wild; chapter 30 covers it and its successors. An attacker flashes last year's signed firmware with a known bug; anti-rollback counters refuse it. A rogue Thunderbolt adapter dumps RAM from a locked laptop unless the IOMMU and Kernel DMA Protection are on. A distributor ships cloned network cards; genuine parts prove identity with manufacturer-signed certificates. Requiring two people and an HSM to sign firmware stops one rogue engineer releasing a backdoor. A café Wi-Fi attacker presents a fake certificate; certificate validation in the browser rejects it.

docs.title: 1.4 #️⃣ Crypto Refresher I: Hashes, MACs & Key Derivation
docs.text:
A hash function turns any data into a short fixed-size fingerprint; change one bit of input and the fingerprint changes completely. A MAC (message authentication code) is a hash mixed with a secret key, so only key holders can produce a valid tag. Key derivation functions (KDFs) turn one secret into many purpose-specific keys. Roots of trust use all three constantly: hashes to measure code, MACs to protect data, KDFs to build key hierarchies.

From one device secret to many keys. A root of trust never uses its master secret directly; it derives purpose-specific keys.

Think of it like…

A hash is a fingerprint: tiny, unique to the person, and you cannot rebuild the person from it. A MAC is a wax seal pressed with a private signet ring. A KDF is a master key cutter that makes a different key for every door from one master blank.

Real-world example

Priya, a firmware engineer at the fictional Kestrel Devices, computes the SHA-256 hash of the new bootloader and gets a 64-hex-digit value. The TPM extends that value into a PCR during boot. Separately, the device's secure element derives a storage key with HKDF from its fused device secret and the label 'config-encryption-v1', and protects the configuration file with an HMAC tag so any tampering is detected at next boot.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Hash: feed in data of any size, get a fixed-size digest (SHA-256 gives 32 bytes).
  2. Compare digests to check integrity — equal digests mean identical data, with overwhelming probability.
  3. MAC: combine a secret key with the data (e.g. HMAC-SHA-256) to get a tag only key holders can compute.
  4. KDF: input a secret plus context labels; output one or more independent keys of the size you need.
  5. Use different derived keys for different purposes so one leaked key does not expose the others.

Who uses it

Firmware, TPM and HSM developers, protocol designers and anyone reading boot logs or certificate fingerprints use hashes, MACs and KDFs daily.

Key takeaway

Know the difference: a hash proves integrity only if the digest itself is protected; a MAC proves integrity and origin among key holders; only a digital signature proves origin to everyone.

Going deeper

  • Digest sizes worth memorising: SHA-1 160 bits (20 bytes), SHA-256 256 bits (32 bytes), SHA-384 384 bits (48 bytes), SHA-512 512 bits (64 bytes). Collision security is roughly half the digest length.
  • SHA-256 and SHA-512 are vulnerable to length-extension if misused as 'hash(key ‖ message)'; HMAC's nested construction avoids this, which is why you should never invent your own keyed hash.
  • TPM PCR extension is itself a hash chain: new PCR = H(old PCR ‖ measurement). Because hashing is one-way, nobody can set a PCR to a chosen value without replaying the exact sequence of measurements.
  • KDFs separate keys by purpose using labels and context. TPM 2.0 uses KDFa (SP 800-108 counter mode with HMAC) for symmetric keys and KDFe (SP 800-56A) for ECDH-derived secrets.
  • Hardware roots of trust usually implement SHA-2 and HMAC in silicon and increasingly SHA-3/SHAKE, because ML-DSA and ML-KEM need Keccak-based functions internally.
  • Constant-time comparison matters: checking a MAC tag byte by byte and stopping at the first mismatch leaks timing that can let an attacker forge tags one byte at a time.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Using a plain hash to protect data from an attacker who can also change the stored hash. Use a MAC or signature, or keep the reference hash in protected storage.
  • Calling hashing 'encryption'. Hashes are one-way and keyless; nothing is decrypted from a digest.
  • Reusing one key for several purposes. Derive separate keys with a KDF and distinct labels.

docs.title: Try it: Hash a file, then make an HMAC of it with a key
docs.text:
echo 'bootloader v1' > boot.bin
sha256sum boot.bin                         # Linux/macOS
openssl dgst -sha256 -hmac 'demo-key' boot.bin
# Windows PowerShell
Get-FileHash .\boot.bin -Algorithm SHA256

Admins confirm a root certificate by comparing its SHA-256 fingerprint with the CA's published value. docs.title: 1.5 Crypto Refresher II: Asymmetric Keys & Digital Signatures
docs.text:
Asymmetric cryptography uses a key pair: a private key kept secret and a public key you can give to anyone. Signing data with the private key produces a digital signature that anyone holding the public key can check, proving who signed and that nothing changed. This is how firmware, bootloaders, certificates and attestation reports prove where they came from.

Signing firmware and verifying it at boot. The device trusts the result only because the public key's hash is fixed in hardware.

Think of it like…

A public key is like a padlock design everyone can recognise; the private key is the one stamp that leaves that exact imprint. Anyone can compare an imprint to the design, but only the stamp's owner can make one.

Real-world example

Kestrel Devices signs every firmware release with an ECDSA P-384 private key kept in an HSM. The matching public key's hash is burned into each chip's fuses at the factory. When a sensor boots, its boot ROM hashes the new firmware, checks the signature with the public key and compares the key's hash to the fuses. A forged image or a swapped public key both fail, so the sensor refuses to run it.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Generate a key pair inside protected hardware (HSM, TPM, secure element).
  2. Publish or embed the public key; keep the private key locked away.
  3. To sign: hash the data, then compute a signature over the digest with the private key.
  4. To verify: recompute the hash and check the signature with the public key.
  5. Trust the public key itself only because it is fused in hardware, pinned, or certified by a trusted CA.

Who uses it

Firmware signers, PKI engineers, release engineers, TPM and HSM developers and anyone validating certificates or code signatures rely on asymmetric crypto.

Key takeaway

Remember: encrypt with the recipient's public key, sign with your own private key — and a signature is only as trustworthy as the way you obtained the public key.

Going deeper

  • Signature sizes matter in boot ROMs and certificates: ECDSA P-256 signatures are about 64 bytes, RSA-2048 256 bytes, ML-DSA-44 2,420 bytes, ML-DSA-87 4,627 bytes and SLH-DSA from about 7.8 KB up to roughly 50 KB.
  • Security levels: RSA-2048 and P-256 give roughly 112- and 128-bit classical security; P-384 about 192-bit. None of them resists a large quantum computer running Shor's algorithm, which is why PQC is being added.
  • FIPS 186-5 (February 2023) added EdDSA and deterministic ECDSA and withdrew DSA for new signatures; FIPS 203, 204 and 205 (August 2024) standardised ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA.
  • ECDSA needs a fresh secret nonce per signature; reusing or leaking nonce bits reveals the private key, as famously happened with Sony's PlayStation 3 signing key in 2010.
  • Hardware roots of trust usually store only a hash of the vendor public key in fuses (to save space) and receive the full key alongside the firmware, checking it against the fused hash first.
  • Hybrid or composite approaches sign with both a classical and a post-quantum algorithm during the transition, so security holds if either remains unbroken.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Saying 'sign with the public key'. You sign with the private key and verify with the public key.
  • Verifying a signature with a public key that arrived alongside the data without anchoring it. An attacker simply signs with their own key and ships it too.
  • Assuming signed means safe. A signature proves who released the code, not that it is free of bugs — old signed versions can still be dangerous.

docs.title: Try it: Make an ECDSA key pair, sign a file and verify it
docs.text:
openssl genpkey -algorithm EC -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -out priv.pem
openssl pkey -in priv.pem -pubout -out pub.pem
openssl dgst -sha256 -sign priv.pem -out fw.sig boot.bin
openssl dgst -sha256 -verify pub.pem -signature fw.sig boot.bin   # Verified OK

An eIDAS qualified signature on a contract is hard to deny because the key lives on a certified device.
