docs.title: 1.6 The Chain of Trust
docs.text:
A chain of trust is a series of steps where each trusted component checks the next one before handing over control or vouching for it. If every link verifies the next, the final result can be trusted as much as the first link. The first link — the one nobody checks — is the root of trust. Boot sequences and certificate chains are both chains of trust.

Two chains of trust on one laptop. Code chains and certificate chains look different but follow the same rule: each link checks the next.

Think of it like…

It is like a relay race where each runner checks the next runner's ID badge before passing the baton. If the first runner is genuine and nobody skips a check, the runner crossing the finish line is genuine too.

Real-world example

When Ana's work laptop starts, the processor's boot ROM verifies the firmware's signature, the firmware verifies the Windows Boot Manager against its Secure Boot database, and the boot manager verifies the Windows kernel. Later, her browser verifies a website certificate against an intermediate CA, which it verifies against a root CA in its trust store. Two different chains — one for code, one for identity — each start from an anchor she never had to check herself.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Start from a root of trust that is trusted by design (immutable ROM, fused key hash, root CA in a trust store).
  2. The current link verifies the next link's signature or measurement before using it.
  3. If verification passes, control (or trust) passes to the next link, which repeats the process.
  4. If any link fails, the chain stops — refuse to boot, fall back to recovery or reject the certificate.
  5. Optionally record each step (measured boot, CT logs) so others can audit the chain later.

Who uses it

Firmware and boot engineers, PKI engineers and anyone troubleshooting 'certificate chain incomplete' or 'secure boot violation' errors work with chains of trust.

Key takeaway

A chain is only as strong as its weakest link and its root: an unsigned stage, a skipped check or a leaked key anywhere breaks everything after it.

Going deeper

  • Two styles exist: a verifying chain (secure boot, certificate validation) blocks bad links, while a measuring chain (measured boot) records each link so a remote verifier can judge later. Many platforms do both.
  • Chains add trust transitively but also add risk: each link's own bugs become part of the TCB. Long chains — such as shim → GRUB → kernel → modules on Linux — need every stage to enforce verification.
  • The root of a boot chain is often split: immutable boot ROM code plus a public-key hash in one-time-programmable fuses. The ROM cannot be patched, but keys can sometimes be revoked by burning additional fuses.
  • Certificate chains are built by the relying party, not dictated by the server; path-building may find alternative routes through cross-signed certificates to different roots (chapter 50 covers path validation).
  • Verify-then-execute must protect against TOCTOU: good designs verify code inside internal SRAM or lock the flash interface so the verified bytes are the bytes that run.
  • Recovery is part of the chain design: NIST SP 800-193 expects a platform to detect corruption and restore authorised firmware automatically rather than leaving the device bricked.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming a chain is secure because the first and last links are signed. One unverified middle stage (an unsigned GRUB module, a missing intermediate check) lets attackers in.
  • Forgetting revocation. A chain that cannot distrust a leaked key or a vulnerable signed image stays exploitable forever.
  • Believing the root of trust is checked by something. By definition it is not; that is why it must be small, immutable or tightly protected.

docs.title: Try it: See a real certificate chain from a website down to a root
docs.text: openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -showcerts </dev/null 2>/dev/null | grep -E 's:|i:'

docs.title: 1.7 Roots of Trust Defined: RTM, RTS, RTR and Friends
docs.text:
A root of trust (RoT) is a component that must behave correctly because nothing can check it — misbehaviour would go undetected. Standards split roots of trust by job: one measures code, one stores secrets, one reports what was measured, and others verify, update, detect and recover. Some roots are immutable (fixed in silicon forever); others are updatable but tightly protected.

The jobs a root of trust can do. TCG names the first three; NIST SP 800-193 adds update, detection and recovery.

Think of it like…

A notary public is a root of trust for signatures: courts accept a notarised document without re-checking, so the notary's integrity matters enormously. A town might have separate trusted officials for measuring land, storing deeds and reporting records — just as a platform has separate roots for measurement, storage and reporting.

Real-world example

In a laptop built by the fictional Corvid Computing, the core root of trust for measurement is the first firmware block, verified by the CPU's boot ROM, which hashes the rest of the firmware. The TPM is the root of trust for storage, holding keys inside shielded locations, and for reporting, signing PCR values in quotes. A separate platform root of trust chip in Corvid's servers acts as the roots for update, detection and recovery of the BIOS flash.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Identify the security function: measuring, storing, reporting, verifying, updating, detecting or recovering.
  2. Assign one small, protected component as the root for each function — often several roots live in one chip.
  3. Decide immutable or updatable: ROM and fuses cannot change; updatable roots need signed, rollback-protected updates.
  4. Build chains of trust from each root outward (measurement chain, key hierarchy, update chain).
  5. Protect each root physically and logically in proportion to the threats you face.

Who uses it

Platform architects, TPM and firmware engineers, chip designers writing security specifications and evaluators reviewing NIST SP 800-193 compliance use these terms.

Key takeaway

Memorise the TCG trio — RTM (measurement), RTS (storage), RTR (reporting) — and the NIST SP 800-193 trio — update, detection, recovery.

Going deeper

  • TCG's definition: a root of trust is a component that must always behave in the expected manner because its misbehaviour cannot be detected. The TPM provides RTS and RTR; the RTM lives in platform firmware or CPU logic.
  • In TCG terms the CRTM is the first measuring code; on modern PCs Intel Boot Guard or AMD's security processor verifies the initial boot block, making the hardware effectively part of the RTM.
  • DRTM (Intel TXT's GETSEC[SENTER], AMD's SKINIT) resets a special set of PCRs (17-22) and measures a fresh launch, reducing reliance on everything the firmware did before.
  • NIST SP 800-193 (May 2018) is the key reference for firmware resiliency and defines RTU, RTD and RTRec alongside chains of trust for each. SP 800-164's draft roots (RTS, RTV, RTI, RTR, RTM) remained a 2012 draft.
  • Immutable versus updatable is a real trade-off: Apple's checkm8 (2019), Nvidia Tegra X1's Fusée Gelée (2018) and Intel's CSME ROM flaw CVE-2019-0090 all showed ROM bugs living forever, so modern designs keep ROM tiny and push logic into updatable stages.
  • DICE (chapter 10) offers a middle path: each updatable layer receives secrets derived from measurements of itself, so updating code automatically changes its identity and old secrets cannot leak to new code.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Calling the TPM 'the' root of trust for everything. A discrete TPM provides storage and reporting; measurement starts in firmware or the CPU, which the TPM cannot check.
  • Assuming immutable means invulnerable. Immutable code can still have bugs — they just can never be patched.
  • Mixing up roots of trust with trust anchors. A trust anchor is a key or certificate; a root of trust is a functioning component that uses or protects such keys.

A data-centre motherboard's PRoT checks BIOS and BMC flash before releasing the CPU from reset.

docs.title: 1.8 Hardware vs Software Trust
docs.text:
Software can be copied, patched and modified by anyone with enough privilege, so software alone cannot fully protect its own secrets. Hardware roots of trust keep keys and checks in silicon that the main processor's software cannot reach. But hardware is harder to update and costs money, so real systems mix the two: hardware anchors the chain, software does the heavy lifting.

Rough isolation strength (illustrative, higher is stronger). Relative ranking only — real strength depends on design, certification and threat model.

Think of it like…

A password written in a notebook (software) can be photocopied by anyone who borrows the notebook. A bank safe-deposit box (hardware) can only be opened in person with the right key, though moving it is much harder.

Real-world example

The fictional startup Finch Pay first stored its payment-signing key encrypted on a server disk, with the decryption password in a config file — effectively software trust. A penetration tester copied both in an afternoon. Finch moved the key into a cloud HSM and its laptops' credentials into TPM-backed storage. Now an attacker who fully compromises a server can ask the HSM to sign while they are present, but cannot walk away with the key.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Decide what must survive a full software compromise: usually long-term keys and the boot chain's anchor.
  2. Place those in hardware — fuses, a TPM, a secure element, an HSM or a security processor.
  3. Keep hardware-resident code small and well-reviewed; implement features in software above it.
  4. Use hardware to verify and measure the software, and to release secrets only to good states.
  5. Plan updates: hardware roots need signed firmware updates and revocation for when bugs appear.

Who uses it

Security architects choosing between software keystores and HSMs, device makers deciding whether to add a secure element, and cloud teams weighing KMS versus HSM tiers make this trade-off.

Key takeaway

Hardware protection's main benefit is non-exportability: even with full admin access an attacker can use a hardware-protected key while present, but cannot copy it to use later.

Going deeper

  • The strongest property hardware adds is non-exportability: an attacker with root can misuse a hardware key only while they control the machine, whereas a stolen software key can be used anywhere, forever.
  • Discrete chips (TPMs, secure elements) offer physical separation and often Common Criteria EAL4+ to EAL6+ certification, but talk over buses (SPI, I²C, LPC) that can be sniffed unless sessions are encrypted.
  • Integrated security processors (Pluton, Apple Secure Enclave, Intel CSME, AMD ASP) avoid exposed buses and can be updated with the platform, but share the die, power and sometimes memory with the main CPU.
  • TEEs isolate code on the main cores using CPU modes and memory encryption; they protect against the OS and hypervisor but have suffered side-channel attacks because they share caches and execution units.
  • Firmware security has to be updatable: AMD and Intel ship security-processor firmware inside BIOS updates, and Microsoft services Pluton firmware through Windows Update.
  • Certification levels help compare options: FIPS 140-3 Levels 1-4 for crypto modules, Common Criteria AVA_VAN.5 for high attack potential, PSA Certified Levels 1-4 and SESIP 1-5 for IoT parts (chapter 10).

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming a hardware-backed key cannot be misused. Host malware can still ask the TPM to sign; hardware stops copying, not misuse — add user presence or policy.
  • Assuming every 'secure chip' is equally strong. A firmware TPM, a discrete TPM and an EAL6+ secure element resist very different attackers.
  • Treating hardware as set-and-forget. Security chips have firmware bugs too and need patching and revocation plans.

New-SelfSignedCertificate -Subject 'CN=tpm-demo' -CertStoreLocation Cert:\CurrentUser\My `
  -Provider 'Microsoft Platform Crypto Provider' -KeyExportPolicy NonExportable
certutil -user -store My tpm-demo

Updatability trade-offDesign principle · Concept · Silicon More logic in immutable hardware means stronger tamper resistance but no fixes; more in firmware means patchable but bigger attack surface. Caliptra keeps a small ROM and moves most functions into signed, updatable firmware. Physical attack resistanceCC AVA_VAN levels, FIPS 140-3 physical security · Concept · Silicon How well hardware resists probing, glitching and side-channel analysis — the main thing extra money buys. A payment card chip resists lab attacks that would extract keys from an ordinary microcontroller in hours. Cost of hardware trustEngineering economics · Concept · Devices & IoT Extra silicon, certification, provisioning and lifecycle management add cost, so designs use hardware where it really matters. A cheap smart bulb may rely on a microcontroller's secure boot; a payment terminal needs certified hardware.

docs.title: 1.9 Secure Boot vs Measured Boot in One Picture
docs.text:
Secure boot is a bouncer: each boot stage checks the next one's signature and refuses to run anything not signed by a trusted key. Measured boot is a notary: each stage hashes the next one and records the result in the TPM, without blocking anything, so the record can be checked later. Most modern PCs, phones and servers do both. Chapter 30 covers the details.

Secure boot vs measured boot

Secure boot Measured boot Question answered May this code run? What exactly ran? Action on bad code Block or recover Record it, keep booting Needs Trusted keys, signatures TPM PCRs, event log Who decides The device itself A verifier, later Catches signed-but-wrong No Yes, if reference values exist Typical use Stop bootkits Attestation, sealing disk keys

They answer different questions, so strong platforms use both.

Think of it like…

Secure boot is a nightclub bouncer turning away anyone without a valid ticket. Measured boot is the CCTV camera at the door — it stops nobody, but afterwards you can prove exactly who came in.

Real-world example

At the fictional Oakridge Hospital, Secure Boot on every workstation blocks a USB bootkit outright. But a misconfigured firmware setting that disables a protection would not be blocked — the firmware is still validly signed. Measured boot records that configuration in the TPM's PCRs, and when the workstation asks the hospital's network for access, the attestation service notices the unusual PCR value and puts it into a quarantine VLAN.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Secure boot: stage N verifies stage N+1's signature against trusted keys; if it fails, stop or recover.
  2. Measured boot: stage N hashes stage N+1 and extends the hash into a TPM PCR, then runs it regardless.
  3. An event log records each measurement so a verifier can replay it and match the PCR values.
  4. Later, the TPM signs a quote of the PCRs; a verifier compares them with known-good values.
  5. Secrets (disk keys) can be sealed to PCR values so they unlock only after a known-good boot.

Who uses it

Endpoint, firmware and platform engineers, Windows and Linux administrators, and anyone deploying BitLocker, Intune compliance or Keylime meet both mechanisms.

Key takeaway

One-line answer for interviews: secure boot enforces (blocks bad code), measured boot reports (records what ran so someone else can decide).

Going deeper

  • PCR extension is order-sensitive and one-way: extending A then B gives a different value from B then A, and no command can set a PCR to an arbitrary value — only reboot resets most PCRs.
  • TCG's PC Client firmware profile assigns PCRs by convention: 0 for core firmware code, 1 for firmware configuration, 2-3 for option ROMs, 4-5 for the boot manager and partition table, 7 for Secure Boot state; chapter 20 lists them all.
  • Measured boot needs reference values to be useful; TCG's Reference Integrity Manifest (RIM) and IETF CoRIM formats let vendors publish expected measurements so verifiers do not have to learn them by trial.
  • Secure boot cannot catch 'signed but wrong' code — an old vulnerable but signed bootloader, as in BlackLotus — unless the image is revoked; measured boot at least records that it ran.
  • Sealing to PCRs is brittle: firmware updates change PCR 0, and Secure Boot database updates change PCR 7, so tools like BitLocker suspend protection or reseal around updates.
  • Mobile platforms mostly use verified boot plus key attestation instead of PCR-style measured boot; Android records verified-boot state into key attestation certificates (chapter 40).

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Thinking measured boot blocks malware. It only records; something else must act on the measurements.
  • Assuming secure boot means the firmware is trustworthy. Secure boot usually starts after firmware; protecting firmware needs a hardware root such as Boot Guard or a platform RoT.
  • Expecting PCR values to be identical across all 'identical' laptops. Firmware versions, settings and option ROMs change them, so reference values must cover each configuration.

docs.title: Try it: Check secure boot state and read the PCRs that measured boot filled
docs.text:
# Linux
mokutil --sb-state
sudo tpm2_pcrread sha256:0,2,4,7
# Windows PowerShell (Administrator)
Confirm-SecureBootUEFI
msinfo32    # look for 'Secure Boot State' and 'PCR7 Configuration'

docs.title: 1.10 Attestation in One Picture
docs.text:
Attestation is how a device proves its identity and state to someone far away. The device (attester) gathers evidence — such as boot measurements — and signs it with a key rooted in hardware. A verifier checks the signature and compares the evidence with known-good reference values, then tells a relying party whether to trust the device. Chapters 20 and 40 go deep; this is the overview.

Remote attestation, background-check model. The nonce makes the evidence fresh; the hardware key makes it believable.

Think of it like…

It is like a sealed health certificate from an accredited lab: the lab (hardware root) signs your test results, the airline's checker (verifier) confirms the lab's seal and compares results with the entry rules, and the gate agent (relying party) lets you board.

Real-world example

Finch Pay's payroll service runs in a cloud confidential VM. Before releasing the database key, Finch's key service sends a random nonce; the VM returns a report signed by the CPU's security processor, including a hash of the VM's initial memory and the nonce. An attestation verifier checks the signature chains to the CPU vendor, the measurement matches Finch's approved build and the nonce is fresh. Only then does the key service release the database key.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The relying party (or verifier) sends a fresh random nonce to stop replay of old evidence.
  2. The attester collects claims — measurements, firmware versions, configuration — plus the nonce.
  3. A hardware-rooted key (TPM AK, CPU attestation key, DICE alias key) signs the evidence.
  4. The verifier checks the signature chain to the manufacturer and compares claims with reference values.
  5. The verifier produces an attestation result; the relying party grants or denies access accordingly.

Who uses it

Zero-trust and endpoint-management teams, confidential-computing engineers, IoT onboarding services and mobile-app security teams use attestation.

Key takeaway

Memorise the three RATS roles from RFC 9334 — Attester, Verifier, Relying Party — and why the nonce matters (freshness).

Going deeper

  • IETF RFC 9334 (January 2023) defines the RATS architecture: attester, verifier, relying party, plus endorser and reference-value provider roles, and the passport and background-check topologies.
  • Evidence formats vary by hardware: TPM quotes (TPMS_ATTEST), Intel TDX quotes, AMD SEV-SNP attestation reports, Arm CCA tokens, PSA tokens (RFC 9783) and SPDM measurement responses.
  • The trust chain of evidence goes back to manufacturing: a device key (EK, DICE DeviceID, CPU VCEK/PCK) is certified by the vendor's CA, so the verifier ultimately relies on the vendor's PKI.
  • Privacy matters: a unique hardware key lets observers track a device. TPMs use separate attestation keys certified via credential activation; schemes such as Direct Anonymous Attestation (DAA) go further.
  • Attestation proves what was measured, not that it is bug-free — reference values must also encode which versions are acceptable, and verifiers need timely updates when vulnerabilities appear.
  • Common deployments: Windows Device Health Attestation and Intune compliance, Keylime for Linux fleets, Android Key Attestation and Play Integrity, and confidential-computing key release services.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Skipping the nonce or timestamp. Without freshness, attackers replay old, healthy-looking evidence.
  • Assuming attestation proves software is safe. It proves which software ran; whether that software is acceptable depends on your reference values.
  • Forgetting the verifier itself is in the TCB. A compromised or misconfigured verifier approves anything.

docs.title: Try it: Produce a TPM quote over PCRs with a nonce (lab machine with tpm2-tools)
docs.text:
tpm2_createek -c ek.ctx -G ecc -u ek.pub
tpm2_createak -C ek.ctx -c ak.ctx -G ecc -g sha256 -s ecdsa -u ak.pub
tpm2_quote -c ak.ctx -l sha256:0,7 -q $(openssl rand -hex 16) -m quote.msg -s quote.sig
tpm2_print -t TPMS_ATTEST quote.msg

docs.text: Name What it does Example Remote attestationTCG, IETF RATS · Concept · Current · General A device proving its identity and software state to a remote party with hardware-signed evidence. A laptop proves its boot state to a VPN gateway before getting network access. AttesterIETF RFC 9334 (2023) · Role · General The entity whose state is being proven; it produces signed evidence. A server's TPM and firmware together act as the attester. VerifierIETF RFC 9334 · Role · General Appraises evidence against endorsements and reference values, then issues an attestation result. docs.title: 1.11 Certificates & PKI in One Picture
docs.text:
A certificate is a digitally signed document saying 'this public key belongs to this name'. A certificate authority (CA) checks the name and signs the certificate. Your browser or operating system holds a small set of root CA certificates it trusts, and accepts other certificates only if they chain back to one of those roots. The people, rules, software and hardware that run all this are called PKI — public key infrastructure. Chapters 50-70 cover it in depth.

A typical web PKI chain. The browser trusts the leaf only because a chain of signatures leads to a root it already holds.

Think of it like…

A certificate is like a passport: a trusted authority (the passport office) checks your identity and issues a tamper-evident document linking your photo to your name. Border officers trust it because they trust the issuing government, not because they know you.

Real-world example

Ravi runs the website of the fictional Willow Bakery. He uses an ACME client that proves to Let's Encrypt he controls willowbakery.example by placing a file on the site, then receives a certificate valid for 90 days. When a customer visits, the browser checks that the certificate's name matches, it has not expired, it chains to the ISRG root in the browser's trust store, and it appears in Certificate Transparency logs. The padlock appears.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Subscriber generates a key pair and a certificate signing request (CSR) containing the public key and name.
  2. A registration authority or automated validation checks the subscriber controls the name.
  3. The CA signs a certificate binding name and public key, with validity dates and permitted uses.
  4. Relying parties build a chain to a trusted root and validate signatures, names, dates and usages.
  5. Certificates are renewed before expiry, and revoked early if keys are compromised.

Who uses it

Web and DevOps engineers, PKI administrators, security operations teams and anyone deploying TLS, VPNs, Wi-Fi 802.1X, code signing or device identity handles certificates.

Key takeaway

Remember the chain: end-entity certificate → intermediate CA → root CA (in trust store) — and that roots stay offline while intermediates do the daily signing.

Going deeper

  • X.509 v3 (1996 onward) added extensions such as Subject Alternative Name, Key Usage, Extended Key Usage and Basic Constraints that tell relying parties exactly what a certificate may be used for.
  • Public TLS certificates are governed by the CA/Browser Forum Baseline Requirements and enforced by browser root programs (Mozilla, Apple, Microsoft, Chrome), with annual WebTrust or ETSI audits.
  • Ballot SC-081 (2025) shrinks maximum TLS validity to 200 days from 15 March 2026, 100 days from 15 March 2027 and 47 days from 15 March 2029, which makes ACME-style automation essential.
  • The same certificate machinery appears inside hardware trust: TPM endorsement-key certificates, DICE certificate chains, SPDM device certificates and UEFI Secure Boot keys are all X.509.
  • Revocation is the weak spot of PKI: CRLs grow large, OCSP leaks browsing data, and many clients soft-fail — one reason the industry is moving to short-lived certificates and browser-pushed revocation lists.
  • Post-quantum PKI is coming: ML-DSA certificates and composite signatures are being standardised, but their size (kilobytes per signature) creates real engineering challenges for TLS and constrained devices.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Thinking the padlock means a site is honest. It means the connection is encrypted to whoever controls that domain name — phishing sites get valid certificates too.
  • Installing a self-signed root on every machine to silence warnings. That makes the private key a powerful trust anchor that must be protected like a real root CA.
  • Forgetting intermediates. Servers must send the intermediate certificate(s); missing intermediates cause 'unable to get local issuer' errors on some clients.

docs.title: Try it: Inspect a website certificate's subject, issuer, dates and SANs
docs.text:
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -dates -ext subjectAltName

docs.title: 1.12 The Big Map: How Hardware RoT, TPM, Boot, TEE & PKI Fit Together
docs.text:
All the topics in this guide fit into one stack. At the bottom, a hardware root of trust in the silicon starts everything. The TPM records and protects. Secure and measured boot carry trust up to the operating system. Trusted execution environments protect code while it runs. Attestation reports all this to others. And PKI — certificates — gives every chip, device, server and website a verifiable identity. This page is the map; the later chapters are the territory.

The trust stack and where each chapter lives. Trust flows upward from silicon; identity and evidence flow outward through PKI and attestation.

Think of it like…

Think of a city: bedrock (silicon RoT) supports foundations (TPM and boot), which support buildings (OS and TEEs); inspectors (attestation) certify the buildings; and the passport office (PKI) issues IDs so visitors can tell who lives where.

Real-world example

Consider a cloud payment service run by the fictional Finch Pay. Server silicon roots of trust verify firmware (chapter 10); a TPM records the boot (chapters 20 and 30); the workload runs in a confidential VM (chapter 40); the VM attests to Finch's key service, which releases keys from an HSM (chapter 40); and customers reach it over TLS using a certificate chaining to a public root CA (chapters 50-70). Remove any layer and the trust story has a hole.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Silicon root of trust: boot ROM, fused keys and crypto engines verify the first firmware.
  2. Boot chain: firmware, bootloader and OS are verified (secure boot) and measured into the TPM.
  3. Runtime protection: TEEs and confidential VMs isolate sensitive code and data while running.
  4. Attestation: hardware-signed evidence lets remote parties check identity and state.
  5. PKI: certificates bind keys to chips, devices, workloads, people and websites so anyone can verify them.

Who uses it

Security architects, platform engineers and students planning a career path use this map to see where TPM work, firmware security, confidential computing and PKI roles sit.

Key takeaway

When you meet a new technology, place it on the map: is it a root, a chain link, a runtime protection, an attestation mechanism or an identity system?

Going deeper

  • The layers reuse the same primitives: hashes for measurement, signatures for verification, and X.509 certificates for identity appear in silicon (DICE, EK certificates), boot (UEFI keys) and the web alike.
  • Every layer has its own root: fused key hashes for firmware, UEFI PK/KEK/db for the OS loader, the TPM EK certificate for attestation, the CPU vendor's CA for TEE reports, and root CAs for TLS.
  • Weaknesses propagate upward: a leaked firmware-signing key undermines secure boot, attestation and any keys sealed to boot state; a mis-issuing CA undermines TLS no matter how secure the hardware is.
  • Industry groups map onto the layers: TCG (TPM, DICE), UEFI Forum (boot), Confidential Computing Consortium and IETF RATS (TEE and attestation), DMTF and OCP (data-centre devices), CA/Browser Forum and root programs (web PKI).
  • Post-quantum migration touches every layer at once: boot ROM signature checks (LMS, ML-DSA), TPM algorithms (TPM 2.0 v1.85 drafts adding ML-KEM and ML-DSA), TEE reports and PKI certificates.
  • Job roles also follow the map: silicon/firmware security engineers at the bottom, platform and endpoint engineers in the middle, PKI engineers and CA compliance staff at the top (chapter 80).

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Treating PKI and hardware trust as separate worlds. Device identity, attestation and secure boot all depend on certificates and CA keys.
  • Securing only one layer. Strong TLS on a server with a compromised BMC or unsigned firmware still leaks data.
  • Assuming the cloud provider handles every layer. Shared-responsibility models leave identity, key policies and attestation checks to the customer.

docs.title: Try it: Touch every layer from your own machine in four commands
docs.text:
# Windows PowerShell (Administrator)
Get-Tpm                                   # TPM / root of trust
Confirm-SecureBootUEFI                    # boot chain
Get-CimInstance -Namespace root/Microsoft/Windows/DeviceGuard -ClassName Win32_DeviceGuard  # VBS isolation
certutil -store -user My                  # certificates (PKI)

docs.title: 1.13 A Short History of Trusted Computing & PKI
docs.text:
Hardware trust and PKI grew up side by side. Smart cards in the 1970s-90s showed that a tiny chip could keep secrets. Public-key cryptography (1976-77) and X.509 (1988) gave us certificates. The Trusted Computing Group (2003) standardised the TPM; UEFI Secure Boot (2011-12) protected the boot chain; Let's Encrypt (2015-16) made HTTPS free; confidential computing arrived around 2015-2019; and NIST published post-quantum standards in 2024.

Milestones in hardware trust and PKI. Each generation reused the ideas of the previous one — and post-quantum is the next rebuild.

Think of it like…

Like the history of locks and passports: first came strongboxes (smart cards), then standard ID documents (X.509), then building codes for vaults (TPM specs), and now everything is being rebuilt to withstand a new kind of lockpick — the quantum computer.

Real-world example

Ana's grandmother's first bank card in the 1990s already held a chip that refused to reveal its key. Ana's 2010 laptop had a TPM 1.2 that nobody used. Her 2022 laptop needed TPM 2.0 for Windows 11, booted with UEFI Secure Boot, and every site she visited had a free certificate. Her 2026 browser negotiates hybrid post-quantum key exchange without her noticing. Each step reused ideas from the step before.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. 1970s: public-key cryptography (Diffie-Hellman 1976, RSA 1977) and the first smart-card patents.
  2. 1980s-90s: X.509 (1988), SSL (1995) and smart cards in phones (GSM SIM) and bank cards (EMV).
  3. 1999-2014: TCPA becomes TCG (2003); TPM 1.2 then TPM 2.0 (2014); UEFI Secure Boot ships with Windows 8 (2012).
  4. 2015-2021: Let's Encrypt, Intel SGX, AMD SEV, Confidential Computing Consortium; Windows 11 requires TPM 2.0.
  5. 2022-2026: open-source silicon roots (OpenTitan, Caliptra), NIST post-quantum standards (2024) and shrinking certificate lifetimes.

Who uses it

Anyone writing reports, giving training or answering 'why is it done this way?' benefits from knowing how and when each piece arrived.

Key takeaway

Anchor dates: TCG 2003, TPM 2.0 2014, Windows 8 Secure Boot 2012, Let's Encrypt public launch 2015-16, Windows 11 TPM 2.0 requirement 2021, FIPS 203/204/205 August 2024.

Going deeper

  • Smart cards evolved from 1970s patents to mass deployment: French telephone cards and bank cards in the 1980s, GSM SIMs from 1991 and EMV payment cards later in the 1990s — the first billions of hardware roots of trust.
  • The Trusted Computing Platform Alliance (1999) produced TPM 1.1b; its successor TCG (2003) published TPM 1.2, standardised as ISO/IEC 11889:2009. TPM 2.0 followed in 2014 and as ISO/IEC 11889:2015.
  • Trusted computing was controversial in the 2000s ('Palladium' / NGSCB debates over user control and DRM); today's designs emphasise owner control, measured rather than restricted boot, and privacy-preserving attestation.
  • UEFI 2.3.1 (2011) defined Secure Boot; Windows 8 certification (2012) required it on by default, and Microsoft's 2011 UEFI CA certificates — now expiring in 2026 — became the de facto trust anchors for PC booting.
  • Let's Encrypt and ACME (RFC 8555, 2019) made automated certificate issuance normal; combined with CT (RFC 6962, 2013) and shorter lifetimes they reshaped the web PKI.
  • Since 2022 the trend is openness and post-quantum readiness: OpenTitan and Caliptra publish RTL, TCG drafts PQC TPM algorithms, and NIST's IR 8547 proposes deprecating quantum-vulnerable algorithms by 2030-2035.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming the TPM is new. It has existed since the early 2000s; Windows 11 simply made TPM 2.0 mandatory.
  • Confusing SSL with TLS. SSL 2.0/3.0 are long deprecated; modern connections use TLS 1.2 or 1.3, though people still say 'SSL certificate'.
  • Thinking post-quantum migration is far away. Standards were published in 2024 and hybrid key exchange is already deployed in major browsers.

docs.title: 1.14 Follow a Laptop from Power-On to an HTTPS Page
docs.text:
This walkthrough follows a single laptop from pressing the power button to showing a padlock in the browser, naming each root of trust and chain as it appears. It ties the whole guide together: silicon checks firmware, firmware checks the bootloader, the TPM records everything and releases the disk key, the user signs in with a hardware-protected key, and the browser checks a certificate chain to a trusted root.

Power button to padlock. Each step trusts the previous one; break any link and Ana sees an error instead of payroll.

Think of it like…

It is like a relay of security checkpoints at an airport: identity check at the door, bag scan, passport control, boarding-pass scan — each trusting the previous checkpoint did its job, until you are finally on the plane.

Real-world example

Ana, an accountant at the fictional Corvid Computing, opens her Windows 11 laptop at 08:55. In about twenty seconds her CPU's security engine verifies the firmware, Secure Boot verifies Windows, the TPM unseals BitLocker's key, Windows Hello unlocks with her face and a TPM key, Intune confirms the device is healthy, and her browser opens the payroll site after validating its certificate and negotiating a hybrid post-quantum TLS key. She notices none of it.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Power-on: the CPU's boot ROM and security engine verify the first firmware block against a key hash in fuses (Intel Boot Guard / AMD PSB).
  2. UEFI firmware runs, measuring itself and settings into TPM PCRs 0-7, then Secure Boot verifies Windows Boot Manager against db/dbx.
  3. Boot Manager verifies and measures the Windows kernel and early-launch anti-malware driver; the TPM unseals the BitLocker key because PCRs match.
  4. Ana unlocks with Windows Hello: her credential is a non-exportable key in the TPM; the device proves its health to Intune via attestation.
  5. Her browser connects with TLS 1.3, receives the server's certificate chain, and validates names, dates, signatures, CT SCTs and revocation status to a root in its trust store.
  6. With the chain valid and keys agreed (e.g. X25519 + ML-KEM-768), the padlock appears and payroll loads.

Who uses it

Help-desk and endpoint engineers diagnosing boot or certificate errors, security architects and interviewers asking 'what happens when you power on and browse?' all use this end-to-end view.

Key takeaway

Practise telling this story in two minutes, naming each root: fused key hash, Secure Boot db, TPM, Windows Hello key, root CA — it is a favourite interview question.

Going deeper

  • On a typical Windows 11 PC, BitLocker seals to PCR 7 and PCR 11 when Secure Boot is on, so ordinary firmware updates that change PCR 0 do not trigger recovery prompts, while Secure Boot policy changes do.
  • Windows also measures into the TPM a log that Device Health Attestation and Intune use; Linux equivalents are the TCG event log plus IMA runtime measurements, verified by tools such as Keylime.
  • The browser's certificate decision involves several independent roots: the root CA in its store, CT log keys built into the browser, and pushed revocation data such as Chrome's CRLSets or Firefox's CRLite.
  • Chrome made hybrid X25519MLKEM768 its default key exchange in late 2024 and other major browsers followed; it protects against 'harvest now, decrypt later' even though certificates themselves are still classical ECDSA or RSA.
  • Failure points map to error messages: 'Secure Boot violation' (boot chain), 'BitLocker recovery' (PCR mismatch), 'device not compliant' (attestation), 'NET::ERR_CERT_DATE_INVALID' or 'unknown issuer' (PKI).
  • Every key in this story was born somewhere: OEM fuses at the factory, Microsoft's UEFI CA keys, the TPM's endorsement key certificate, Ana's Hello key at enrolment and the website's key at certificate issuance.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Thinking the TPM verifies the bootloader. Firmware verifies it (secure boot); the TPM only records measurements and releases sealed keys.
  • Assuming the browser trusts the OS root store everywhere. Chrome and Firefox ship their own root stores on most platforms.
  • Believing a padlock means post-quantum security. Key exchange may be hybrid post-quantum, but certificate signatures are still classical in 2026.

docs.title: Chapter 5: Trusted Execution, Confidential Computing & Attestation
docs.text: This chapter moves from checking how a machine booted to protecting what it does while it runs. It explains trusted execution environments — from phone TrustZone TEEs and Intel SGX enclaves to whole confidential VMs on AMD SEV-SNP, Intel TDX and Arm CCA — and the confidential GPUs now protecting AI. It then covers how anything proves its state remotely (IETF RATS, EAT and attestation services), how devices get trustworthy identities, where keys live (HSMs and cloud KMS), how phones and passkeys attest, and what a decade of TEE attacks teaches.

docs.title: 5.1 TEEs Explained: Protecting Data While It Is Being Used
docs.text:
A Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) is a walled-off area inside a processor where code and data are protected even from the computer's own operating system, hypervisor and administrators. Data is normally encrypted on disk (at rest) and on the network (in transit); a TEE also protects it in memory while it is being processed (in use). Doing this with hardware, and proving it with attestation, is called confidential computing.

Ordinary VM vs enclave vs confidential VM

Ordinary VM Enclave (e.g. SGX) Confidential VM Hypervisor trusted? Yes, fully No No What is protected Nothing extra Part of one app Whole guest OS + apps Code changes None Split app or library OS Few (CVM-aware OS) Trusted base Host + guest CPU + enclave code CPU, firmware, guest OS What is attested Nothing (vTPM optional) Enclave code hash Firmware + boot measurements Examples Standard cloud VM Intel SGX SEV-SNP, TDX, Arm CCA

Confidential VMs trade a bigger trusted base for far easier adoption, which is why clouds favour them.

Think of it like…

A TEE is like a private viewing room inside a bank: the bank (the cloud host) owns the building and its staff walk the corridors, but only you hold the key to the room, and a sealed inspection certificate on the door proves the room was built to specification.

Real-world example

Kestrel Health wants to train a cancer-detection model on patient scans in a public cloud, but its regulator worries about cloud staff seeing the data. Kestrel runs the training job in a confidential VM whose memory is encrypted by the CPU with a key the hypervisor never sees. Before releasing the key that decrypts the scans, Kestrel's key server checks a hardware-signed attestation report proving the VM's firmware and image match the approved build. A curious administrator dumping the host's RAM sees only ciphertext.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The CPU creates an isolated container — an enclave inside one process or a whole confidential VM — and gives it a memory-encryption key held only inside the processor.
  2. Hardware access checks stop the OS, hypervisor and devices reading or remapping the protected memory; data leaving the chip for DRAM is encrypted.
  3. As code is loaded, the processor measures (hashes) it into a launch measurement that cannot be changed afterwards.
  4. On request, the CPU's security firmware signs a report containing that measurement and a caller-supplied value, using a key certified by the chip maker.
  5. A remote verifier checks the signature chain and measurement against expected values, then releases secrets — keys, data, model weights — only to a genuine, correctly configured TEE.

Who uses it

Cloud security architects, platform engineers, privacy engineers in healthcare and finance, AI infrastructure teams and mobile security engineers all design around TEEs.

Key takeaway

Memorise the three states of data — at rest, in transit, in use — and the Confidential Computing Consortium's definition: confidential computing protects data in use by computing in a hardware-based, attested TEE.

Going deeper

  • Memory-encryption engines in the memory controller encrypt cache lines with AES (usually XTS mode with an address tweak) at full speed; integrity differs — client SGX used a Merkle tree, while SEV-SNP and TDX mainly rely on hardware ownership tables.
  • TEE threat models normally trust the CPU package and its firmware, distrust the host OS, hypervisor, other tenants and DMA devices, and exclude many side channels and some physical attacks — always read the vendor's stated model.
  • Process enclaves (SGX) need applications split into trusted and untrusted halves or wrapped in a library OS; confidential VMs (SEV-SNP, TDX, Arm CCA) run mostly unmodified guests, so lift-and-shift became the dominant cloud model.
  • Every protected guest still depends on the untrusted host for I/O, interrupts and time; those interfaces (hypercalls, #VC/#VE exceptions, shared bounce buffers) are where many real-world bugs and attacks live.
  • Measured overheads are typically a few percent for CPU-bound work; I/O-heavy workloads pay more because data is copied through shared, unencrypted buffers unless trusted I/O (PCIe TDISP) is available.
  • A TEE without attestation is encryption you cannot verify: the security value comes from relying parties refusing to release secrets until hardware-signed evidence matches expected measurements.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Believing a TEE makes code bug-free: a vulnerable app inside an enclave is still exploitable through its own inputs; the TEE only removes the host from the attack surface.
  • Assuming encrypted memory alone defeats a malicious host: without integrity, replay protection and attestation, a hypervisor can still remap, replay or substitute pages.
  • Treating TPM measured boot and TEEs as the same thing: a TPM reports what booted, while a TEE isolates running code and data from the host.

docs.title: Try it: Check whether your Linux machine or VM exposes TEE features
docs.text:
grep -o -w -E 'sgx|sev|sev_es|sev_snp|tdx_guest' /proc/cpuinfo | sort -u   # CPU / guest flags
sudo dmesg | grep -i -E 'memory encryption|sev|tdx'   # inside a CVM: shows SEV-SNP or TDX active
ls /dev/sev-guest /dev/tdx_guest 2>/dev/null          # guest attestation devices

docs.text: Name What it does Example TEE attestation key hierarchyIntel PCK, AMD VCEK/VLEK, Arm CCA platform key, NVIDIA device keys · Concept · Trusted execution Chip-unique secrets fused at manufacture derive or certify the keys that sign a TEE's attestation reports. An SNP report is signed by a VCEK derived from fused chip secrets and certified by AMD's ARK and ASK chain. Security version numbers (TCB versions)Intel CPUSVN/TEE_TCB_SVN, AMD reported TCB, Arm CCA platform claims · Concept · Trusted execution Version fields for microcode and security firmware included in attestation, letting verifiers reject unpatched platforms. Kestrel's verifier requires the SNP firmware version shipped after a 2025 bulletin, so unpatched hosts fail attestation. EnclaveIntel SGX, Keystone and other enclave designs · Concept · Trusted execution A protected region inside one application's address space; only enclave code can read its memory, not even the OS. A password manager keeps its vault-decryption routine in an SGX enclave so a kernel rootkit cannot scrape the master key. Confidential VM (CVM)AMD SEV-SNP, Intel TDX, Arm CCA Realms · Concept · Current · Cloud A whole virtual machine whose memory and CPU state are encrypted and isolated from the hypervisor, with hardware-signed launch measurements. Mira's team moves an unchanged Ubuntu database VM to an SEV-SNP confidential VM by ticking one option in the cloud console. Data in useConfidential computing terminology · Concept · Trusted execution Data while it is loaded in memory and processed by the CPU — the state that disk and TLS encryption leave exposed. A memory dump of a normal VM reveals decrypted card numbers mid-transaction; the same dump of a confidential VM shows ciphertext. Memory encryption engineAMD SME/SEV, Intel TME-MK, Arm MEC · Hardware · Current · Silicon AES hardware in the memory controller that encrypts every cache line written to DRAM with a per-VM or per-enclave key. When a TDX guest writes to RAM, the controller tags the line with the guest's key ID and encrypts it with AES-XTS automatically. Launch measurementEvery TEE (names differ by vendor) · Concept · Trusted execution A hash of the code and configuration loaded into a TEE at creation, recorded by hardware and included in attestation reports. SGX calls it MRENCLAVE, TDX calls it MRTD and SEV-SNP calls it MEASUREMENT; a verifier compares each with the expected value. Attestation report / quoteIntel, AMD, Arm, NVIDIA (vendor-specific formats) · Format · Trusted execution A hardware-signed statement of a TEE's measurements, security versions and caller-supplied data, verifiable through the chip maker's certificate chain. An app puts the hash of its TLS public key in REPORT_DATA so the verifier knows that key lives inside the attested TEE. Enclave sealingSGX, TrustZone and other TEEs · Concept · Trusted execution Encrypting data with a key the CPU derives from the TEE's identity, so only the same TEE or signer can decrypt it later. An SGX enclave seals its database key to MRSIGNER so later vendor-signed versions of the enclave can still unseal it. Untrusted-host threat modelVendor TEE threat models · Concept · Trusted execution The assumption that cloud administrators, the hypervisor and host OS may be malicious, while the CPU package and its firmware are trusted. Aurora Cloud's technicians can reboot or pause a confidential VM, but by design they should not be able to read its memory. Lift-and-shift vs partitioned appsConfidential computing adoption patterns · Concept · Trusted execution Two styles: run an unmodified VM or container in a CVM, or split an app so only a small trusted part runs in an enclave. Startup Lumen partitions its signing service into a 2,000-line enclave, while its larger web app simply runs inside a confidential VM. Side channelComputer-architecture security research · Concept · Trusted execution Leaking secrets indirectly through timing, caches, power or page-access patterns rather than by reading protected memory directly. A malicious hypervisor watches which enclave pages fault to infer which branch of a decryption routine ran.

docs.title: 5.2 Arm TrustZone TEEs: OP-TEE, Trusty, QSEE and Trusted Apps
docs.text:
Almost every phone, and many IoT devices, run a second, hidden operating system beside Android or Linux. Arm TrustZone hardware splits the processor into a normal world and a secure world; a small TEE operating system in the secure world runs trusted applications (TAs) that handle keys, fingerprints, payments and video DRM. The normal world can ask TAs to do work but cannot read their memory.

Arm A-profile exception levels with a TEE. Requests cross between worlds only through the EL3 monitor via SMC; secure memory is invisible to the normal world.

Think of it like…

It is like a bank branch with a public hall and a vault room behind a hatch: customers (normal apps) pass requests through the hatch, staff in the vault (trusted apps) do the sensitive work, and the hatch never opens wide enough to climb through.

Real-world example

When Priya unlocks her Android phone with a fingerprint, the sensor data is routed to a trusted app in the phone's TEE rather than to Android. The TA compares it with the enrolled template and, only on a match, tells the KeyMint TA to unlock the keys protecting her credential-encrypted storage. Android only ever learns 'match' or 'no match', and even malware with root in the Android kernel cannot copy the stored templates or keys.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. At boot, secure firmware (Trusted Firmware-A at EL3) loads and verifies the TEE OS into secure memory before the normal-world OS starts.
  2. Memory and peripherals such as the fingerprint sensor or a crypto engine are marked secure by TrustZone controllers, making them invisible to the normal world.
  3. A normal-world app calls a client library (GlobalPlatform TEE Client API), and the kernel's TEE driver issues an SMC (Secure Monitor Call).
  4. The secure monitor switches worlds; the TEE OS dispatches the request to the trusted application identified by its UUID.
  5. The TA performs the sensitive operation with keys that never leave the secure world and returns only the result.

Who uses it

Android and embedded-Linux security engineers, mobile payment and DRM teams, SoC vendors and IoT device makers write, integrate and audit trusted applications.

Key takeaway

Know the stack from the bottom up — EL3 secure monitor (TF-A), TEE OS (OP-TEE, Trusty, QSEE/QTEE, Kinibi, TEEgris), trusted apps — and that GlobalPlatform standardises the TEE APIs and protection profile.

Going deeper

  • GlobalPlatform defines the TEE Client API (normal-world side), the TEE Internal Core API (TA side) and a TEE Protection Profile for Common Criteria certification, letting payment schemes and banks trust a device's TEE.
  • OP-TEE, now maintained under TrustedFirmware.org, is the reference open-source TEE for Arm Cortex-A; trusted apps are signed binaries loaded by UUID, often stored in the normal-world filesystem and verified on load.
  • Android requires a TEE-backed Keystore: KeyMint, Gatekeeper and Weaver run as trusted apps, and StrongBox can move keys into a separate secure element for higher resistance to physical attack.
  • Arm FF-A (Firmware Framework for A-profile) standardises messaging between worlds and partitions, and S-EL2 lets a secure partition manager such as Hafnium isolate several secure services from one another.
  • Android's protected KVM (pKVM) and Android Virtualization Framework add isolated protected VMs in the normal world, an alternative to piling ever more code into the TrustZone TEE.
  • TrustZone alone provides no remote attestation or tenant isolation; vendors add attestation by provisioning keys into the TEE (as Android Key Attestation does) and keep secure memory in on-chip RAM or protected DRAM regions.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming TrustZone code is small and therefore safe: commercial TEE OSes and trusted apps have had serious vulnerabilities, and a secure-world exploit defeats every TA on the device.
  • Confusing TrustZone-A (application processors, secure monitor at EL3) with TrustZone-M (microcontrollers, secure states without a monitor): designs, firmware and tools differ.
  • Thinking TrustZone protects cloud tenants from each other: it gives a device one secure world controlled by the maker, which is the gap Arm CCA Realms fill.

docs.title: 5.3 Intel SGX: Enclaves, Attestation and the Retreat From PCs
docs.text:
Intel Software Guard Extensions (SGX), launched with 6th-generation Core processors in 2015, lets an application create an enclave: a protected region of its own memory that even the OS and hypervisor cannot read. SGX was removed from consumer Core chips from the 11th generation (2021) onward but lives on in Xeon servers, and its attestation machinery also signs Intel TDX quotes.

Life of an SGX enclave. The measurement is fixed at EINIT; everything a verifier later trusts traces back to it.

Think of it like…

SGX is like a safe-deposit box bolted inside your own flat: the landlord (the OS) controls the building and the doors, but only the box's own mechanism opens it, and the bank can certify exactly which box model you have.

Real-world example

Tessera Pay runs its card-tokenisation code in an SGX enclave on Xeon servers. Before its HSM cluster provisions a tokenisation key, Tessera's key service asks the enclave for a DCAP quote. It checks that MRENCLAVE matches the audited build, MRSIGNER matches Tessera's signing key, debug mode is off and the platform's TCB is up to date. Only then is the key sent to the enclave over a channel bound to the quote.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The developer builds and signs the enclave, producing SIGSTRUCT with the expected measurement (MRENCLAVE), signer and security version.
  2. The OS driver creates the enclave (ECREATE), adds pages (EADD) and measures them (EEXTEND); EINIT checks the result against SIGSTRUCT.
  3. The application enters the enclave through ECALLs; the enclave asks the untrusted OS for files and networking through OCALLs.
  4. EREPORT produces a local report MACed for another enclave on the same CPU; the Quoting Enclave turns it into a signed quote.
  5. A remote verifier checks the quote with Intel's PCK certificate chain (DCAP) and compares MRENCLAVE, MRSIGNER and security versions with policy.

Who uses it

Fintech, blockchain and privacy-technology developers and security researchers still work with SGX, and its DCAP attestation stack is shared with Intel TDX.

Key takeaway

Learn the pair MRENCLAVE (exactly this code) versus MRSIGNER (anything signed by this author) — it appears in most SGX interview questions and sealing policies.

Going deeper

  • Enclave memory lives in the Enclave Page Cache (EPC); client SGX had a small EPC (128 MB class) with an integrity tree, while Scalable SGX on Xeon (3rd Gen onward) offers hundreds of gigabytes but drops replay-protecting integrity.
  • Intel discontinued the EPID-based Intel SGX Attestation Service on 2 April 2025, leaving DCAP — ECDSA quotes, PCK certificates from Intel's Provisioning Certification Service, cached locally by a PCCS — as the supported path.
  • TCB recovery: after a microcode or SGX bug fix Intel raises security version numbers and publishes new TCB information, and verifiers report older platforms as OutOfDate until they are patched.
  • Library OSes such as Gramine and Occlum let unmodified Linux programs run in enclaves, cutting porting work but enlarging the trusted code base and the side-channel surface.
  • Removing SGX from 11th-Gen-and-later Core processors broke Ultra HD Blu-ray playback on new PCs, a reminder that DRM was one of SGX's main consumer uses.
  • SGX's threat model excludes most side channels, so developers must write constant-time code; Foreshadow, SGAxe and Downfall were each answered with microcode fixes plus TCB recovery.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming SGX is dead: it is deprecated on client PCs but still shipped and supported on Xeon servers, and the TDX quoting stack is built on it.
  • Sealing data to MRENCLAVE and then upgrading: the new build has a different measurement and cannot unseal old data — seal to MRSIGNER with a security version instead.
  • Accepting a quote without checking TCB status and the DEBUG attribute: a debug enclave's memory can be read with a debugger.

docs.title: 5.4 Intel TDX: Trust Domains on Xeon
docs.text:
Intel Trust Domain Extensions (TDX) turns a whole virtual machine into a confidential trust domain (TD). The hypervisor still schedules the TD and gives it virtual devices, but an Intel-signed component called the TDX Module, running in a special CPU mode, sits between them and keeps the TD's memory and CPU state encrypted and off-limits. TDX became generally available with 5th Gen Xeon in December 2023 and continues on Xeon 6.

Who trusts whom in Intel TDX. The hypervisor must go through the TDX Module with SEAMCALLs; it never touches TD private memory directly.

Think of it like…

TDX is like a hotel where guests' rooms are run not by hotel staff but by a sealed, independent concierge robot the hotel cannot reprogram: staff can ask it to move a guest, but only the robot opens doors, and it gives each guest a signed receipt proving which room they got.

Real-world example

Orion Insurance moves its claims-analytics VMs to Intel TDX confidential VMs in the cloud. At boot, the TD's virtual firmware is measured into MRTD, and the kernel and command line are measured into RTMRs. Orion's key broker requests a TD quote, verifies it through Intel's certificate chain and checks MRTD, RTMRs and the TDX Module version against policy before releasing the disk-encryption key. The host can still pause and schedule the VM but cannot read its memory.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Platform firmware loads the Intel-signed TDX Module into a protected range (SEAMRR) through the SEAM loader, which verifies its signature.
  2. The hypervisor asks the TDX Module (via SEAMCALL) to create a TD; the module assigns a private key ID so TME-MK encrypts the TD's memory.
  3. Initial pages are added and measured into MRTD; at run time the guest extends RTMR0-3 with firmware, kernel and application measurements.
  4. The guest requests a TDREPORT, which the host's TD Quoting Enclave converts into an ECDSA-signed TD quote.
  5. A verifier checks the quote chain to Intel's root, the TDX Module security version, MRTD and RTMRs, then releases secrets.

Who uses it

Cloud and HPC platform engineers, Linux/KVM developers, confidential-AI teams and security architects at banks, insurers and government agencies work with TDX.

Key takeaway

Remember TDX's trusted base: the CPU, the Intel-signed TDX Module and your own guest image — the hypervisor, host OS, BIOS and cloud administrators are outside it.

Going deeper

  • By common convention MRTD covers the initial TD image (the virtual firmware), RTMR0 firmware configuration, RTMR1 the OS loader and kernel, RTMR2 the command line and initrd, and RTMR3 is left for applications — similar in spirit to TPM PCRs.
  • Private memory is encrypted with TME-MK (AES-XTS) using per-TD key IDs; memory shared with the host for I/O uses a host key, so guests explicitly convert pages and bounce data through them.
  • Early TDX on 4th Gen Xeon was limited to custom SKUs for selected cloud providers; general availability came with 5th Gen Xeon (Emerald Rapids) in December 2023 and continues on Xeon 6.
  • TDX Module 1.5 added live migration (using Migration TDs) and TD Partitioning for nested VMs; a five-month Google–Intel review in 2025 found five vulnerabilities, including CVE-2025-30513 that could turn a migratable TD debuggable, all patched by February 2026.
  • TDX Connect brings trusted I/O using PCIe TDISP and IDE link encryption, so attested GPUs or NICs can DMA directly into TD private memory instead of through bounce buffers.
  • Clouds often add a vTPM inside the confidential VM; attestation then combines the hardware TD quote with TPM quotes over the boot chain — PCR and quote mechanics are covered in the TPM chapter.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Trusting host-supplied inputs inside the TD: interrupts, MMIO, ACPI tables and virtio devices are attacker-controlled and need hardened guest drivers.
  • Pinning only MRTD: it covers the virtual firmware, not your kernel or application — also check RTMRs or a vTPM event log.
  • Assuming any 4th Gen Xeon in your rack supports TDX: early TDX SKUs went only to selected clouds; check the CPU model, BIOS settings and TDX Module version.

docs.title: Try it: Inside a TDX guest: confirm TDX and find the attestation interfaces
docs.text:
dmesg | grep -i tdx                         # e.g. 'Memory Encryption Features active: Intel TDX'
ls /dev/tdx_guest                          # TDX guest attestation device
ls /sys/kernel/config/tsm/report 2>/dev/null   # configfs-tsm: generic report/quote interface
trustauthority-cli --help                  # Intel Trust Authority CLI: collect and verify quotes

docs.title: 5.5 AMD SEV, SEV-ES and SEV-SNP
docs.text:
AMD Secure Encrypted Virtualization (SEV) encrypts each virtual machine's memory with its own key, managed by the AMD Secure Processor inside the EPYC chip. It grew in three steps: SEV encrypted memory, SEV-ES also encrypted the CPU register state, and SEV-SNP added integrity protection so a malicious hypervisor cannot remap or replay a VM's pages. SEV-SNP is what clouds use for AMD confidential VMs today.

AMD memory-encryption generations. Each EPYC generation closed attacks the previous one allowed, ending in SNP's integrity protection.

Think of it like…

SEV is like a shipping company giving every customer a container with its own lock (SEV), then also sealing the paperwork in the cab (SEV-ES), and finally keeping a tamper-evident register of which container sits in which slot so nobody can swap them (SEV-SNP).

Real-world example

Halden Bank runs payment reconciliation on a cloud VM with AMD SEV-SNP enabled. At launch, the AMD Secure Processor measures the initial guest firmware. Inside the VM, the snpguest tool requests an attestation report containing that measurement and a fresh nonce. Halden's verifier checks the report's signature against the chip's VCEK certificate, chained to AMD's ARK and ASK roots, confirms debug is disabled and firmware versions are current, then releases the database key.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The hypervisor asks the AMD Secure Processor (ASP) firmware to launch a guest; the ASP creates a VM-specific key held in the memory controller.
  2. Initial guest pages (usually OVMF firmware) are encrypted and measured; the launch digest is recorded for attestation.
  3. The Reverse Map Table (RMP) records the owner of every physical page; hardware blocks the hypervisor from writing or remapping guest-owned pages.
  4. Register state is saved encrypted in the VMSA (from SEV-ES), and the guest uses the shared GHCB page to pass only what the host needs.
  5. The guest requests an attestation report signed with a VCEK or VLEK, and a verifier validates it through AMD's certificate chain.

Who uses it

Cloud and virtualisation engineers running EPYC fleets, Linux/KVM and Hyper-V developers, and security architects choosing between SEV-SNP and TDX work with SEV.

Key takeaway

Remember the ladder: SEV = encrypted memory, SEV-ES = plus encrypted registers, SEV-SNP = plus memory integrity (RMP) and robust attestation.

Going deeper

  • Guest keys never leave the AMD Secure Processor, an Arm-based security core inside the EPYC SoC; its SEV firmware enforces guest policy flags such as no-debug and minimum firmware versions, which appear in the signed report.
  • VCEK is unique per chip and derived from the current TCB versions (bootloader, TEE, SNP firmware, microcode), so patching changes it; VLEK is a cloud-loaded alternative; both chain to AMD's ARK and ASK roots served by the Key Distribution Service.
  • Virtual Machine Privilege Levels (VMPL0-3) let a small Secure VM Service Module such as COCONUT-SVSM run at VMPL0 inside the guest, providing a vTPM the hypervisor cannot tamper with.
  • Zen 5 (EPYC 9005) adds Ciphertext Hiding, preventing the hypervisor from reading guest ciphertext, which blocks a family of deterministic-encryption side channels; AMD also cites PMC virtualisation for counter-based leaks.
  • Azure (DCasv5/v6, ECasv5/v6), Google Cloud (N2D Confidential VMs) and AWS (M6a, C6a and R6a) offer SEV-SNP guests, and mainline Linux carries both guest and KVM host SNP support.
  • Reported overheads for SNP guests on EPYC 9005 are typically a few percent for CPU-bound work, more for I/O because data passes through shared, unencrypted SWIOTLB bounce buffers.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Relying on plain SEV or SEV-ES against a hostile host: without SNP's RMP, the hypervisor can remap or replay encrypted pages, and such guests have been broken repeatedly.
  • Caching one VCEK forever: it changes whenever firmware or microcode TCB versions change, so fetch the certificate matching each report's TCB.
  • Checking only the signature: also verify the guest policy (debug off), TCB versions, launch measurement and your nonce in REPORT_DATA.

docs.title: Try it: Request and verify an SEV-SNP attestation report inside a guest
docs.text:
dmesg | grep -i sev          # 'Memory Encryption Features active: AMD SEV SEV-ES SEV-SNP'
sudo snpguest report report.bin request.bin --random   # report with a random 64-byte nonce
snpguest fetch ca pem ./certs genoa                     # AMD ARK + ASK for your EPYC family
snpguest fetch vcek pem ./certs report.bin             # VCEK for this chip and TCB from AMD KDS
snpguest verify certs ./certs && snpguest verify attestation ./certs report.bin
# argument order varies between snpguest versions: check snpguest --help

docs.title: 5.6 Arm CCA Realms and RISC-V Confidential Computing
docs.text:
Arm's Confidential Compute Architecture (CCA) adds a new Realm world to Armv9 processors, so virtual machines called Realms can be isolated from the hypervisor, the host OS and even the TrustZone secure world. RISC-V is following with its own designs: Keystone for enclaves and CoVE for confidential VMs. Both were moving from emulators and research prototypes toward real silicon in 2025-26.

The four worlds of Arm CCA. Every physical granule belongs to exactly one world, enforced by Granule Protection Table checks on each access.

Think of it like…

If TrustZone gave a building one locked back office, CCA turns it into a building with four separate wings — public, back office, rentable private suites and a tiny security control room — with a guard who checks a floor-plan map at every door.

Real-world example

Nadia, a cloud-platform intern, builds a Realm VM on Arm's free Fixed Virtual Platform emulator using TF-A, TF-RMM and a CCA-enabled Linux kernel. She asks the Realm for an attestation token, which comes back as a CBOR bundle of a platform token and a realm token. She feeds it to a Veraison verifier running in a container, which checks it against reference values and returns a result marking the platform trustworthy.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Root world: EL3 firmware (TF-A) owns the Granule Protection Table, which tags every physical memory granule as Normal, Secure, Realm or Root.
  2. The Normal-world hypervisor asks the Realm Management Monitor (RMM) through the RMI interface to create a Realm and delegate pages to it.
  3. The RMM measures the Realm's initial contents into its Realm Initial Measurement (RIM); the Realm can extend Realm Extensible Measurements (REMs) later.
  4. Every memory access is checked against the GPT; a Normal-world access to a Realm page raises a granule-protection fault.
  5. Through the RSI interface the Realm requests an attestation token: a realm token plus a platform token signed by the hardware root of trust.

Who uses it

Arm server and SoC engineers, hypervisor developers, cloud architects evaluating Arm confidential VMs and RISC-V security researchers work on these architectures.

Key takeaway

Remember CCA's four worlds — Normal, Secure, Realm and Root — and that the RMM, not the hypervisor, is the trusted manager of Realms.

Going deeper

  • RME (Realm Management Extension) is an optional Armv9.2-A feature; Arm's Neoverse V3 was the first Neoverse core to support CCA, so CCA-capable server silicon only began reaching the market in 2025-26.
  • Linux Realm-guest support is upstream, but KVM host support for running Realms was still under review in 2026 (a 15th revision of the patch series was posted in July 2026), so most hands-on work uses the FVP or QEMU.
  • CCA attestation tokens are CBOR/COSE structures profiled from EAT (RFC 9711); the platform token follows Arm's PSA token format (RFC 9783), and Veraison provides open-source verification.
  • Memory Encryption Contexts (MEC), a later RME extension, let different Realms use different memory-encryption keys instead of one shared Realm key.
  • RISC-V Keystone (UC Berkeley, EuroSys 2020) builds enclaves using Physical Memory Protection (PMP) and a small machine-mode security monitor — an open, customisable research platform.
  • RISC-V CoVE (Confidential VM Extension) defines a TEE Security Manager (TSM) and ABI for confidential VMs; the AP-TEE task group's specification was still in development in 2025-26, alongside Supervisor Domains and the Smmtt memory-tracking extension.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Equating CCA with TrustZone: TrustZone has one secure world owned by the device maker; CCA lets any tenant create attested Realms at run time.
  • Assuming every Armv9 chip supports Realms: RME is optional, and many phones and servers ship without it — check the specific core, SoC and firmware.
  • Treating RISC-V CoVE as a finished product: it is a specification in progress with research prototypes, not yet a widely deployed cloud service.

TF-RMM validates every RMI call from KVM before touching a Realm's page tables. RealmArm CCA · Concept · Trusted execution A CCA-protected VM whose memory and registers the Normal-world hypervisor cannot read or modify. A Realm running a payment service keeps cardholder data private from the Arm server's host OS. RMI and RSIArm CCA · Specification · Trusted execution Realm Management Interface (hypervisor to RMM) and Realm Services Interface (Realm to RMM, for attestation and measurements). A Realm's kernel uses an RSI call to extend REM0 with the hash of the container image it is about to run. CCA attestation tokenArm (EAT-based) · Format · Emerging · Trusted execution CBOR token pairing a realm token (RIM, REMs, challenge) with a platform token signed by the hardware root of trust. A key broker checks the realm token's RIM matches the approved image and the platform token's firmware is current. RIM and REMsArm CCA · Concept · Trusted execution The Realm Initial Measurement of the starting image, plus four Realm Extensible Measurements the Realm extends at run time. Nadia's verifier rejects a Realm whose RIM changed because the kernel image was rebuilt with a different configuration. Memory Encryption Contexts (MEC)Arm (RME extension) · Hardware · Emerging · Silicon Extension letting different Realms use different memory-encryption keys rather than sharing one Realm-world key. With MEC, one Realm's encryption key cannot be used to decrypt another Realm's pages captured from DRAM. Arm Fixed Virtual Platform (FVP)Arm · Tool · Current · Trusted execution Arm's free-to-download system simulator used to run the full CCA software stack before RME hardware is widely available. Students boot TF-A, TF-RMM, a host kernel and a Realm on the FVP following Arm's published learning path. KeystoneKeystone project (UC Berkeley origin) · Software · Current · Trusted execution Open-source framework for customisable RISC-V enclaves using PMP and a machine-mode security monitor. A university lab builds Keystone enclaves on a RISC-V board to study enclave design without vendor NDAs. RISC-V CoVE / AP-TEERISC-V International AP-TEE task group · Specification · Emerging · Trusted execution RISC-V confidential-VM architecture in which a TEE Security Manager isolates confidential VMs from the host hypervisor and attests them. Researchers have prototyped CoVE in emulation, running a confidential Linux guest whose memory the host KVM cannot read. RISC-V PMP and SmmttRISC-V International · Hardware · Silicon Physical Memory Protection restricts memory per privilege mode; Smmtt adds supervisor-domain memory tracking for confidential VMs. Keystone's security monitor reprograms PMP entries on every enclave switch so the OS cannot touch enclave memory.

docs.title: 5.7 Confidential VMs and Containers in the Cloud
docs.text:
All three big clouds rent out confidential computing. You can choose a confidential VM backed by AMD SEV-SNP or Intel TDX, run containers inside small per-pod confidential VMs, or, on AWS, carve an isolated enclave out of an instance with Nitro Enclaves. Each option comes with attestation so keys are released only to a verified environment.

Confidential computing on the big three clouds

Azure Google Cloud AWS CPU TEEs SEV-SNP and TDX CVMs SEV, SEV-SNP and TDX CVMs SEV-SNP on M6a/C6a/R6a Other isolation Confidential containers on ACI Confidential GKE Nodes Nitro System, Nitro Enclaves GPU option NCCadsH100v5 (H100) A3 confidential (H100 + TDX) Attestable AMIs incl. GPU instances Attestation Microsoft Azure Attestation Google Cloud Attestation Nitro attestation docs, NitroTPM Key release Secure Key Release Workload Identity Federation + KMS KMS attestation conditions

Names differ, but each cloud pairs hardware isolation with an attestation service and attestation-aware key release.

Think of it like…

It is like choosing a hotel room: a normal room (ordinary VM), a room with your own lock plus a signed inspection certificate (confidential VM), or a windowless safe room inside your room that only talks through a slot (Nitro Enclave).

Real-world example

Larkspur Analytics deploys its Kubernetes fraud-scoring service with Confidential Containers: each pod runs in its own small SEV-SNP or TDX VM via Kata Containers. When a pod starts, its guest agent sends hardware evidence to Trustee, Larkspur's self-hosted attestation and key-broker service. Only when policy checks pass does Trustee release the key that decrypts the container image and model, so the cluster's node administrators never see either.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Choose a confidential-capable machine family, such as Azure DCasv6 or DCesv6, Google Cloud N2D or C3 Confidential VM, or AWS M6a with SEV-SNP.
  2. Enable the confidential option at creation; the platform boots trusted virtual firmware and usually a vTPM inside the guest.
  3. Bind disk encryption to attestation, for example Azure confidential OS-disk encryption or your own key broker.
  4. At start-up the workload collects hardware evidence and obtains an attestation token from a verifier.
  5. Your key service — cloud KMS policy, Azure Secure Key Release or Trustee — releases secrets only to tokens that match policy.

Who uses it

Cloud architects, Kubernetes platform teams, DevSecOps engineers and compliance leads in banking, health care and government use these services.

Key takeaway

Know the three cloud models: confidential VMs (whole guest), confidential containers (one CVM per pod via Kata) and AWS Nitro Enclaves (an isolated slice of an EC2 instance with signed attestation documents).

Going deeper

  • Azure: DCasv5/ECasv5 (3rd Gen EPYC) and DCasv6/ECasv6 (4th Gen EPYC) use SEV-SNP; DCesv6/ECesv6 (5th Gen Xeon) use TDX; confidential OS-disk encryption binds disk keys to the VM's vTPM state.
  • Google Cloud offers Confidential VMs with SEV (N2D, C2D), SEV-SNP (N2D) and TDX (C3), Confidential GKE Nodes, and A3 confidential VMs combining TDX with H100 GPUs; Confidential Space builds an attested container host on top.
  • AWS's Nitro System moves virtualisation into dedicated Nitro cards and a minimal hypervisor without interactive operator access; Nitro Enclaves carve CPU and memory from a parent instance into a VM with no network or storage, only a vsock channel.
  • AWS EC2 instance attestation (generally available September 2025) uses NitroTPM and Attestable AMIs: you build an AMI with a reference measurement, and AWS KMS can refuse keys to instances whose measurements differ.
  • Confidential Containers (CoCo), a CNCF project, runs each pod in its own CVM through Kata Containers, pulls and decrypts images inside the guest, and uses Trustee for attestation; Red Hat ships it in OpenShift sandboxed containers.
  • IBM Secure Execution for Linux on IBM Z and LinuxONE, with the Hyper Protect services built on it, shows confidential computing is not only an x86 or Arm feature.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming a confidential VM size alone is enough: if your application never checks attestation before using secrets, a misconfigured ordinary VM would work just as well.
  • Forgetting the control plane: the Kubernetes API server, logging agents and sidecars outside the CVM can still leak data or inject configuration.
  • Confusing AWS Nitro System operator-access restrictions with hardware memory encryption against the host: they are different guarantees backed by different evidence.

docs.title: Try it: Inspect a Nitro Enclave image and list Azure confidential VM sizes
docs.text:

nitro-cli build-enclave --docker-uri myapp:latest --output-file myapp.eif   # prints PCR0/1/2
nitro-cli describe-enclaves
# Azure CLI: confidential VM sizes in a region
az vm list-skus --location westeurope --resource-type virtualMachines \
  --query "[?contains(name,'DCas') || contains(name,'DCes')].name" -o tsv
